articles.title: Heterogeneity of entrepreneurial intention among vocational college students: a new perspective on the intention-behavior gap through vocational capital
paragraphs: Heterogeneity of entrepreneurial intention among vocational college students: a new perspective on the intention-behavior gap through vocational capital
Lei Hao ●Chunna Hou
Received: 21 March 2026 / Accepted: 13 October 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Entrepreneurial intention is an important antecedent of entrepreneurial action, yet individuals may vary substantially in how they translate entrepreneurial goals into implementation tendencies. This study adopts a person-centered perspective to investigate the latent heterogeneity of entrepreneurial intentions among 934 vocational college students in China. Latent proﬁle analysis identiﬁed ﬁve distinct goal-implementation proﬁles, suggesting that entrepreneurial intentions may be characterized by qualitatively different conﬁgurations rather than a homogeneous construct. Multinomial logistic regression analyses further revealed that psychological and social capital were signiﬁcantly associated with proﬁle membership, with students reporting higher levels of these resources being more likely to belong to proﬁles characterized by stronger goal-implementation alignment. In contrast, prior entrepreneurial experience was associated with a lower likelihood of belonging to the low-goal/low-implementation, high-goal/low- implementation, or moderate proﬁles, whereas human capital and demographic characteristics showed limited associations with proﬁle membership. These ﬁndings provide a person-centered perspective on entrepreneurial intention research by moving beyond variable-centered approaches and highlighting the associations of individual psychological and social resources with differentiated entrepreneurial goal-implementation patterns among vocational college students.
Introduction

The rapid transformation of global industries has intensiﬁed employment challenges among young adults due to the growing misalignment between acquired skills and labor market demands (Figueiredo et al., 2017). In this context, entrepreneurship represents an alternative developmental pathway that enables youth to exercise agency and pursue self-directed career goals (Entrialgo & Iglesias, 2016). Entrepreneurial intention (EI), deﬁned as an individual's conscious commitment to establishing a new business venture, is widely recognized as a key precursor of future entrepreneurial action (Krueger et al., 2000). Despite its established role as an antecedent of entrepreneurial action, research has consistently documented a gap between students' EIs and subsequent behaviors (Gelderen et al., 2018). Many young people report strong intentions, yet only a small proportion develop EIs. In China, future entrepreneurial action among students remains relatively rare and often delayed, complicating direct assessment of sustained action. Rather than assuming a uniform

progression from intention to behavior, it is important to recognize that youth may differ in how closely entrepre- neurial goals align with implementation tendencies during emerging adulthood. Variable-centered approaches may obscure meaningful subgroups characterized by distinct goal-implementation conﬁgurations, thereby limiting understanding of the intention-behavior discrepancy. Moreover, although entrepreneurship education has become increasingly integrated into vocational education systems in China, existing entrepreneurship research has dis- proportionately focused on university students in academic institutions, leaving the entrepreneurial cognition and intention formation processes of vocational college students comparatively underexplored (Handayati, 2020). Therefore, examining vocational college students provides an important opportunity to understand how young individuals with distinct educational and employment backgrounds develop different patterns of alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. Compared with traditional university students, they often face greater employment pressure but may also demonstrate stronger risk sensitivity in early venture stages (Du & Shen, 2024; Wu & Tian, 2022; Chen et al., 2023). These factors suggest that, as part of the youth population, vocational college students may exhibit heterogeneous patterns in the alignment between their entrepreneurial goals and implementation efforts. Moreover, resource-related factors may be associated with these patterns. Building on the Rubicon Model of Action Phases (MAPs), EIs can be understood as reﬂecting individuals' pre-action psychological structures, char- acterized by the dynamic interplay between motivational orientations and volitional tendencies. Accordingly, indi- viduals with similar entrepreneurial aspirations may differ in how these psychological components are organized, potentially corresponding to distinct proﬁles of goal implementation. Career capital, including human, social, and psychological capital, may serve as an important antecedent to such heterogeneity by shaping individuals' motiva- tional and volitional orientations through the accumulation of knowledge, social connections, and psychological resources. However, little research has explored how career capital inﬂuences the development of distinct goal- implementation proﬁles among vocational students. The present study adopts a person-centered approach to identify latent proﬁles that reﬂect different combinations of entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies, and to examine the predictors of membership in these proﬁles. Figure 1 presents the conceptual framework of this study. Drawing on the theory of rational goal pursuit (Ajzen & Kruglanski, 2019), the framework integrates entrepreneurial attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control as key psychological mechanisms underlying EI proﬁles. It further illustrates the role of career capital dimensions (i.e., human, social, and psychological capital) and demographic factors in explaining variations across EI proﬁles.
Heterogeneity of EI among vocational college students

Although previous research on EI has extensively examined its antecedents and the alignment between entrepre- neurial goals and implementation tendencies (Wilson et al., 2010), relatively limited attention has been paid to the

intrinsic heterogeneity of EI itself. Identifying latent subgroups based on goal-implementation conﬁgurations helps address the limitations of traditional variable-centered approaches, which often assume homogeneity across indivi- duals and may obscure meaningful intra-individual discrepancies (Gelderen et al., 2018). Variable-centered methods are limited in explaining why some individuals with high EIs may exhibit different patterns of goal-implementation alignment, as they aggregate responses and overlook individual differences in the conﬁguration of entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. In contrast, person-centered approaches such as latent proﬁle analysis (LPA) allow the identiﬁcation of distinct EI patterns, offering a more nuanced understanding of entrepreneurial development among vocational college students (Jebsen et al., 2023). Recent studies integrating qualitative and person-centered approaches provide evidence of the multidimensional nature of EI. Geldhof et al. (2014) identiﬁed three intention proﬁles through semi-structured interviews: a lifestyle- oriented proﬁle emphasizing autonomy and work-life balance; a small high-proﬁt proﬁle focused on efﬁciency and lean operations; and a high-growth proﬁle characterized by ambitions to scale ventures into major industry positions. Similarly, Douglas et al. (2021) identiﬁed four subtypes of EI: proﬁt-oriented, social impact-oriented, psychological compensation-oriented, and innovation-oriented, highlighting the diversity of motivational conﬁgurations. These classiﬁcations highlight the inﬂuence of social and contextual factors on entrepreneurial motivation. However, qualitative typologies often depend on small sample sizes, which may limit generalizability and introduce potential classiﬁcation bias. To overcome these limitations, recent large-scale quantitative studies have employed person-centered techniques. Gao et al. (2022) identiﬁed three EI latent proﬁles among 918 Chinese university students: Low Goal/Low Imple- mentation (20.6%), Moderate Goal/Implementation (59.3%), and High Goal/High Implementation (20.1%). Bu et al. (2023), using a sample of 8467 students from 46 Chinese universities and vocational colleges, identiﬁed two dominant proﬁles: high-intention and low-intention, indicating a polarization in entrepreneurial aptitude. Addition- ally, Douglas et al. (2021) used fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis to demonstrate that speciﬁc EI conﬁg- urations were linked to demographic characteristics. For example, younger students were more likely to exhibit innovation-business hybrid proﬁles, while older men were predominantly proﬁt-driven. Collectively, these ﬁndings suggest that EIs are structurally diverse rather than uniformly distributed. Despite this progress, vocational college students have often been overlooked as a distinct population, leaving unclear how heterogeneous goal-implementation conﬁgurations may characterize their pre-action psychological structures (Geldhof et al., 2014). Compared with university students, vocational college students develop EIs within distinct educational and career contexts characterized by different learning pathways, resource conditions, and career transition demands (Bu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). These contextual characteristics may inﬂuence how entre- preneurial goals are combined with implementation intentions, thereby contributing to heterogeneous pre-action psychological structures. Therefore, examining latent EI proﬁles among vocational college students is essential for identifying distinct goal-implementation conﬁgurations and understanding how different psychological patterns may be associated with varying levels of readiness for entrepreneurial action (he et al., 2022).
The association between career capital and heterogeneous EIs among vocational college students

The theory of rational goal pursuit posits that goal pursuit occurs when individuals' evaluations of a goal's desirability and feasibility reach a critical threshold (Ajzen & Kruglanski, 2019). This framework suggests that goal pursuit depends not only on the strength of individuals' current goals but also on their perceived feasibility of achieving these goals. Accordingly, individuals may exhibit different pre-action psychological structures depending on how their entrepreneurial goals and perceptions of feasibility are structured. Those with strong entrepreneurial goals but limited perceived feasibility may exhibit weaker implementation tendencies, whereas those who perceive entrepreneurship as both desirable and attainable are more likely to exhibit stronger goal-implementation alignment. Individual factors, such as personality traits, achievement motivation, and psychological resources, inﬂuence goal desirability and feasibility, whereas external factors, including family background, education, and social networks, shape access to entrepreneurial resources (Bieleke et al., 2020; DiRenzo, 2010). Career capital integrates these

internal and external resources and may facilitate goal pursuit by enhancing individuals' feasibility perceptions and supporting their movement beyond the goal threshold. Career capital is a multidimensional construct that includes human capital, social capital, and psychological capital (PsyCap). Human capital refers to knowledge, skills, and competencies acquired through education, work experience, and training (Becker, 1985), enabling vocational college students to explore entrepreneurial opportunities and assess their feasibility. Social capital, based on trust, reciprocity, and network ties (Afandi et al., 2017), provides access to information and resources, facilitating opportunity identiﬁcation and mobilization. PsyCap is related to intrinsic motivation, adaptive coping, and resilience in pursuing entrepreneurial goals, which may be relevant to translating intentions into implementation tendencies (Luthans & Youssef-Morgan, 2017). Although these dimensions are theoretically interconnected and mutually supportive, they represent distinct resource pathways. Human capital primarily strengthens perceived competence, social capital enhances perceived accessibility of entrepreneurial resources, and psychological capital promotes conﬁdence and persistence in goal pursuit. Through these com- plementary pathways, career capital may be associated with differences in how individuals organize entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies, thereby corresponding to heterogeneous pre-action psychological structures. These dimensions represent complementary forms of career capital, and previous research has reported a positive association between career capital and EI (Luthans et al., 2007). Career capital may show differential associations with goal-implementation proﬁles across its human, social, and psychological dimensions among vocational college students. From the perspective of rational goal pursuit, career capital represents a resource foundation that may be related to individuals' feasibility perceptions and to the extent to which entrepreneurial goals are supported by available resources in relation to the goal threshold. Human capital enhances perceived competence, social capital provides access to entrepreneurial resources, and psychological capital strengthens conﬁdence and persistence in pursuing entrepreneurial goals. Therefore, differences in career capital may be associated with heterogeneity in goal-implementation proﬁles. Individuals with greater career capital report higher perceived control over uncertainty and a smaller gap between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies (Sokol-Hessner & Rutledge, 2018). Prior studies indicate that human, social, and psychological capital inﬂuence high-intention and low-intention proﬁles differently (Bu et al., 2023). Cross-national evidence shows that in contexts of low economic freedom, human capital is more associated with survival-oriented intentions, whereas PsyCap primarily supports stress management rather than directly altering survival needs (Korunka et al., 2003). PsyCap also contributes to balancing social risks and mission-related conﬂicts in hybrid intentions (Mahfud et al., 2020), and prosocial abilities may explain more variance in EI than knowledge alone (Bacq & Alt, 2018). Social capital can facilitate the translation of psychological resources into implementation beliefs (Hockerts, 2017). Moreover, PsyCap, including entrepreneurial self-efﬁcacy, is closely linked to growth- oriented goals and the likelihood of surpassing action thresholds (Ajzen & Kruglanski, 2019; Sansone et al., 2024). Previous studies conﬁrm that career capital promotes EI, but its differential impact across goal-implementation proﬁles remains underexplored. Most research focuses on university students, but vocational college students differ in career capital accumulation and institutional support (D'Amico et al., 2019). They may leverage career capital gained from entrepreneurship education to better align entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. In China's vocational education system, skills-based career capital is particularly predictive of EI, increasing goal- implementation alignment (Ning & Ge, 2017). According to the theory of rational goal pursuit, insufﬁcient career capital may be associated with greater difﬁculty in surpassing action thresholds, while negative emotions, such as fear of failure, may be associated with a weaker alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies (Martina, 2019). The present study identiﬁes latent goal-implementation proﬁles of EI among Chinese vocational college students and investigates how distinct dimensions of career capital contribute to membership in these proﬁles. Building on the rational goal pursuit framework, we conceptualize EI as a heterogeneous pre-action psychological structure shaped by the interaction between current entrepreneurial goals and perceived feasibility. Accordingly, individuals with similar entrepreneurial aspirations may differ in their implementation tendencies due to variations in their perceptions of resource-based feasibility. By integrating a person-centered perspective with career capital, the study aims to clarify differential pathways through which internal and external resources may be associated with students' entrepreneurial

goals and implementation tendencies. Findings are expected to deepen understanding of intention-behavior patterns and inform the development of developmentally appropriate, targeted entrepreneurship education in vocational contexts. In summary, this study examined 934 Chinese vocational college students and used LPA to identify naturally occurring goal-implementation proﬁles. It further explored the psychological patterns underlying discrepancies between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies and examined the associations between career capital and these proﬁles. Based on these ﬁndings, we propose the following hypotheses: H1. EIs among vocational college students exhibit latent heterogeneity, with distinct goal-implementation proﬁles reﬂecting different conﬁgurations of entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. H2. Psychological capital is signiﬁcantly associated with membership in goal-implementation proﬁles among vocational college students, such that students with higher levels of psychological capital are more likely to belong to proﬁles characterized by stronger alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies.
Method
Participants

Participants were recruited from ﬁve public vocational colleges in central and northeastern China, including two in Henan Province and three in Jilin Province. No exclusion criteria were applied based on students' entrepreneurial interest or prior entrepreneurial experience. Given that this study aimed to identify heterogeneous pre-action psy- chological structures underlying EI rather than to predict entrepreneurial participation, all students who completed the survey and provided valid responses were retained for analysis. This approach allowed the LPA to identify the range of goal-implementation conﬁgurations represented in the sample. A total of 934 valid responses were obtained, including 678 women (72.6%) and 256 men (27.4%). Participants were aged 18–21, representing different academic years and ﬁelds of study, and varied in prior exposure to entrepreneurial activities and family socio-economic background. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, detailing their rights and potential risks of participation. Participation was voluntary and anonymous.
Measures

EI was measured using the EI Scale developed by Li (2011) for Chinese undergraduate students. The scale comprises 12 items divided into two subscales: Entrepreneurial Goal Intentions (6 items), which assess individuals' commitment to entrepreneurship as a future career goal (e.g., “My career goal is to become an entrepreneur”), and Entrepreneurial Implementation Intentions (6 items), which assess individuals' readiness to translate entrepreneurial goals into action under speciﬁc situational conditions (e.g., “If I ﬁnd a suitable partner, I will start a business”). Participants responded to each item on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Higher scores reﬂect stronger EI. Cronbach's alpha for the scale was 0.91, indicating excellent internal consistency. In addition, a con- ﬁrmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to assess the construct validity of the EI scale. The results indicated an acceptable model ﬁt (CFI = 0.933, RMSEA = 0.078, SRMR = 0.055). Human capital was measured using the Human Capital Scale developed by Bu et al. (2023) for Chinese university students. The scale includes 12 items across two dimensions: Experiential Learning (6 items; e.g., “I can learn from my mistakes”) and Entrepreneurial Education (6 items; e.g., “My university provides high-quality and diverse learning experiences in innovation and entrepreneurship”). Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Higher scores reﬂect greater human capital. Cronbach's alpha was 0.89, indicating good internal consistency. In addition, a CFA was conducted to assess the construct validity of the HC scale. The results indicated an acceptable model ﬁt (CFI = 0.943, RMSEA = 0.060, SRMR = 0.047).

Social capital was assessed using the 40-item Internet Social Capital Scale (ISCS; Williams et al., 2006). The scale comprises two dimensions: Bonding Social Capital (20 items; e.g., “I have close friends I can trust completely”) and Bridging Social Capital (20 items; e.g., “Interacting with friends helps me stay informed about current events”). Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Higher scores reﬂect greater social capital. Cronbach's alpha was 0.91, indicating excellent reliability. In addition, a CFA was conducted to assess the construct validity of the SC scale. The results indicated an acceptable model ﬁt (CFI = 0.916, RMSEA = 0.041, SRMR = 0.053). Previous research has also provided empirical support for the applicability of the ISCS among Chinese college students (Dong et al., 2023). PsyCap was measured using the 24-item Psychological Capital Questionnaire (PCQ; Luthans et al., 2007). The scale comprises four dimensions: Self-Efﬁcacy (6 items; e.g., “I can always solve problems I encounter in my work”), Optimism (6 items; e.g., “I can analyze long-term problems and ﬁnd solutions”), Hope (6 items; e.g., “I can always see the positive side of things at work”), and Resilience (6 items; e.g., “I can recover from difﬁcult situations”). Items were rated on a 6-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree). Higher scores indicate greater PsyCap. Cronbach's alpha was 0.87, indicating good internal consistency. In addition, a CFA was conducted to assess the construct validity of the PsyCap scale. The results indicated an acceptable model ﬁt (CFI = 0.901, RMSEA = 0.048, SRMR = 0.053). Entrepreneurial attitude was assessed using the Entrepreneurial Attitude Scale (Liñán et al., 2009), developed within a cross-cultural context. The scale comprises ﬁve items reﬂecting a single dimension (e.g., “For me, becoming an entrepreneur has more advantages than disadvantages”). Participants responded on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Cronbach's alpha was 0.85, indicating good internal consistency. In addition, a CFA was conducted to assess the construct validity of the Entrepreneurial Attitude scale. The results indicated an acceptable model ﬁt (CFI = 0.973, RMSEA = 0.078, SRMR = 0.026). Subjective norms were measured using the Subjective Norms Scale (Liñán et al., 2009), developed within a cross- cultural context. The scale includes three items reﬂecting a single dimension (e.g., “To what extent does your family support your decision to develop entrepreneurial action readiness?”). Items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Cronbach's alpha was 0.80, indicating acceptable internal consistency. In addition, the construct validity of the Social Norm scale was assessed through standardized factor loadings, composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE), as the three-item one-factor CFA model was just-identiﬁed (df = 0); the results showed signiﬁcant factor loadings, with CR = 0.82 and AVE = 0.65, sup- porting the reliability and convergent validity of the scale. Perceived behavioral control was assessed using the Perceived Behavioral Control Scale (Liñán et al., 2009), developed within a cross-cultural context. The scale comprises six items reﬂecting a single dimension (e.g., “I feel ready to start a business”). Items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Higher scores indicate greater perceived behavioral control. Cronbach's alpha was 0.89, indicating good internal consistency. In addition, a conﬁrmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to assess the construct validity of the Perceived Behavioral Control Scale. The results indicated an acceptable model ﬁt (CFI = 0.977, RMSEA = 0.068, SRMR = 0.022).
Research procedure

After obtaining written informed consent, questionnaires were distributed and collected in person during class time. Trained research assistants provided instructions, answered questions, and monitored data collection to ensure protocol adherence. All research assistants were graduate students in psychology (master's or doctoral level) who had completed standardized training. Participants had ~40 minutes to complete the questionnaire. Upon completion, each received a small gift as a token of appreciation.

Assessment of common method bias

After data collection, Harman's single-factor test was conducted through exploratory factor analysis to assess com- mon method bias (CMB). The results revealed 19 factors with eigenvalues >1, with the ﬁrst factor accounting for 20.79% of the total variance, well below the 40% threshold commonly used to indicate bias. These ﬁndings suggest that CMB was unlikely to constitute a major concern in the present data, although Harman's single-factor test does not rule out the possibility of CMB.
Data analysis

Data analysis was conducted in multiple stages using SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 7.4. Key antecedent variables were then analyzed in SPSS 26.0 to examine differences across the EI latent proﬁles and to further characterize the identiﬁed proﬁles. EI and related scales were treated as continuous variables, and missing data were handled using Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML). Next, LPA was performed in Mplus 7.4 to identify distinct EI subgroups. Key antecedent variables were then analyzed in SPSS 26.0 to examine differences across the EI latent proﬁles and to further characterize the identiﬁed proﬁles. Finally, multinomial logistic regression in SPSS 26.0 was used to examine the associations of gender, entrepreneurial experience, only-child status, place of residence, and career capital with EI proﬁle membership.
Results
Preliminary analysis

Table 1 presents the means, standard deviations, and zero-order correlations for all study variables. Positive corre- lations were observed among entrepreneurial goal intention, entrepreneurial implementation intention, human capital, social capital, and PsyCap (r = 0.25–0.69, p <0.001), providing preliminary evidence of associations among the variables considered in the subsequent proﬁle analyses. The two subdimensions of EI, namely goal intention and implementation intention, showed a moderate correlation (r = 0.69). This high correlation is theoretically justiﬁed: Gelderen (2008) suggests that stronger entrepreneurial goals are closely related to stronger implementation tenden- cies, reﬂecting the theoretical connection between these two dimensions. Action phase theory further posits that goals correspond to the goal-setting stage, while implementation tendencies align with the action-planning stage in translating intentions into behavior (Gollwitzer, 1999). These theoretical distinctions provide a meaningful basis for differentiating latent EI subtypes. In the present study, adjusted R² values for the proﬁles exceeded 0.5, indicating that the scale effectively distinguishes between goal-implementation proﬁles.

Subgroups of EI among vocational college students

To further assess model ﬁt, a Bootstrap Likelihood Ratio Test (BLRT) was conducted. The results indicated sig- niﬁcant p values for all ﬁve models, with model ﬁt improving as the number of latent categories increased. As shown in Table 2, the ﬁve-proﬁle solution provided the most favorable ﬁt among the solutions considered, with the lowest AIC (39067.29), BIC (39435.09), and aBIC (39193.72) values, high classiﬁcation accuracy (entropy = 0.875), and signiﬁcant LMR (p = 0.013) and BLRT (p < 0.001) results. The smallest class accounted for 9.10% of the sample, exceeding the 5% threshold often used to ensure reliable estimation. Beyond statistical indices, the ﬁve-proﬁle solution demonstrated clear theoretical interpretability by capturing distinct conﬁgurations of entrepreneurial goal intention and implementation intention. Therefore, this solution was retained as it best represented the heterogeneous psychological structures underlying EI during the pre- action phase, providing insights into differentiated pathways from intention formation to potential entrepreneurial behavior. Figure 2 plots ﬁve latent proﬁles based on entrepreneurial goal intention (x axis) and implementation intention (y axis), where categories are organized from Category 1 at the bottom (Low Goal/Low Implementation) to Category 5 at the top (High Goal/High Implementation). In conclusion, the results identiﬁed ﬁve distinct goal-implementation proﬁles among vocational college students, indicating heterogeneity in EIs. These proﬁles represent different conﬁgurations of entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies, thereby supporting Hypothesis 1. The ﬁndings suggest that vocational college students do not constitute a homogeneous group in their EIs, but instead exhibit diverse patterns in the alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies.
Characteristics and variations of antecedent variables across subtypes of EI among vocational college students

A one-way ANOVA examined differences in entrepreneurial attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control across the ﬁve latent classes identiﬁed in the vocational college students. The purpose of this analysis was to further characterize the identiﬁed latent proﬁles by examining differences in key antecedent variables. Table 3 shows signiﬁcant between-class differences in entrepreneurial attitude [F (4, 929) = 100.89, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.30]; sub- jective norms [F (4, 929) = 66.38, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.22]; and perceived behavioral control [F (4, 929) = 74.97, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.24]. These ﬁndings further characterize the differences among the ﬁve proﬁles identiﬁed by LPA and provide additional evidence that the proﬁles differ meaningfully on these key antecedent variables.
Associations of demographic variables with EI proﬁle membership among vocational college students

Multinomial logistic regression was used to examine the associations between demographic factors and membership in the ﬁve goal-implementation proﬁles. Demographic variables (e.g., entrepreneurial experience, only-child status, residence, and gender) served as predictors, with proﬁles as the dependent variable. Results indicated that prior entrepreneurial experience was associated with lower odds of membership in the high-goal/low-implementation, moderate, and low-goal/low-implementation proﬁles, relative to the reference proﬁle. Only-child students had higher odds of membership in the high goal/high implementation proﬁle than in the high goal/low implementation proﬁle. Residence and gender were not signiﬁcantly associated with proﬁle membership. These ﬁndings suggest that some demographic characteristics are associated with differences in goal-implementation proﬁles, whereas others show limited associations with membership in these proﬁles.

The predictive impact of career capital on EI subtypes

As shown in Tables 4 and 5, multinomial logistic regression analyses were conducted to examine whether demo- graphic variables and career capital dimensions predicted membership in different EI (EI) proﬁles. Higher human capital was associated with lower relative odds of membership in the moderate- and low-goal/high-implementation proﬁles (OR = 0.62, 95% CI [0.40, 0.90]), with the direction of the association depending on the reference category speciﬁed in the multinomial model. Higher social capital was associated with higher odds of membership in the moderate (OR = 2.60, 95% CI [1.67, 4.05]), high goal/low implementation (OR = 3.04, 95% CI [1.92, 4.83]), and high goal/high implementation proﬁles (OR = 3.72, 95% CI [2.16, 6.41]), relative to the Low Goal/Low Imple- mentation proﬁle. PsyCap was signiﬁcantly associated with membership in multiple proﬁles, with a particularly strong association observed for the high goal/high implementation proﬁle (OR = 15.80, 95% CI [9.14, 27.32]). Higher PsyCap was associated with higher odds of membership in the high goal/high implementation, high goal/low implementation, and moderate proﬁles relative to the low goal/high implementation proﬁle. These ﬁndings suggest that higher PsyCap is associated with stronger goal-implementation alignment across the identiﬁed proﬁles.
Associations of PsyCap dimensions with EI proﬁle membership among vocational college students

Table 6 presents the results of the multinomial logistic regression examining the extent to which PsyCap predicted students' membership in the ﬁve EI proﬁles, with PsyCap showing signiﬁcant associations with proﬁle membership. Four separate logistic models examined how the dimensions of PsyCap (self-efﬁcacy, hope, resilience, and optimism) predicted membership in proﬁles. Results showed that self-efﬁcacy, resilience, and optimism were signiﬁcantly associated with proﬁle membership, whereas hope was not. Self-efﬁcacy: higher self-efﬁcacy was associated with higher odds of membership in the High goal/high imple- mentation (OR = 2.95, 95% CI [1.71, 5.07]), high goal/low implementation (OR = 2.37, 95% CI [1.53, 3.69]), and low goal/high Implementation proﬁles (OR = 3.26, 95% CI [1.86, 5.73]). Higher self-efﬁcacy was associated with lower odds of membership in the moderate proﬁle (OR = 0.38, 95% CI [0.23, 0.61]) relative to the speciﬁed reference proﬁle. Resilience: Higher resilience was associated with higher odds of membership in the low goal/high implementation proﬁle relative to the low goal/low implementation proﬁle (OR = 1.79, 95% CI [1.04, 3.01]). Optimism: Higher optimism was signiﬁcantly associated with lower odds of membership in the high goal/high implementation proﬁle relative to the moderate proﬁle (OR = 0.55, 95% CI [0.38, 0.80], p = 0.002). Similarly, higher optimism was signiﬁcantly associated with lower odds of membership in the High Goal/High Implementation proﬁle relative to the Low Goal/High Implementation proﬁle (OR = 0.60, 95% CI [0.38, 0.94], p = 0.026) and relative to the Low Goal/Low Implementation proﬁle (OR = 0.56, 95% CI [0.36, 0.86], p = 0.009). In addition, higher optimism was signiﬁcantly associated with lower odds of membership in the high goal/low implementation proﬁle relative to the moderate proﬁle (OR = 0.75, 95% CI [0.57, 0.99], p = 0.043). These ﬁndings provide support for Hypothesis 2, suggesting that PsyCap dimensions, particularly self-efﬁcacy, resilience, and optimism, are signiﬁcantly associated with goal-implementation proﬁle membership. Higher PsyCap was associated with greater odds of membership in several proﬁles characterized by stronger entrepreneurial goals and/or implementation tendencies. These ﬁndings indicate that PsyCap is signiﬁcantly associated with distinct goal- implementation proﬁles, particularly proﬁles characterized by stronger entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies.
Discussion

Based on the theory of rational goal pursuit, this study explores potential reasons why different EI proﬁles may not consistently correspond to entrepreneurial implementation tendencies among vocational college students. Using LPA,
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-09584-9 Article in Press

ﬁve distinct goal-implementation proﬁles were identiﬁed. Higher career capital, particularly self-efﬁcacy, resilience, and optimism, was associated with membership in proﬁles characterized by relatively greater alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. The ﬁve proﬁles were: low goal/low implementation (13.06%), low goal/high implementation (9.10%), moderate (31.69%), high goal/low implementation (29.98%), and high goal/ high implementation (16.17%).
Varied expressions of EI among vocational college students

This study identiﬁes signiﬁcant heterogeneity in EI proﬁles among vocational college students. Using a ﬁve-class model, we found the following categories: low goal/low implementation (13.06%), low goal/high implementation (9.10%), moderate (31.69%), high goal/low implementation (29.98%), and high goal/high implementation (16.17%). These results are consistent with theoretical expectations and reﬂect diverse patterns of goal-implementation align- ment. In particular, the Low Goal/High Implementation group (9.10%) represents a distinct misalignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. Rather than reﬂecting impulsive, action-oriented individuals, this proﬁle indicates individuals with relatively strong action-planning tendencies but insufﬁcient commitment to entrepreneurial goals. According to the MAP (Gollwitzer, 1990, 1999), these individuals may possess greater volitional readiness while remaining at an earlier stage of motivational commitment. This pattern suggests that EI may encompass distinguishable motivational and volitional components that can show different levels of develop- ment across individuals. Moreover, the high goal/low implementation proﬁle (29.98%), representing the second largest subgroup, provides important insight into the psychological basis of the EI-behavior gap. Individuals in this proﬁle exhibit strong entrepreneurial goals but relatively limited implementation tendencies, suggesting that strong entrepreneurial aspirations do not necessarily translate into sufﬁcient preparation for action. From the perspective of MAP, these individuals may have established clear entrepreneurial goals but may experience difﬁculties transitioning from the motivational phase to the volitional phase, in which concrete planning and action regulation are required. Thus, this proﬁle represents a pre-action psychological structure characterized by high motivational commitment but insufﬁcient implementation readiness, offering a potential explanation for why some individuals remain at the intention stage despite strong entrepreneurial aspirations. Together, these four main proﬁles accounted for 86.94% of the sample, indicating considerable variability in students' EIs, consistent with recent ﬁndings in Chinese higher education (He et al., 2022). The Moderate proﬁle, which comprises 31.69% of students, represents a balanced level of both entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. This ﬁnding is broadly comparable with earlier studies reporting that a sub- stantial proportion of students exhibit moderate levels of EI or related goal-implementation patterns (Gao et al., 2022). Rather than representing merely an intermediate level of EI, this proﬁle reﬂects a distinct pre-action psy- chological structure in which entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies have not yet reached a high level of alignment. From the perspective of the MAPs (Gollwitzer, 1990, 1999), individuals in this proﬁle may have developed initial entrepreneurial goals but have not yet transformed them into concrete implementation intentions. This ﬁnding extends previous research by suggesting that the Moderate proﬁle may represent a meaningful goal- implementation conﬁguration rather than simply an intermediate position on a unidimensional intention continuum. Therefore, identifying this proﬁle provides further insight into why some individuals maintain entrepreneurial goals yet experience difﬁculties achieving alignment between goals and implementation during the transition toward entrepreneurial action. The High Goal/High Implementation proﬁle (16.17%) shares conceptual similarities with the 'natural entrepreneurs' described by Li et al. (2011), particularly in terms of relatively high levels of entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. These ﬁndings contribute to understanding EI not only in terms of intensity but also in terms of the internal alignment between motivational and volitional processes. Rather than treating EI as a homogeneous construct, this study reveals heterogeneous pre-action psychological conﬁgurations that may be associated with different levels of entrepreneurial implementation readiness.
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-09584-9

While previous research has mainly examined EI as a continuous construct, the present study emphasizes the importance of identifying distinct goal-implementation conﬁgurations to explain why some students exhibit stronger entrepreneurial implementation tendencies, whereas others show greater discrepancies between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. Students with family business backgrounds may have greater exposure to entre- preneurial activities and opportunities, which could be associated with stronger tendencies to implement entrepre- neurial goals (Martina et al., 2011). Moreover, vocational training and personalized guidance may contribute to stronger alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies, particularly when such support is closely integrated with students' professional development needs. Our ﬁndings show that alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies is inﬂuenced by key factors from the theory of rational goal pursuit (Ajzen & Kruglanski, 2019). Students with stronger entrepre- neurial attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control were more likely to be classiﬁed into proﬁles characterized by higher goal and implementation intentions. These results provide empirical support for the ﬁve- proﬁle structure of EI and highlight the importance of career capital, including psychological, human, and social capital, which is associated with differences in goal-implementation alignment. Higher career capital was associated with stronger implementation tendencies among students classiﬁed into proﬁles with higher entrepreneurial goals. Future research should further examine how varying levels of career capital relate to different goal-implementation proﬁles and investigate the role of entrepreneurship education in shaping goal-implementation alignment.
Associations of demographic variables, career capital, and social capital with EI variants

Only-child status, prior entrepreneurial experience, and career capital were signiﬁcantly associated with membership in EI proﬁles, whereas gender and place of residence were not. This pattern differs from ﬁndings reported by Bu et al. (2023), who observed regional and gender differences. This discrepancy may reﬂect differences in the research context and theoretical focus. Unlike Bu et al. (2023), who examined the antecedents of EI in a broader university population, this study focused on vocational college students and identiﬁed heterogeneous pre-action psychological structures underlying EI. Thus, demographic factors may show weaker associations with goal-implementation alignment in vocational college samples, although this possibility requires examination across different populations and research contexts. The theory of rational goal pursuit suggests that subjective evaluations, such as risk tolerance and achievement motivation, may contribute to gender differences in goal pursuit. In addition, the regional entre- preneurial environment may shape EI indirectly by inﬂuencing perceptions of feasibility (Yukongdi et al., 2017). Students with prior entrepreneurial experience or only-child status were more likely to be classiﬁed into speciﬁc EI proﬁles. This is consistent with Sieger et al. (2011), who reported that prior entrepreneurial experience reduces fear of failure and enhances opportunity recognition. Only children may have access to different patterns of family resources and parental support, which may be associated with EI; however, the present study does not directly examine the mechanisms underlying this association. Interestingly, human capital did not signiﬁcantly differentiate EI proﬁles in the present study. This ﬁnding does not suggest that entrepreneurial education or experiential learning lacks importance; rather, it highlights a potential boundary condition in the translation of entrepreneurial resources into pre- action psychological structures. Drawing on the MAPs (Gollwitzer, 1990, 1999), human capital primarily provides individuals with knowledge and cognitive resources for understanding entrepreneurial opportunities and developing relevant competencies, whereas the formation of implementation tendencies requires additional motivational, voli- tional, and contextual resources. In vocational education contexts, entrepreneurship education may show weaker associations with EI proﬁle differentiation when learning experiences are insufﬁciently practice-oriented or poorly integrated with students' professional development needs, thereby restricting the transformation of entrepreneurial knowledge into concrete implementation plans (Martin et al., 2013; Nabi et al., 2017). Therefore, the non-signiﬁcant role of human capital in distinguishing EI proﬁles suggests that possessing entrepreneurial-related resources does not necessarily guarantee action readiness. Instead, it highlights the importance of examining how cognitive resources interact with psychological and social resources in shaping goal-implementation alignment.
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-09584-9 Article in Press

Our ﬁndings further provide evidence that social and psychological capital are associated with membership in EI proﬁles, thereby shaping goal-implementation alignment. Students with higher career capital were more likely to belong to the Moderate proﬁle rather than the Low Goal/High Implementation proﬁle, suggesting that knowledge and skills may help sustain balanced EIs under external pressures. The study also indicates that social capital is associated with membership in EI proﬁles. Family support may be associated with lower perceived entrepreneurial risk, while emotional support may be associated with greater will- ingness to explore entrepreneurial opportunities. Bridging social capital, involving access to external resources and credibility building, is associated with membership in higher-goal-oriented proﬁles (Bu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2011).
Associations of PsyCap with EI proﬁle membership

The theory of rational goal pursuit suggests that individuals with limited resources face signiﬁcant barriers in achieving their goals, with negative emotions such as fear of failure hindering entrepreneurship (Kautonen et al., 2015). In this study, PsyCap emerged as the strongest predictor of the alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation. Students with higher levels of career capital were more likely to belong to the High Goal/High Implementation, High Goal/Low Implementation, and Moderate proﬁles, supporting prior research that highlights PsyCap's role in managing risk-related stress and enhancing goal commitment (Bu et al., 2023). This study contributes by demonstrating that PsyCap dimensions show differential associations with EI proﬁle membership. Consistent with Gao et al. (2022), self-efﬁcacy was a signiﬁcant predictor of proﬁle differentiation. Among students with low-EI proﬁles, higher self-efﬁcacy was associated with stronger implementation tendencies despite resource constraints. In the Moderate proﬁle, self-efﬁcacy was associated with a relatively more favorable goal-implementation conﬁguration. For students in high-EI proﬁles, self-efﬁcacy was associated with membership in proﬁles characterized by relatively high entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies (Hao et al., 2021). In contrast to previous studies (Hao et al., 2024), resilience emerged as a predictor only for the low goal/high implementation and low goal/low implementation classes. One possible explanation is that, among vocational stu- dents with relatively limited entrepreneurial experience, resilience may become particularly relevant when students perceive entrepreneurial challenges or potential failure as consequential. For these students, resilience appeared to enhance their readiness to take on entrepreneurial challenges. Interestingly, hope did not emerge as a signiﬁcant predictor, which differs from some prior ﬁndings (Cheavens et al., 2018). This inconsistency may reﬂect contextual differences in vocational settings, where more immediate factors such as social norms and self-efﬁcacy may play a stronger role (Martinez-Gonzalez et al., 2019). Although hope was not signiﬁcant, it may remain relevant for sustaining long-term entrepreneurial motivation. Consistent with Giacomin et al. (2016), optimism was signiﬁcantly associated with EI proﬁle membership and was related to a greater likelihood of membership in proﬁles characterized by more favorable goal-implementation conﬁgurations.
Practical implications

The ﬁndings clarify the association between career capital and EI subtypes and offer implications for entrepre- neurship education among youth in vocational colleges. Career capital was associated with stronger goal- implementation alignment and may be relevant to reducing inconsistencies between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies. Given the heterogeneity of EI proﬁles identiﬁed in this study, entrepreneurship edu- cation may beneﬁt from moving beyond uniform approaches toward more proﬁle-sensitive interventions. Students with low goal orientation may beneﬁt from activities that develop entrepreneurial awareness and foster psycholo- gical capital, whereas those with high goals but low implementation tendencies may require greater emphasis on implementation planning and action regulation. Students with high goal-implementation alignment may beneﬁt more from advanced entrepreneurial practice, mentorship, and resource integration. Importantly, the Moderate proﬁle, which was the largest subgroup identiﬁed in this study, was characterized by moderate levels of entre- preneurial goals and implementation tendencies. This proﬁle may represent an important group for educational
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-09584-9

support, particularly in facilitating the transition from general entrepreneurial consideration to more concrete entrepreneurial preparation. Rather than focusing solely on increasing EI intensity, entrepreneurship education could emphasize students' progression from general consideration of entrepreneurship toward more concrete preparation by supporting goal clarity, implementation planning, and career capital accumulation. Developing stratiﬁed training models and school-based career capital curricula may provide opportunities for students to develop and mobilize intangible resources, while also addressing concerns related to fear of failure and risk aversion (he et al., 2022). The PsyCap components of career capital show differentiated associations with EI subtypes. Self-efﬁcacy was associated with stronger persistence in the face of intermediate barriers, consistent with the broader expectations of social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1989). Optimistic explanatory styles may support motivation, persistence, and positive expectations for future outcomes, as suggested by the relevant theoretical literature (Seligman, 1991). Resilience was associated with lower perceived disruption costs and more sustained implementation tendencies, consistent with prior research (Giones et al., 2020). Institutional and cultural contexts in China may also be relevant to students' risk perceptions, PsyCap, and goal-implementation patterns and therefore warrant further investigation. Accordingly, future entrepreneurship education should integrate career capital development with targeted psychological support, emphasizing the transition from entrepreneurial aspiration to actionable pre- paration rather than simply increasing EI. Incorporating contextual factors and adopting differentiated inter- ventions for distinct EI subtypes may enhance practical effectiveness.
Limitations and future directions

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although this study used validated self-report measures, the reliance on self-reported data may still introduce common method variance and social desirability bias, which could affect the observed associations among the study variables. Future research could incorporate multi- source assessments, behavioral indicators, or implicit measures to further strengthen measurement validity. Second, the ﬁndings are based on vocational college students from selected regions of China, which may limit the generalizability of the identiﬁed proﬁles and their correlates to students from other regions, educational institutions, or national contexts. Future studies should examine whether the identiﬁed goal-implementation proﬁles are replicated across diverse demographic groups, regions, and institutional contexts. Third, the cross- sectional design limits conclusions regarding the temporal stability and developmental ordering of the identiﬁed proﬁles and does not permit conclusions about whether these intention proﬁles translate into subsequent entrepreneurial preparation, engagement, or actual entrepreneurial behavior. Longitudinal research, including repeated assessments or latent transition analyses where appropriate, is needed to examine the temporal stability and possible transitions among these proﬁles and to determine whether membership in a proﬁle is associated with subsequent entrepreneurial preparation, engagement, and actual entrepreneurial behavior. Finally, although psychological capital was signiﬁcantly associated with EI proﬁle membership in the multinomial logistic regression analysis, the mechanisms underlying these associations remain unclear. Future studies could adopt longitudinal or intervention designs to further explore how psychological resources shape the development of entrepreneurial goal-implementation patterns.
Conclusion

This study employed a person-centered approach using LPA to examine heterogeneity in EIs among vocational college students. The ﬁndings identiﬁed ﬁve distinct goal-implementation proﬁles, indicating that EIs may be characterized by heterogeneous conﬁgurations rather than a single homogeneous pattern. Further multinomial logistic regression analyses showed that psychological capital was signiﬁcantly associated with proﬁle mem- bership. Students with higher levels of psychological capital had higher relative probabilities of belonging to proﬁles characterized by stronger alignment between entrepreneurial goals and implementation tendencies.
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-09584-9 Article in Press
These ﬁndings contribute to EI research by highlighting the importance of recognizing individual heterogeneity and considering psychological resources when examining differentiated patterns of EI.

articles.title: Development of an evaluation system of neighborhood culture based on multi-source data
paragraphs: Development of an evaluation system of neighborhood culture based on multi-source data
Lixia Guo · Yu Gao · Yanxin Qiao · Ling Zeng
Received: 30 April 2026 / Accepted: 8 October 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract In the process of rapid urban development, neighborhoods, as spatial units for residents’daily lives, work, and leisure, are an important part of urban renewal. However, the lack of awareness of local regional his­ tory and neighborhood culture among developers has resulted in homogenous appearance and lack of cultural presence in many neighborhoods. The present study aimed to protect and optimize neighborhood culture and used public perception as the research perspective to evaluate the cultural perception of the neighborhood, to clarify the perceived strength of each cultural element and provide a scientific basis for cultural conservation. Considering the Da Zhao Historical District of Hohhot as an example, a cultural perception evaluation system was developed by integrating subjective perception analysis and objective spatial data measurement. Drawing on existing literature to identify evaluation factors and criteria, the system was grounded in multi-source data by obtaining field research, geospatial, and online text data to analyze the public’s cultural perceptions of the built environment and subjective perceptions of the neighborhood’s architectural style, street space, and envi­ ronmental atmosphere. The present study provides a scientific and effective method for evaluating the cultural perceptions of neighborhoods with a view toward promoting the construction of a better life.
Keywords Cultural perception · Neighborhoods culture · Historic districts · Multi-source data · Evaluation system
Introduction

With rapid urbanization, the distinctive features of cities are gradually fading, rendering homogeneity a prevalent issue across numerous urban areas. As spatial carriers of urban cultural characteristics and important places for the public’s daily life, leisure and entertainment, historic and cultural districts play a pivotal role in preserving urban cultural heritage, shaping urban spatial features and fostering urban spiritual identity. Unfortunately, many historic and cultural districts have recently been plagued by problems such as declining vitality and insufficient cultural expression. While scholars have conducted extensive research on the protection of historic and cultural districts and urbanization development, yielding fruitful results1, the homogenization of urban construction and the loss of cultural connotation in historic districts have made research on neighborhood cultural preservation and

Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75696-6 Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75696-6

cultural perception an urgent academic and practical task. As a core component of neighborhood cultural pres­ ervation research, in-depth exploration of cultural perception is critical to reversing the urban homogenization dilemma and revitalizing historic and cultural districts. Existing research on historic and cultural district protection and neighborhood cultural preservation can be systematically categorized into two dimensions: physical and psychological, replacing the traditional approach of listing individual scholars’ work. In the physical dimension, research has experienced a long evolutionary process, shifting from the protection of a single physical entity to the holistic protection of the spatial environ­ ment, with the core focus on the evaluation and protection of urban physical space and tangible cultural carriers. Wilson approached the protection of cultural relics and monuments and renovated architectural features within a district2, and Xi delved into sensory aspects such as vision and hearing, employing laboratory simulations and other methodologies to analyze users’ sensory experiences of neighborhood spaces3, laying a solid foundation for the physical protection of historic districts yet lacking effective connection with human psychological needs. In the psychological dimension, the concept of preservation has evolved continuously, shifting the focus from physical space to human subjectivity, with the core being the exploration of people’s emotional connection, perception and cognition of historic and cultural districts. Jacobs emphasized the importance of considering the psychological aspects of people as primary users in communities4. Building on this foundation, scholars such as Steele explored individuals’ emotional attachment to places, arguing that the interaction between people and their surroundings generates a sense of place identity, dependence, and belonging5,6. Scholars such as Getz approached the topic from both tourists’ and residents’ perspectives, investigating their perceptions and cognitions of tourist destinations and recognizing the significance of understanding their viewpoints7–9. These studies have enriched the psychological perspective of cultural preservation research but are often decoupled from physical dimension research, failing to form a holistic research framework. In the field of cultural perception, which is an important branch of neighborhood cultural preservation, domestic and international psychological research on cultural per­ ception originated in the 1960s10, and has evolved through three stages: the proposal of perception theories11, preliminary research on cultural perception12,13 and rapid development of cultural perception14–17. Reception provides a conceptual bridge between the physical and psychological dimensions of historic district research by explaining how tangible environmental features are transformed into intangible cognition. In this study, cultural perception refers to the process through which individuals recognize, interpret, and emotionally respond to cultural meanings embedded in physical environments. Unlike general environmental satisfaction, cultural perception emphasizes the interaction between spatial characteristics, cultural symbols, social activities, and human experiences in shaping people’s understanding of a place. This concept is closely associated with the theories of sense of place, place identity, and place attachment. Sense of place emphasizes that physical settings acquire meanings through continuous interactions between people and environments5,18. Place identity theory suggests that environmental characteristics and cultural symbols contribute to individuals’ cognitive recognition of places6. Place attachment further explains the emotional bonds and feelings of belonging developed through long-term interactions with meaningful environments19. Therefore, cultural perception in historic districts can be understood as an integrated outcome involving spatial recognition, cultural interpretation, and emotional connec­ tion. However, existing cultural perception studies have rarely incorporated these theoretical perspectives into evaluation frameworks, particularly in multi-ethnic historic districts where religious symbols, ethnic traditions, and urban spatial characteristics jointly shape cultural cognition. Research methods for cultural perception and historic district protection can be clearly divided into traditional and emerging approaches, with distinct advantages and limitations. Traditional research methods are mainly based on on-site investigation and manual data collection, including questionnaire surveys, interview records and basic urban image analysis. Hong et al. constructed a customer perception satisfaction evaluation system, collected questionnaire data, and utilized Likert scale analysis and exploratory factor analysis to quantitatively study customer satisfaction20. The strengths of traditional methods lie in their ability to directly obtain first- hand subjective information from research subjects, ensure the authenticity of individual perception data, and
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75696-6 Article in Press

demonstrate strong operability in small-scale research. However, their limitations are prominent: the research scope is narrow, they consume substantial time and labor costs, and subjective biases are difficult to avoid in data collection and analysis, making it hard to reflect the overall perception characteristics of large groups. Emerging research methods have developed rapidly with the popularization of the Internet and advances in information technology, mainly including multi-source textual content analysis, laboratory simulation and big data analysis. Gao et al. used textual materials such as online travelogues and reviews and conducted content analysis of the intentions of domestic and international tourists toward historical neighborhoods21. These methods can expand the research scope, realize large-scale data collection and analysis, reduce manual intervention and improve the objectivity and efficiency of research. Nevertheless, they also have drawbacks: they require professional techni­ cal support for multi-source data processing and analysis, the authenticity of data needs to be verified, and it is difficult to deeply explore the internal psychological motivations of individual perception. Traditional and emerg­ ing methods are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. However, simply combining questionnaires, GIS, street-view imagery, POI data, and online reviews does not in itself constitute a theoretical contribution. The more important challenge is to clarify how these data sources jointly represent the relationship between tangible spatial characteristics and intangible cultural cognition. A systematic review of existing literature reveals three key theoretical and methodological gaps in historic dis­ trict cultural perception research. First, the relationship between physical environments and cultural perception remains insufficiently explored. Existing studies mainly focus either on physical spatial characteristics, such as architectural features, spatial morphology, and environmental quality, or on residents’ and visitors’ subjective per­ ceptions22. However, how tangible spatial environments are transformed into cultural meanings and public per­ ception has not been fully explained, limiting a comprehensive understanding of cultural perception formation in historic districts. Second, current evaluation approaches remain insufficiently connected with theoretical frame­ works. Although traditional methods, such as questionnaires and interviews, and emerging approaches based on GIS, street-view imagery, POI data, and online reviews have expanded the measurement of urban perception23,24. Third, existing cultural perception evaluation systems have mainly focused on conventional historical towns, commercial heritage districts, or relatively homogeneous cultural landscapes25. However, northern ethnic historic districts, where religious culture, ethnic traditions, and contemporary commercial activities coexist, may demon­ strate distinctive cultural perception characteristics that remain insufficiently studied26. Based on these research gaps, this study aims to address three key questions: how cultural perception in multi- ethnic historic districts can be theoretically understood from the perspectives of physical environment, sense of place, place identity, and place attachment; how multi-source spatial data and public perception data can be inte­ grated to construct a comprehensive and localized cultural perception evaluation framework for northern ethnic historic districts; and how spatial characteristics and cultural elements shape differentiated public cultural percep­ tions and generate implications for historic district conservation and renewal. Accordingly, this study makes three contributions. First, it provides a theoretical interpretation of cultural perception in historic districts by integrating sense of place, place identity, and place attachment theories, conceptualizing cultural perception as an interactive process through which physical environments, cultural symbols, and human experiences jointly construct cultural meanings. Second, it develops a localized cultural perception evaluation framework for northern multi-ethnic historic districts by integrating physical spatial characteristics and subjective public cognition. By combining multi-source spatial data with perception-based evaluation, the proposed framework extends traditional historic district assessment approaches that mainly focus on physical conservation and provides a systematic method for understanding public cultural cognition. Third, this study explores the formation mechanisms of differentiated cultural perceptions by examining how spatial characteristics and cultural elements influence public cognition. The findings demonstrate how architectural features, street environments, and religious-cultural symbols contrib­ ute to cultural recognition and emotional experiences, thereby providing evidence-based strategies for historic district conservation and sustainable renewal.

Area overview and research methodology
Overview of the study area

The Da Zhao historic and cultural district is located in an old city on both sides of Danan Street in Yuquan Dis­ trict of Hohhot City, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. It is a historical and cultural area with streets having Ming and Qing dynasty architectural styles, such as Sesame Street, Moon Tower, Alatan Khan Square, and Jiujiu Street, and the Da Zhao Temple at its core, covering an area of 35.28 hectares. The Da Zhao historic and cultural district(Fig. 1) inherits the historical context of Hohhot City and is home to cultural relics, such as the Da Zhao Temple, Caishen Temple, Hongqing Temple, Tumote Confucian Temple, and Guanyin Temple. Historic districts showcase diverse cultural elements including history, religion, ethnicity, customs, and commerce and represent the unique regional and ethnic features of an old city.

Data sources and processing

Traditional, geographic, and big data were used in this study. Traditional small data were obtained through field surveys, geographic data were downloaded from official websites, and big data were acquired through web crawling. 1) Road network data. We obtained Open Street Map (OSM) road network data from the official website(OpenStreetMap Ireland – The home of the OpenStreetMap community on the island of Ireland) and converted and classified them. Topo­ logical processing was performed on the road network, and the unconnected road network was processed by extending the roads. To ensure the accuracy of the quantitative values and comparative analysis of the vitality of the surrounding plots, the research scope was expanded by approximately 700 m to establish a road network axis model, the 700-meter extension is more consistent with the actual spatial characteristics of the Da Zhao Historic District and results in a relatively low sampling density. 2) Street-view imagery data. Road network data were obtained from the OSM website, using GIS-based spatial analysis tools, sampling points were generated along the road network at 50 m intervals, resulting in 451 street view locations. The coor­ dinates were converted into the format supported by the Baidu Street View API to obtain corresponding images. To ensure data consistency and comparability, all images were collected using standardized parameters, including a resolution of 1024 × 512 pixels, an acquisition height of approximately 2.5 m, a pitch angle of 0°, and a field of view (FOV) of 90°. The heading angle was adjusted according to road direction to maintain consistent observa­ tion of street corridors. After acquisition, images with severe occlusion, blurring, abnormal exposure, or insufficient spatial infor­ mation were removed. The valid images were then processed using the DeepLabv3 + deep learning semantic segmentation model for pixel-level recognition. Based on the characteristics of historic districts, image elements were classified into semantic categories including building, road, sky, vegetation, and other street elements28. The pixel proportion of each category was calculated to derive spatial environmental indicators, which were used to quantify street-level spatial features. 3) POI data POI data were collected through the Baidu Map Open Platform Web Service API using the place.search inter­ face. The parameters output=json and scope = 2 were configured to obtain comprehensive structured informa­ tion, including place names, geographic coordinates, addresses, business hours, and other attributes. During data retrieval, both location-related keywords (e.g., “Da Zhao,” “Da Zhao Temple,” “Saishang Old Street,” and “Da Zhao Historic Cultural Tourism Area”) and functional keywords (e.g., restaurants, hotels, shops, scenic spots, and banks) were used to ensure comprehensive coverage of different types of facilities within the study area. The collected raw POI dataset was systematically preprocessed through data cleaning procedures, including missing value handling, format standardization, anomaly detection, and duplicate record removal. Subsequently, the valid POI points were classified according to their functional attributes. After data cleaning and classification, a total of 714 valid POI records were retained within the study area, including 157 catering service facilities, 511 shopping facilities, 16 cultural and educational facilities, 8 leisure service facilities, 11 accommodation facilities, and 11 residential service facilities. 4) Questionnaire interview data. The questionnaire used a closed-ended format to investigate public perceptions of the cultural significance of the Da Zhao district in terms of interest, uniqueness, recognition, vitality, and other cultural aspects. A total of 200 online and offline questionnaires were distributed, and 187 valid responses were obtained after quality screen­ ing. Questionnaires with complete information that can support subsequent analysis and data processing, as well as valid responses, were retained. Questionnaires with perfunctory responses were excluded, including those in which the same score was selected for all items or answers were chosen randomly and irregularly. This ensured

Online review data were collected from publicly available review platforms, covering user ratings and textual comments related to architecture, catering services, leisure and entertainment, cultural exhibition spaces, and other relevant categories within the study area. During data collection, several parameters were established, including the review period (2010–2025), minimum review length threshold (≥ 5 Chinese characters), and rating information requirements (including overall ratings and sub-item ratings). Constructing the evaluation system
Determination of factors

The evaluation framework was developed based on the theoretical relationship between physical environments and public cultural perception. According to the theory of sense of place, cultural perception in historic districts is not only determined by the existence of physical cultural resources but also by the ways in which individuals recognize, interpret, and emotionally connect with these resources. The physical environment provides tangible cultural carriers, such as architectural forms, spatial structures, and landscape elements, while public perception reflects the cognitive and emotional responses generated through interactions with these environmental features. Therefore, cultural perception can be regarded as a comprehensive process integrating physical characteristics, experiential evaluation, and cultural cognition. Based on this theoretical perspective, the evaluation framework was constructed from two complementary dimensions: the physical characteristics of the material environment and the subjective cognitive experiences of the public. The physical dimension represents the tangible carriers of cultural information and includes the architectural characteristics and spatial organization of historic districts. The subjective dimension reflects the public’s understanding, emotional experience, and overall cognition of cultural meanings embedded in the place. This classification is consistent with place-related theories, in which physical environments provide the basis for place identity formation, while continuous interaction and experience contribute to place attachment and emo­ tional connection. Accordingly, four evaluation dimensions were established: architectural style, street space, environmental atmosphere, and perceived impression. Among these dimensions, architectural style and street space represent the physical foundation of cultural perception, environmental atmosphere reflects users’ experi­ ential and emotional responses, and perceived impression represents the integrated cognitive representation of the historic district. Specifically, the four dimensions correspond to different stages in the formation of cultural perception. Archi­ tectural style represents the symbolic and visual foundation of cultural recognition, which is consistent with place identity theory emphasizing the role of distinctive environmental features in shaping place recognition. Street space reflects the spatial interaction process between individuals and historic environments, corresponding to the sense of place perspective that meanings are generated through continuous human–environment interactions. Environmental atmosphere represents the emotional and experiential dimension of cultural perception, which is closely related to place attachment theory emphasizing emotional bonds and belonging. Perceived impression reflects the final cognitive outcome after visiting and experiencing historic districts, corresponding to destination image theory, which explains how individuals form overall evaluations and memories of places. The selection of evaluation indicators followed a three-step procedure. First, previous studies related to historic district conservation, cultural perception assessment, tourist experience evaluation, and place-related theories were reviewed to identify potential indicators describing both physical environments and psychological percep­ tions. Second, field investigations were conducted in the Da Zhao Historic and Cultural District to supplement locally specific cultural characteristics, including religious landscapes, ethnic cultural symbols, traditional com­ mercial activities, and spatial experience features. Third, a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire was distributed to the public to identify the spatial and cultural elements that positively influence cultural perception. Respondents were asked to rate whether each candidate indicator enhanced their understanding, recognition, and emotional experience of the historic district, with scores ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Based on the evaluation results, indicators with stronger perceived contributions were selected and further examined through factor analysis.Indicators with a mean score below 3.5 were removed, whereas conceptually overlapping indicators were merged or revised. The retained indicators were subsequently examined through questionnaire- based statistical validation and exploratory factor analysis.
