The indicators were assessed in terms of theoretical relevance, conceptual distinctiveness, local applicability, and measurability. Indicators with substantial conceptual overlap were merged or refined where necessary.Based on literature review, field investigation, theoretical relevance, local applicability, and measurability, 14 indicators were selected for questionnaire evaluation and exploratory factor analysis. To verify the rationality of the indicator system, exploratory factor analysis was conducted using questionnaire data. The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) test and Bartlett’s test of sphericity were first applied to examine whether the data were suitable for factor extraction. The KMO value was 0.888, and the significance level of Bartlett’s test was 0.000, indicating that significant correlations existed among the variables and that the questionnaire data were appropriate for factor analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA) was subsequently performed to identify the underlying dimensions of public cultural perception. Highly correlated indicators were transformed into independent common factors, and four components with eigenvalues greater than one were extracted. These four components explained 58.673% of the total variance, demonstrating their explanatory ability for the cultural perception evaluation system. Factor loadings were then used to examine the relationship between individual indicators and extracted factors. Based on both statistical results and theoretical meanings, four common factors consisting of 14 evaluation indicators were identified (Table 4).Unlike other dimensions containing multiple observable indicators, perceived impres­ sion was used as an overall evaluation indicator reflecting the final cognitive synthesis of architectural, spatial, and experiential perceptions. The four evaluation items in factor group A describe the basic attributes of building form, property, color, and quality in the district. Therefore, the group was named “Architectural Style.” Factor group B with four evaluation items describes the spatial layout, block texture, street scale, and support facilities, and was named “Street Space.” The five evaluation items in factor group C describe public perceptions of interest, uniqueness, recognizability, and other factors. Therefore, the group was named “Environmental Atmosphere.” One evaluation item in factor group D describes public perception of the image of the district, and the group named “Perception Impression.”

Cultural perception analysis of the da zhao historic district
Analysis of perceptual factors
Evaluation of architectural style perception

Architectural style perception was evaluated based on image recognition from four perspectives: architectural quality, form, attributes, and colors (Fig. 3). Overall, the architectural quality perception was relatively good, with a primarily first-class rating. The build­ ings were perceived to have rich details such as façade reliefs, hollowed-out windows, and gilded paintings, which may have provided visitors and residents with a good perception of the block’s culture. The buildings depict diverse styles, including Buddhist, Qing Dynasty, and Han-style architecture, narrow courtyards typical of Shanxi, and unique Mongolian yurts. The combination of different building types creates a diverse and unique architecture that provides good visual and perceptual experiences. The district has various building types, such as religious, residential, and commercial. The building attributes are diverse, among which Da Zhao Temple has a prominent religious nature, weakening public perception of the district’s other functions. Religious culture is part of the cultural perception of the public; therefore, the percep­ tion evaluation of architectural attributes was good. The district is mainly characterized by three colors: gray, yellow, and red. The gray floor, yellow sloping roof, and red walls constitute the color tone of the district, which is different from modern urban spaces composed of asphalt roads, glass curtain walls, and flat roofs. Therefore, the public had a good perception of the architectural color. The high architectural style perception indicates that visible cultural symbols play an important role in shaping place identity. The coexistence of Tibetan Buddhist temples, Mongolian traditional forms and Qing-style build­ ings provides distinctive visual differences from contemporary urban environments. These symbolic architectural elements function as cultural anchors, enabling visitors to quickly recognize the historical and cultural identity of the district.

As shown in Fig. 4, the integration and depth value analysis maps presented a yellow-green color tone, indicating low accessibility and relatively loose con­ nections within the block. Closeness of spatial connections is an important factor that affects public perception of street-space patterns, explaining the weak perception of the spatial pattern. Street and alley textures were analyzed based on the OSM road network’s selection degree and connectivity. The selection degree map reflects spatial attractiveness and connectivity map reflects the street space permeabil­ ity. As shown in Fig. 4, the selection degree and connectivity maps exhibited a cool color tone, indicating weak spatial attractiveness and permeability. Relatively few cultural and educational industries are present, and promotion of the district’s culture is relatively weak. By analyzing the proportion and layout of the district’s industries, public perception of support facilities was found to be weak.

The importance and satisfaction levels of the 15 indicators were analyzed, and an importance-performance analy­ sis (IPA) diagram was produced (Fig. 7). The first quadrant included elements such as “humanistic sentiment,” “folk activities,” “street architecture,” “cultural elements,” “cultural fusion,” “exhibition venues,” and “cultural

Evaluation of impression

The word (Table 7) frequency analysis revealed that the positive evaluations featured high frequencies of “reli­ gion,” “antique,” “Da Zhao Temple,” “architecture,” and “characteristic,” reflecting the street block’s unique features, such as its religious, antique, and Mongolian characteristics. The negative evaluations contained words such as “business,” “scenic area,” “memory,” “almost,” and “don’t understand,” indicating issues such as the commercialization, limited business types, and unclear public perception of the block’s cultural significance. Based on the analysis of public perception of a street block’s image, the religious and ethnic culture of the block could easily perceived, but their understanding was limited. The display of the block’s cultural background lacks depth, and public perception was blurry. Religious culture became the dominant cultural symbol because religious landmarks possess strong symbolic meaning and emotional resonance. Da Zhao Temple functions not only as a physical landmark but also as a cultural memory carrier, strengthening public recognition of the district. However, frequent appearance of words such as “hard to understand” indicates that symbolic recognition has not fully transformed into cultural understanding. Hohhot was established during the late Ming and early Qing dynasties, a period when Tibetan Buddhist culture became highly influential in the northern grassland region. Temple complexes and their surrounding commercial areas developed into important urban centers during this period. The architectural forms, color characteristics, and spatial patterns of these historic environments reflect the integration of grassland culture, religious traditions, and Central Plains culture, demonstrating the distinctive cultural landscape characteristics of historic districts in multi-ethnic regions.
Public perception evaluation score

As shown in Table 8, the overall perception score for cultural image was moderate at 3.28. These results suggest that public perception of the physical space was higher than that of environmental atmosphere. Among the physi­ cal space attributes, architectural style received the highest perception score of 3.91, indicating that the public could visually appreciate the architecture. However, the perception of street space was unsatisfactory, with a score of 3.01. Specifically, the perception of support facilities was the weakest, reflecting the low proportion of cultural venues and symbol, which weakened the role of cultural promotion. Regarding subjective perception, environmental atmosphere scored 3.15, with the highest score for cultural perception and lowest for interest per­ ception. This reflected a weak perception of the existing commercial and leisure atmosphere in the block and a weak play ability, suggesting adjustment needs for the industrial type.

Research conclusions
Strong presence of religious culture, but occasional public perception

As a well-known Tibetan Buddhist architecture in China, Da Zhao Temple attracts many followers and tourists for worship and sightseeing. Therefore, the mosque maintains long-term operations, and the income from fol­ lowers and tourists can support the mosque in regularly holding religious and folk activities. Organization of these events and iconic architectural features, such as yellow roofs, red walls, and pagodas, can give the public a good perception of religious culture. However, organization of events is time-limited, and cultural vitality due to religious and folk activities can only be felt at specific times; hence, deep perception of the religious culture is occasional. This result highlights that the Da Zhao Historic District has formed a unique multi-ethnic architectural fusion feature that is different from the single-style architectural districts in other regions, but the lack of detailed cul­ tural expression inside the buildings leads to the public’s only superficial perception of architectural culture, which is a prominent shortcoming distinguishing it from the high-scoring historic districts in previous studies.
Building culture is compatible but lacks detailed expression

The block features diverse building styles, including Buddhist architecture, Mongolian yurts, Qing Dynasty build­ ings, Han-style buildings, and modern architecture. Different architectural styles blend well, allowing the public to appreciate various architectural forms. While a block has many architectural styles, each building style differs only in terms of form, color, size, and other aspects. The decoration, industry type, and spatial layout inside the buildings are highly similar, lacking internal spatial construction and detailed expressions. Therefore, the public had a good perception of the architectural style, but a surface-level understanding of culture.
Despite cultural exchange in business and trade, homogeneity exists in the development of food culture

The public generally had a negative perception of the industries. The block’s main industries include antiques, calligraphy, painting, ethnic handicrafts, tea, and dining. While these industries reflect the historical and cul­ tural significance of the Great Mosque historical and cultural block, they appeal mainly to middle-aged and older people. Younger generations are less interested in these industries and tend to focus on the dining culture.
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75696-6

Unfortunately, the block’s efforts to create unique dining experiences have been weak, resulting in an overabun­ dance of restaurants and popular snacks. This has led to a lack of authentic Mongolian cuisine and local specialty dishes, contributing to the homogeneity of the dining culture in the area.
Ethnic cultural integration is achieved, but public perception requires the foundation of cultural understanding

The Da Zhao historical and cultural block is a neighborhood in which diverse cultures converge and blend. It includes various cultural elements, such as religion, Mongol Yuan, Silk Road, Shanxi merchants, and revolution­ ary culture, due to its long history. These cultures are reflected in the architecture, industries, and neighborhood cuisine, making it a unique cultural hub. However, the data analysis showed that, while the public could sense the difference between the Da Zhao historical and cultural block and other neighborhoods, they had difficulty under­ standing and recognizing their culture. There are issues such as “not being able to comprehend,” “not understand­ ing,” and “not being familiar” with the neighborhood culture. If the public had a basic understanding of culture, they could appreciate it better. Cultural recognition is necessary for the public to fully comprehend and appreciate the cultural diversity of their neighborhoods.
Summary and Discussion
Summary of main findings

The present study developed a multi-dimensional cultural perception evaluation framework for historic districts by integrating physical spatial characteristics and public cognitive experiences. Taking the Da Zhao Historic and Cultural District in Hohhot as a case study, this research combined field investigation, geographic spatial data, street-view imagery, POI data, questionnaire surveys, and online review data to evaluate how historical environ­ ments are perceived by the public. Unlike traditional evaluation approaches that focus mainly on physical preser­ vation or subjective satisfaction, this study considered cultural perception as a comprehensive outcome generated through interactions between spatial characteristics, cultural symbols, and human experience. The evaluation results indicate that the cultural perception of the Da Zhao Historic District is generally moder­ ate, with strong cultural recognition in some dimensions but insufficient depth of cultural understanding. The dis­ trict demonstrates a relatively strong perception of architectural style due to the coexistence of Tibetan Buddhist, Mongolian, Qing Dynasty, and traditional Chinese architectural characteristics. These distinctive architectural elements provide strong visual cultural symbols and contribute to public recognition of the district’s historical identity. However, street space perception remains relatively weak, mainly because insufficient spatial conti­ nuity, limited pedestrian-scale experience, and an unbalanced functional structure restrict continuous cultural experiences. The findings further reveal that cultural resources alone do not automatically lead to deep cultural perception. Although religious culture, especially the symbolic influence of Da Zhao Temple, strongly enhances cultural rec­ ognition, online review analysis shows that many visitors can identify the cultural characteristics of the district but lack deeper understanding of their historical and cultural meanings. Similarly, although diverse architectural forms create a distinctive visual image, the internal cultural narratives and detailed expressions of buildings remain insufficient, resulting in a relatively superficial perception of cultural value. In addition, the study identifies a contradiction between cultural inheritance and commercial development. Commercial activities contribute to maintaining neighborhood vitality; however, the current concentration of catering and shopping functions weakens cultural diversity and increases the risk of functional homogenization. Therefore, improving cultural interpretation, strengthening spatial experience, and balancing commercial activi­ ties with cultural functions are essential for enhancing cultural perception in historic districts.
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75696-6 Article in Press
Theoretical implications and comparison with previous studies

This study contributes to existing historic district perception research in several aspects. First, previous studies on historic district evaluation have often examined either physical spatial characteristics or residents’ subjective perceptions separately. By integrating material environment and public cognition within a unified framework, this study provides empirical evidence that cultural perception is not simply determined by the existence of historical resources, but is formed through the interaction between spatial carriers and human interpretation. This finding extends the application of sense of place theory by demonstrating how architectural symbols, street environments, and cultural activities jointly influence public cultural cognition. Second, compared with previous studies focusing mainly on conventional historic towns and commercial heritage areas, this study provides evidence from a northern multi-ethnic historic district where Tibetan Bud­ dhist culture, Mongolian traditions, and urban commercial functions coexist. The results indicate that strong cul­ tural symbols can effectively enhance place recognition, but symbolic recognition does not necessarily develop into deeper cultural understanding without effective interpretation and experiential engagement. This finding highlights the importance of distinguishing between cultural visibility and cultural comprehension in heritage conservation. Third, existing big-data-based perception studies have increasingly adopted street-view images, POI data, and online reviews to evaluate urban environments. However, many studies mainly emphasize technical measure­ ment and lack theoretical explanations of why certain spatial characteristics influence perception. By integrating multi-source data with place-related theories, this study provides a more interpretive framework for understand­ ing cultural perception formation in historic districts.
Planning and cultural governance implications

The findings provide several implications for the conservation and renewal of historic and cultural districts. First, cultural conservation should shift from physical preservation toward cultural interpretation. Although Da Zhao Historic District possesses abundant architectural and religious resources, public understanding of cultural meanings remains limited. Therefore, additional cultural explanation systems, including exhibition spaces, digi­ tal interpretation platforms, and interactive cultural activities, should be introduced to transform visible cultural symbols into deeper cultural knowledge. Second, spatial renewal strategies should focus on improving continuous cultural experiences. The relatively weak perception of street space indicates that historical resources alone cannot guarantee positive cultural experi­ ences. Improving pedestrian-scale environments, strengthening spatial connections between cultural nodes, and increasing distributed cultural facilities can enhance interaction between visitors and historical spaces. Third, commercial development should be coordinated with cultural preservation. The current concentration of catering and shopping functions provides economic vitality but also contributes to cultural homogenization. Future renewal strategies should encourage locally distinctive cultural industries, traditional crafts, and ethnic cultural activities to maintain the authenticity and diversity of the historic district. Finally, the evaluation framework developed in this study can support dynamic cultural governance. By con­ tinuously integrating spatial data, public feedback, and online perception information, local governments can establish monitoring mechanisms to identify changes in cultural perception and provide evidence-based guidance for historic district management.
Limitations and future research

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study adopts a cross-sectional research design and mainly reflects cultural perception characteristics during a specific period. Future research could incorporate long-term
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75696-6

monitoring data to examine temporal changes in cultural perception caused by seasonal tourism, cultural activi­ ties, and urban renewal processes. Second, this study focuses on one representative ethnic historic district. Although the case provides valuable insights into northern multi-ethnic cultural environments, comparative studies involving different historic dis­ tricts are needed to further examine the applicability of the proposed framework. Third, cultural perception involves multi-sensory experiences beyond visual perception. Future research could incorporate auditory, tactile, and behavioral data to develop a more comprehensive understanding of how people perceive and interact with historic cultural environments.

Individuals often rely on friends’ advice when making mate-choice decisions under uncertainty, yet how such advice is integrated into decision-making remains unclear. Using fNIRS hyperscanning, we simultaneously recorded neural and behavioral activity from 66 adult friend dyads (33 female dyads)1234567890():,; 1234567890():,; during interactive advice phases. Only the bidirectional Social Information Processing (SIP) computational model best ﬁt the behavioral data, indicating that social inﬂuence arises from reciprocal interaction rather than one-way transmission. Behaviorally, positive advice from in the relationship advisors increased mate-choice intention, whereas negative advice from single advisors more strongly inﬂuenced decision-making. Both conditions elicited enhanced interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), linked to risk evaluation, and in the left superior and middle temporal gyri (l-STG, l-MTG), associated with semantic processing and value transformation. Machine learning analyses showed that task-level INS robustly forecasted overall advice inﬂuence. Together, these ﬁndings demonstrate that friend advice inﬂuence emerges from dynamic brain-to-brain alignment in control and semantic networks—reﬂecting emotional sharing during positive advice and risk re-evaluation during negative advice. Check for updates
Jade Seguin 1 & Mathias Pessiglione 1

Students may learn their course material for different types of motives: because the material is interesting or because they aim at a good grade. A common intuition is that performing tasks because they are interesting (under intrinsic motivation) requires less effort than performing tasks because they are instrumental for obtaining some beneﬁts (under extrinsic motivation). Yet, this notion is not1234567890():,; 1234567890():,; incorporated in current effort allocation models, which were developed in the context of instrumental behaviour. These same-cost models would consider intrinsic and extrinsic motivation as targeting two types of rewards through the same kind of effortful process. Here, we introduce a different-cost model, in which intrinsic motivation improves task performance by providing effortless direct drive, whereas extrinsic motivation improves performance through the exertion of effortful cognitive control. We tested the predictions of this model across a series of behavioural experiments, during which volunteers (n = 147 in total) memorized lists of information, with various levels of self-reported interest and various amounts of monetary reward associated to correct recall. Behavioural results indicate that both interest and reward (intrinsic and extrinsic motivation) improve memory performance, with no interaction between the two effects. Computational analyses show that these behavioural effects are best captured by the different-cost model, rather than the same-cost model. Moreover, pupillometry validated the key prediction of the different-cost model: for a similar improvement in performance, increasing interest triggers lesser effort exertion compared to increasing reward. Together, these ﬁndings suggestthat working under intrinsic motivation mightrelax the demand on cognitive effort and help preventing fatigue and burnout syndromes.

articles.title: Rubric-anchored large language model feedback for academic argumentation revision
paragraphs: Rubric-anchored large language model feedback for academic argumentation revision
Jing Wei
Received: 27 March 2026 / Accepted: 3 November 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Generative AI can provide rapid, detailed feedback for student writing, yet its organization may affect how students use feedback during short classroom revision windows. This study examined descriptive outcome and process patterns across rubric-anchored LLM feedback (RA), non-anchored LLM feedback (NA), and an active criteria-aligned self-revision comparison in a four-week intact-class quasi-experiment with 105 Chinese second-year Economics students (three classes, one per condition). Two practice tasks used Draft-Review-Revi­ sion cycles, whereas baseline (T0) and posttest (T1) assessments were completed without feedback. Rubric- scored argumentation performance was summarized using covariate-adjusted posttest means, with a maximum possible score of 24. Descriptive adjusted means were highest under RA (14.64), followed by NA (14.21) and Control (14.05). The naive individual-level ANCOVA did not yield a statistically significant Condition term. Descriptive revision-activity summaries based on words added, words deleted, and net word change showed greater textual change under RA across both practice tasks on several indicators. In an exploratory subsample of 24 students, the proportion of suggestions targeting Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, or Counterargument that were adopted or partially adopted was descriptively higher under RA (75.0%) than NA (69.0%). Given the one-class-per-condition design and condition-specific prompts, these findings do not isolate a causal effect of rubric anchoring. Within the GPT-4o-based implementation examined here, rubric-aligned organization war­ rants further investigation as a design feature for time-limited classroom revision.
Keywords Generative AI · Large language models · Rubric-anchored feedback · Academic argumentation · Revision activity · Feedback uptake
Introduction

The rapid uptake of generative AI has intensified interest in how AI reshapes writing support, feedback practices, and assessment in higher education1,2. In writing instruction, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for idea generation, outlining, language polishing, and feedback seeking, all of which intersect with core stages of process writing and revision. This shift has moved the pedagogical question from whether AI can generate

feedback to how the design of that feedback shapes learners’ understanding, agency, and revision-oriented par­ ticipation in authentic classroom tasks. In educational settings, these tools also raise practical and ethical concerns, including over-reliance, shallow revision, opacity of system reasoning, and academic integrity risks, especially in take-home or lightly proc­ tored writing2,3. In routine classroom instruction, however, a more immediate pedagogical bottleneck is whether students can use AI-generated feedback effectively within a short revision window. LLMs can produce rapid, detailed suggestions, but when feedback is presented as long, weakly organized lists, learners may struggle to triage what matters, connect suggestions to assessment criteria, and complete higher-order revisions under time pressure. The present study therefore examines presentation format as a concrete instructional design variable and asks whether it makes LLM feedback more usable at the point of revision. Writing improvement depends not simply on receiving feedback, but on learners’ uptake of that feedback through interpretation, relevance judgments, prioritization, and enactment4–6. When feedback is extensive but loosely organized, the coordination work required to map suggestions onto goals and plan a revision sequence can become the limiting step. This problem is especially acute in source-based academic argumentation, where surface edits, such as local wording or grammatical corrections, may improve correctness without strengthening criterion-relevant links among claims, evidence, and warrants across sources, and where revision quality depends on higher-order decisions about claims, evidence selection, and warrant justification7,8. Accordingly, the present study focuses on an organizing layer that makes criterion links explicit at the point of revision. This framing is referred to here as structure as scaffolding.
Literature review

This section reviews the conceptual and empirical foundations for the study. Following the problem logic estab­ lished in the Introduction, the review focuses on three strands central to the present design: decision overhead in feedback use, rubric anchoring as a scaffold for criterion-referenced revision, and the role of feedback structure in GenAI-supported writing revision. Together, these strands clarify why feedback organization may matter when students revise source-based academic argumentation under classroom time constraints.
Decision overhead in AI feedback

In writing instruction, feedback matters when it helps learners narrow the gap between current performance and intended goals. Formative assessment scholarship treats feedback as a lever for improvement rather than judge­ ment, emphasising clarity about the goal, the current state, and the next actions that move learning forward4,5,9. Recent conceptual work on hybrid intelligent feedback likewise underscores that AI feedback needs explicit pedagogical framing if it is to support meaningful improvement rather than merely generate more comments1. In higher-education writing, the constraint is the work required to use feedback well within limited time. Writ­ ers decide what deserves attention first, how suggestions relate to criteria, and how to translate advice into changes that strengthen the text. Research on feedback recipience and feedback literacy shows that uptake depends on interpretation, judgement of relevance, and student agency, not simply exposure to feedback6,10,11. When feed­ back arrives as a long, ungrouped list, students must supply the structure themselves. They sort suggestions into categories, infer the target dimension, and reconcile overlapping demands. That coordination absorbs attention and makes quick, local edits more attractive than integrative work. This tension is amplified in source-based academic argumentation. Classic revision research distinguishes surface-level editing from meaning-changing revision that reorganises claims, evidence relations, and reason­ ing7,8. Stronger argumentation depends on moves that integrate information across sentences and paragraphs, including explicit warrants and credible counterargument with rebuttal. These moves remain demanding even with helpful feedback. Cognitive load theory predicts that when a complex task is paired with additional search
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-79755-w Article in Press

and classification demands, extraneous load competes with the processing needed for conceptual integration12. A feedback format that increases decision burden can consume learners’ limited revision time. As a result, students may spend less time on higher-order argumentation work, even when the suggestions themselves are valid.
Rubric anchoring as a scaffold

Rubrics are widely used to make quality criteria visible to learners. They can support planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation by clarifying what good writing looks like and by giving writers a stable reference for revision decisions13–15. Evidence syntheses suggest that rubrics are especially helpful when students can translate criteria into concrete actions on argument-relevant dimensions such as claim, evidence, reasoning, and counterargu­ ment16. However, this translation step is also where many writers stall, because they may sense that an argument is weak but cannot readily diagnose whether the gap lies in the claim itself, the selection or integration of evi­ dence, the warrant linking evidence to the claim, or the adequacy of the rebuttal. Scaffolding theory helps explain why the organization of criteria and feedback matters during revision. Effec­ tive scaffolds reduce coordination demands so learners can concentrate on the substantive work of improving performance17,18. Rubric anchoring applies this logic by organizing feedback under rubric-aligned headings so that the target dimension is explicit. This organization can make criterion links easier to locate and may reduce some of the coordination work involved in deciding what to address first. The latter is treated here as a proposed account rather than a directly measured cognitive mechanism. When the target dimension is explicit, writers can decide more efficiently what to revise first and how to check whether a change meets the criterion. This aligns with feedback literacy research showing that productive uptake depends on students’ interpretation, judgement, and self-regulation rather than on receiving comments alone6,10,19. In this sense, rubric anchoring is intended to make criterion-referenced next steps easier to see and easier to carry out during time-limited revision. Importantly, rubric anchoring here does not simply mean provid­ ing students with a rubric alongside feedback. It uses rubric criteria as the organizational layer of the feedback itself, grouping draft-specific LLM suggestions under explicit criterion headings at the point of revision. The design question is therefore narrower than whether rubrics or structured feedback are beneficial in general: it con­ cerns whether the learner-facing organization of LLM-generated feedback is associated with different revision patterns when compared with feedback presented as a flat list under common constraints on length, suggestion count, and intended dimensional emphasis.
Why structure matters in GenAI feedback

Research on automated writing evaluation and automated feedback shows that technology-supported feedback can improve writing, but effects vary with system design, task type, and instructional context20–24. Scalable systems tend to support grammar and mechanics more reliably than higher-order concerns such as content development, organization, and critical thinking, which often require stronger pedagogical framing or human mediation25,26. This line of work makes a basic point clear: having feedback is not the same as having feedback that learners can use to improve complex writing goals. Generative AI changes the landscape by producing fluent, draft-sensitive suggestions at scale. Recent studies report measurable benefits for some writing outcomes, while also showing that GenAI can alter feedback and revision dynamics in ways that do not automatically translate into better final performance3,27–30. Abundance shifts the bottleneck: the challenge becomes helping writers interpret, prioritise, and enact advice responsibly under classroom constraints. Methodological work in adjacent AI domains similarly shows that choices con­ cerning information organization, component coordination, and resource allocation can shape system perfor­ mance. Cheng et al. examine large-small model collaboration under heterogeneous computational constraints, highlighting the role of coordination and resource allocation31. Zhang et al. adopt a coarse-to-fine framework with multi-granularity relationship modeling to organize complex cross-document information32, while Zhang et
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-79755-w

al. combine curriculum learning with difficulty-aware mixture-of-experts routing to coordinate processing across problem spaces of differing complexity33. Although these studies address technical AI systems, they collectively highlight the methodological significance of how complex information and processing components are structured and coordinated under constraints. This broader design perspective provides a useful basis for considering how the organization of LLM-generated feedback may likewise shape its usability during time-limited revision. Rubric-aligned organization can influence feedback use through several distinguishable routes. First, head­ ings may improve navigability by segmenting a feedback report into recognizable categories. Second, explicit rubric labels may increase the visibility of assessment criteria by making the target of each suggestion easier to identify. Third, these structural cues may reduce the coordination demands involved in deciding what to prioritize and how to translate feedback into revision actions. These routes are related but conceptually distinct: naviga­ bility and criterion visibility concern the organization and accessibility of the feedback itself, whereas decision overhead concerns the cognitive work involved in using that feedback. Decision overhead therefore offers one interpretive account of why feedback organization may matter during time-limited revision. Decision overhead is used here in a narrower, task-specific sense than several related constructs. Cognitive load refers more broadly to the mental demands placed on limited processing resources, whereas decision overhead refers specifically to the coordination involved in identifying, prioritizing, and translating feedback suggestions into revision actions. Feedback literacy concerns learners’ capacities to interpret, evaluate, and act on feedback, whereas decision overhead concerns the situational demands encountered while doing so. Suggestion-level uptake is an observable behavioral outcome indicating whether feedback was enacted, not a measure of the cognitive effort required to reach that decision. Perceived difficulty would represent a learner’s subjective judgment of task demands and was not operationalized as an analytic variable in the present study. Accordingly, decision overhead is not treated as a separately measured construct, but as an interpretive account linking feedback organization to the observed revision-process patterns.
The present study

The present study examines whether descriptive outcome and process patterns differ across two LLM feedback implementations that vary in how feedback is organized in relation to rubric criteria. The contribution there­ fore lies not in testing rubric use or LLM feedback efficacy in general, but in examining rubric alignment as a learner-facing organizational feature of draft-specific LLM feedback under time-limited revision. Both LLM conditions used the same ChatGPT web interface and GPT-4o model option and were constrained by the same feedback-length limit, number-of-suggestions requirement, and intended distribution across writing dimensions: approximately 70% of suggestions were intended to target Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, and Counterargument, and approximately 30% Organization and Academic Language. The RA prompt required rubric-aligned head­ ings, whereas the NA prompt required a flat numbered list without rubric headings or category labels. These common constraints were intended to maintain broad consistency in feedback volume and emphasis, while the condition-specific prompts allowed variation in the diagnostic content generated for individual drafts. The active comparison condition used a seven-item criteria-aligned self-revision checklist followed by a brief revision plan. Because conditions were assigned at the class level with one class per condition, outcome contrasts are treated as design-relevant descriptive patterns rather than confirmatory evidence of causal effects. Revision activity and suggestion-level uptake are examined as separate process indicators that characterize what students did during revision; neither is treated as a direct measure of decision overhead or as a comprehensive measure of revision engagement.

Research questions

RQ1. What descriptive differences in rubric-scored argumentation performance are observed across RA, NA, and Control after adjustment for baseline performance and task order? RQ2. How are the descriptive between-condition patterns distributed across Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, Counterargument, Organization and Academic Language? RQ3a. How does the magnitude of between-draft revision activity differ descriptively across RA, NA, and Control during the two practice tasks? RQ3b. In the exploratory LLM subsample, how do suggestion-level uptake patterns differ descriptively between RA and NA?
Methods

This section describes the quasi-experimental design, tasks, intervention conditions, measures, and analytic approach used to characterize descriptive differences in writing outcomes and revision processes across the three classroom conditions. The instructional context and four-week unit are outlined first, followed by the source- based writing tasks, intervention conditions, outcome and process measures, and the analytic strategy used to summarize patterns while acknowledging the limitation of class-level assignment (K = 3). Detailed replication materials are provided in the Supplementary Information.
Design and context

I conducted a three-condition intact-class quasi-experiment to examine descriptive differences in rubric-scored argumentation performance and revision processes across rubric-anchored LLM feedback (RA-LLM), non- anchored LLM feedback (NA-LLM), and an active criteria-aligned self-revision comparison (N = 105; K = 3). Three administratively formed intact classes were allocated to one condition each. Here, K = 3 denotes the three class-level assignment units, with only one intact class representing each condition. The study was implemented as a four-week instructional unit embedded in the regular course schedule at a single institution. Participants were Chinese second-year undergraduates enrolled in an EAP-adjacent academic argumentation writing course; all were Economics majors distributed across three intact classes (Class 1 n = 35; Class 2 n = 33; Class 3 n = 37). Course instruction emphasized source-based argumentation, rubric-guided revi­ sion, and classroom-based drafting and revising under time limits. The course met twice per week; each meeting consisted of two 50-minute blocks separated by a 10-minute break. All three classes were taught by the same instructor using a common syllabus, pacing, and assessment rou­ tines. In-class instructions, timing cues, and submission procedures were standardized through a shared execution protocol. Condition differences were confined to the Review phase of the two practice tasks (B1 and B2), where students received RA feedback, NA feedback, or the active self-revision checklist, respectively. In Week 1, students completed a 40-minute English diagnostic test (30 items) assessing reading comprehension and vocabulary/grammar; raw accuracy was recorded as a supplementary proficiency index. The diagnostic test was used to characterize general English proficiency across the three intact classes and to define the proficiency strata used for the exploratory uptake subsample. Class-level descriptive means were closely aligned (Class 1: M = 20.97; Class 2: M = 21.15; Class 3: M = 21.32; maximum = 30). Baseline writing performance was captured separately by the T0 writing task administered in the same week. The four-week unit then proceeded with B1 and B2 in Weeks 2 and 3 and the T1 posttest in Week 4. With one intact class representing each condition, condition and class membership were completely con­ founded. The 105 students therefore do not constitute independent replications of the three conditions, and

Ethics statement

All methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. The study protocol and implementation arrangements were reviewed and approved by the College of Educational Sciences, Northwest Normal University (Project No. NWNU20250006B; approval dated 3 April 2025), before the instructional unit and research data collection began. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before research data collection. Before student drafts were entered into the ChatGPT web interface, names, student numbers, and other identifying information were removed and coded study IDs were used. Quantitative results are reported in aggregate form, and no individual student can be identified from the reported results.
Tasks and procedure

All writing tasks were source-based academic argumentation prompts. Each task package included two contrast­ ing briefs and a small data table. Students were instructed to state an evidence-based claim, integrate informa­ tion across sources, explain reasoning, and address a counterargument with rebuttal. To reduce dependence on supplementary files, the task set is summarized here: the two assessment prompts addressed mandatory intern­ ships and hybrid-by-default work policies, whereas the two practice prompts addressed an AI literacy module and congestion pricing. Across the unit, tasks followed a common structure with two task types: assessments (T0, T1; no feedback) and practice tasks (B1, B2; Draft-Review-Revision with condition-specific support). Accord­ ingly, condition-specific feedback was used only for formative revision during the two practice tasks and was not provided during the baseline or posttest assessments. The four-week schedule and the within-task workflow are summarized in Fig. 1.
Assessments (T0, T1)

Baseline (T0) and posttest (T1) were administered as single uninterrupted, proctored 50-minute writing blocks with no feedback. Although each class meeting contained two 50-minute blocks separated by a break, assessments

Practice tasks (B1, B2)

The intervention was delivered during two practice tasks (B1 and B2), each implemented across two class meet­ ings using a fixed Draft-Review-Revision workflow. In the first meeting for each practice task, students produced Draft 1 during a dedicated 50-minute block under classroom time limits. In the subsequent meeting, students completed a mandatory 15-minute Review phase, during which they read the RA/NA feedback or the checklist depending on condition, followed immediately by a 35-minute revision period to produce Draft 2. Across classes, the instructor followed a standardized lesson script and timing checklist to keep instructions, timing cues, and submission procedures constant; no additional condition-specific guidance was provided beyond the assigned feedback format during Review.
Four-week flow

Week 1 included the diagnostic test and T0 baseline writing. Weeks 2–3 implemented B1 and B2, respectively (Draft 1 in one meeting; Review-Revision to Draft 2 in the next). Week 4 administered the T1 posttest writing task and collected a brief post-unit reflection. Assessment task order was counterbalanced within each class: RA, A→C n = 18 (51.4%) and C→A n = 17 (48.6%); NA, A→C n = 16 (48.5%) and C→A n = 17 (51.5%); Control, A→C n = 18 (48.6%) and C→A n = 19 (51.4%). Overall, 52 students (49.5%) followed A→C and 53 (50.5%) followed C→A. The full schedule and within-task workflow are summarized in Fig. 1.
Conditions and design validation

The three conditions compared two LLM feedback implementations that organized feedback differently in rela­ tion to rubric criteria and an active criteria-aligned self-revision comparison. The two LLM conditions used the same ChatGPT web interface and GPT-4o model option and were constrained by the same feedback-length limit, number-of-suggestions requirement, and intended distribution across writing dimensions. Because RA and NA feedback were generated using condition-specific prompts, the substantive diagnostic content of individual reports was not experimentally held identical across conditions.
RA-LLM (rubric-anchored)

Students received LLM feedback grouped under six rubric-aligned headings. Reports were capped at 400 words and constrained to six to eight actionable suggestions. The prompt specified an intended distribution in which approximately 70% of suggestions targeted Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, and Counterargument and approxi­ mately 30% targeted Organization and Academic Language. Each suggestion was required to identify what to revise, where or how to revise it, and a criterion for judging completion.
NA-LLM (non-anchored)

Students received LLM-generated feedback as a flat numbered list without rubric headings or category labels. Reports were subject to the same 400-word limit, six-to-eight-suggestion requirement, and intended distribution across writing dimensions as RA. The NA prompt imposed these common constraints while omitting rubric- based organizational grouping.

Control (active criteria-aligned self-revision comparison)

Students completed a mandatory 15-minute self-review using a structured seven-item checklist aligned with the same assessment criteria used across the study. The checklist prompted students to examine claim clarity and con­ sistency, evidence use from both briefs and the data table, reasoning, counterargument and rebuttal, organization and transitions, academic language, and data accuracy. Students then produced a three-bullet revision plan before revising Draft 1 into Draft 2. Thus, the Control condition provided structured criterion exposure, protected review time, and an explicit planning activity while withholding individualized draft-specific diagnostic feedback. This checklist-based procedure was designed for the present study as an active non-LLM comparison aligned with the same assessment criteria; it was not intended to reproduce the class’s usual evaluation practice.
LLM implementation, quality control, and reproducibility

De-identified student drafts and condition-specific prompts were entered individually into the ChatGPT web interface using GPT-4o. Model generation settings were left at the platform defaults. The prompts required veri­ fication of numerical statements against the provided data table, prohibited invented numerical information, and prohibited full-essay rewriting. Before classroom delivery, each generated report was screened using a stan­ dardized quality-control checklist covering the 400-word limit, six-to-eight-suggestion requirement, condition- specific format, numerical accuracy, consistency with the task briefs and data table, source attribution, accurate reference to the student draft, diagnostic relevance, and compliance with the prohibition on full-essay rewriting. Reports containing factual inaccuracies, source misrepresentation, clear diagnostic mismatches, or output-con­ straint violations were rejected and regenerated using the same condition-specific prompt and procedure. I did not substantively rewrite or selectively edit individual suggestions. Once a report passed screening, all sugges­ tions in that accepted report were presented to the student without further substantive modification, and the exact accepted report was archived under the corresponding de-identified study ID. The manipulation check examined whether the intended structural distinction between RA and NA was real­ ized and whether the sampled reports showed broadly similar profiles on selected properties. I randomly sampled 24 feedback reports per condition (12 from B1 and 12 from B2), de-identified them, and presented them in ran­ domized order. Two coders, who were not provided with condition labels, rated structural navigability, rubric- alignment visibility, segmentation clarity, actionability, and diagnostic depth on anchored 1–5 scales. Because the organizational format remained visible, complete perceptual blinding to condition could not be ensured, and awareness of the visible format could have influenced the actionability and diagnostic-depth ratings. Word count and number of suggestions were also recorded as objective descriptive indicators. The check was used to docu­ ment structural differentiation and selected report properties, not to establish semantic or substantive equivalence between RA and NA feedback.
Measures and analysis

The study combined an outcome measure of rubric-scored argumentation performance with two complementary process indicators: between-draft revision activity and suggestion-level uptake. The outcome measure summa­ rizes performance on the six prespecified rubric dimensions, whereas the process indicators characterize the amount of textual change and the enactment of individual LLM suggestions. The two process indicators are not treated as interchangeable measures of a single engagement construct.
Outcome measure: rubric-scored argumentation performance

Writing performance was assessed using a six-dimension analytic rubric covering Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, Counterargument, Organization, and Academic Language. Each dimension was scored from 0 to 4, yielding a

total score from 0 to 24; complete descriptors for all five score points are presented in Table 1. Raters assigned the single best-fitting score for each dimension based on the overall preponderance of evidence and used the lower score when performance was mixed across adjacent descriptors. Two trained raters independently scored all T0 and T1 essays blind to condition and timepoint following a calibration session. Inter-rater reliability for the total score was assessed on the independent ratings before discussion or adjudication using a two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficient. Disagreements were subsequently resolved through discus­ sion, with adjudication as needed, following the rubric decision rules.
Process indicator 1: revision activity

For each practice task (B1 and B2), Draft 1 and Draft 2 were compared using the Compare function in Microsoft Word. The comparison was used to identify inserted and deleted text, from which the numbers of words added and words deleted were recorded. Net word change was calculated as words added minus words deleted. These indicators summarize the extent of textual change between Draft 1 and Draft 2.

Process indicator 2: suggestion-level uptake

To examine RQ3b, I used an exploratory stratified subsample of 24 students from the two LLM conditions, com­ prising 12 students from RA and 12 from NA. The subsample size reflected the stratified sampling scheme: four students were selected from each of three proficiency strata within each of the two LLM conditions (4 × 3 × 2 = 24), providing equal representation across strata and conditions. Week 1 English diagnostic-test scores were used to define three proficiency strata (Low, Medium, and High) within each condition. Within each stratum, students were ranked by diagnostic-test score, and four students were selected at approximately equally spaced ranks across the ordered score distribution. This procedure yielded equal representation of the three proficiency levels within each condition and provided coverage across the ordered score distribution within each stratum. The sub­ sample was used for exploratory descriptive analysis rather than population-level inference. For each selected student, feedback suggestions targeting Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, or Counterargument were linked to Draft 2 and coded as Adopted, Partially adopted, Ignored, or Misinterpreted using the predefined codebook. For sec­ ondary descriptive summaries, successful uptake was defined as Adopted plus Partially adopted. The successful uptake percentage was calculated within each condition as the number of Adopted plus Partially adopted sugges­ tions divided by the total number of coded suggestions × 100. The resulting dataset contained 60 such suggestions in RA and 58 in NA. Because students contributed multiple suggestion units, suggestions were nested within students and were not treated as independent observations. Coders were not given condition labels, although the visible organizational format prevented complete perceptual blinding.
Analytic strategy and design limitations

Data were checked for completeness, valid score ranges, task labels, and consistency of study IDs before analy­ sis. All participants had complete T0 and T1 scores and revision-activity records for B1 and B2. Descriptive sta­ tistics and covariate-adjusted posttest summaries were obtained using IBM SPSS Statistics 26. Posttest estimated marginal means were derived from an individual-level general linear model adjusting for baseline writing perfor­ mance and assessment task order. These EMMs have no inferential role in the present design; they are used only to summarize the observed posttest pattern after adjustment for baseline writing performance and assessment task order. Because conditions were assigned at the class level with one class per condition (K = 3), these adjusted means were interpreted descriptively and were not used to estimate an independently identified treatment effect; cluster-robust inference was not attempted. For transparency, a naive individual-level ANCOVA is included in the supplementary materials. Dimension-level adjusted means were treated as descriptive decompositions of the overall rubric score rather than six independent confirmatory tests. Revision activity and suggestion-level uptake were used to characterize revision processes and to inform interpretation of the descriptive outcome patterns.

Manipulation check

The manipulation check examined the realized properties of the two LLM feedback formats (Table 3). RA reports were rated higher than NA reports on structural navigability, rubric-alignment visibility, and segmentation clarity. To address RQ3b, I examined the distribution of the four uptake categories in the exploratory stratified subsample of 24 students from the two LLM conditions (Table 7). Among the 60 suggestions targeting Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, or Counterargument coded in RA, 53.3% were Adopted, 21.7% were Partially adopted, 18.3% were Ignored, and 6.7% were Misinterpreted. Among the 58 suggestions coded in NA, the corresponding proportions were 46.6%, 22.4%, 22.4%, and 8.6%, respectively. The clearest descriptive separation occurred for full adop­ tion, which was higher under RA, whereas partial adoption was similar across the two conditions. When Adopted and Partially adopted were combined as a secondary descriptive summary, successful uptake was descriptively higher in RA (75.0%) than in NA (69.0%). Because suggestion units were nested within 24 students, these per­ centages are interpreted as exploratory descriptive patterns. The two vignettes below illustrate the coding categories and make the distinction between successful enact­ ment and misinterpretation concrete. They are included as coding examples and are not used to estimate preva­ lence or to establish a cognitive mechanism.
Vignette 1 (RA; successful uptake-reasoning)

A mid-proficiency student’s Draft 1 stated a clear position and cited a table value, but the logic connecting the evidence to the claim was implicit. Under the Reasoning heading, the RA report prompted the student to explain what the statistic meant in context and how it supported the central claim. In Draft 2, the student added two sen­ tences that interpreted the number and explicitly linked it to the claim while keeping the overall structure stable. The case was coded as successful uptake because the revision addressed the intended reasoning requirement.
Vignette 2 (NA; misinterpretation)

An NA student received feedback as an ungrouped numbered list. One item bundled several demands: integrate ideas from both briefs, cite a percentage from the table, and explain what the number showed. In revision, the student inserted the requested statistic and restated the percentage but did not explain its argumentative implica­ tion or connect it to the claim. This was coded as Misinterpreted because the revision addressed a surface ele­ ment of the suggestion by inserting and restating the statistic, while leaving its core intended reasoning function unfulfilled.
Discussion

This study examined descriptive differences in rubric-scored argumentation performance and revision processes across three classroom conditions, including two feedback implementations generated using GPT-4o through the ChatGPT web interface. The discussion distinguishes directly observed patterns from interpretive explanations and limits conclusions to the present class-level design, prompt implementation, and source-based argumentation tasks.
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-79755-w
Key findings

Descriptive covariate-adjusted posttest means were highest under RA, followed by NA and the active self-revi­ sion comparison. Given the one-class-per-condition design, this ordering should be read as a between-condition pattern observed in the present sample, with class-level influences remaining an alternative explanation. The active comparison also provided structured exposure to assessment criteria, protected review time, and an explicit revision-planning activity; contrasts involving Control therefore compare individualized LLM-generated diag­ nostic feedback with structured criteria-aligned self-revision, rather than with no instructional support. At the dimension level, the largest descriptive separation occurred for Reasoning, with smaller differences for Claim, Evidence, and Counterargument. The outcome measure was intentionally aligned with the six dimensions used to structure RA feedback. This alignment makes the assessment criteria directly relevant to the targeted writing skills, but it also narrows interpretation: rubric-aligned headings increased the visibility of the same dimensions used in scoring, so greater criterion salience may have contributed to the RA pattern. The adjusted means should therefore be interpreted as performance on the rubric dimensions assessed in these source-based argumentation tasks, not as evidence of broad improvement in academic writing ability. Revision activity and suggestion-level uptake provide complementary descriptions of revision behavior. The task-specific trace summaries quantify the amount of between-draft textual change, whereas uptake coding records whether individual LLM suggestions were enacted in an exploratory subsample. The larger revision magnitudes observed under RA indicate more extensive textual change only and do not establish that those revi­ sions were more productive, more cognitively engaged, or more effective. The uptake coding provides a more differentiated view: full adoption was descriptively higher under RA (53.3% vs. 46.6%), partial adoption was similar across conditions (21.7% vs. 22.4%), and ignored and misinterpreted suggestions were somewhat less frequent under RA. These uptake differences remain preliminary because suggestions were nested within a small student subsample.
Decision overhead as an interpretive account

The observed process patterns are consistent with a decision-overhead account, although the study did not directly measure the cognitive processes involved in feedback use. During time-limited revision, students must identify which suggestions deserve attention, determine how individual suggestions relate to assessment criteria, and translate feedback into concrete revision actions. Rubric-aligned headings make the intended criterion target more visible and may reduce some of this coordination work. Three related explanations should nevertheless be distinguished. First, rubric-aligned headings may improve navigability by making feedback easier to scan and locate. Second, they may increase the visibility of assessment criteria by explicitly identifying the rubric dimension associated with a suggestion. Third, clearer organization may reduce the cognitive or decision demands involved in prioritizing and enacting feedback. The manipulation check provides direct evidence for the first two properties of the feedback materials, particularly navigability and rubric visibility, but the third concerns students’ internal processing and was not directly measured. Revision activity and suggestion-level uptake also do not directly capture cognitive load, decision difficulty, processing time, prioritization, comprehension, or attentional allocation. Decision overhead is therefore used as an interpre­ tive account of the observed patterns rather than an established mechanism.
Boundary conditions and alternative explanations

Several alternative explanations remain compatible with the observed patterns. Because one intact class repre­ sented each condition, class-level influences remain an alternative explanation for the observed between-condi­ tion patterns. Rubric headings also made assessment categories more salient, which may have increased attention to the scoring criteria without reducing cognitive load. Novelty associated with AI feedback may have influenced
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-79755-w Article in Press

revision behavior. In addition, RA and NA reports were generated through condition-specific prompts; although common constraints limited broad differences in length, suggestion count, and intended emphasis, they did not ensure identical diagnostic content. Observed RA-NA differences therefore cannot be attributed exclusively to organizational format. Criterion salience and decision overhead are related but distinct explanations. Rubric headings directly increase the visibility of assessment categories, whereas a reduction in decision overhead would concern the cognitive effort required to prioritize and enact suggestions. The present study directly documents differences in feedback organization and selected process behaviors but does not identify which internal cognitive process produced the observed dimension-level pattern. The two process indicators should also remain conceptually separate. Revision-activity measures quantify the amount of textual change, whereas suggestion-level uptake records whether specific feedback suggestions were enacted. Their descriptive patterns can be considered together, but they are not interchangeable measures of a single engagement construct.
Design implications for classroom feedback

Within the GPT-4o implementation conducted through the ChatGPT web interface, the descriptive patterns point to several design features that merit further testing in classroom feedback. Rubric-aligned headings can make the intended criterion target more visible at the point of revision and provide a clearer structure for locating relevant suggestions. Constraining feedback length and the number of suggestions can keep reports manageable during short revision periods, while actionable suggestions that identify what to revise, where or how to revise it, and how to judge completion can provide a clearer pathway from feedback to revision action. These features are best treated as design hypotheses arising from the present implementation. Their value requires further testing across language models, model versions, prompt designs, student populations, disciplines, instructors, and revision contexts. The present study therefore supports continued investigation of rubric-aligned organization as a classroom feedback design option rather than establishing a general principle for LLM-based writing feedback.
Limitations and future work

Most importantly, conditions were assigned at the class level with one class per condition. Condition and class membership were therefore completely confounded, and the observed between-condition differences cannot be separated from pre-existing or unmeasured class-specific influences. Although the three classes shared the same instructor, syllabus, pacing, assessment procedures, and closely aligned diagnostic means, these controls do not eliminate class effects as an alternative explanation. Future studies should include multiple independently assigned classes per condition. A second design limitation concerns the comparison between the two LLM conditions. RA and NA feedback were generated using condition-specific prompts that imposed different organizational requirements. The prompts shared the same intended feedback length, number of suggestions, and distribution across writing dimensions, and the manipulation check documented realized structural differences and similarity on selected rated proper­ ties. These controls do not establish equivalence of the substantive diagnostic content. Accordingly, observed differences between RA and NA cannot be attributed exclusively to rubric headings. A stronger future test would generate a common set of feedback content and experimentally vary only its organizational presentation. The study did not directly measure the cognitive processes proposed in the decision-overhead account. Direct measures of cognitive load, decision difficulty, prioritization, feedback comprehension, and processing time were not collected during the Review phase. Revision-activity indicators also quantify textual change rather than revision quality, and direct coding of the quality of individual B1/B2 revisions was not conducted. Future work
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-79755-w

should combine feedback-organization manipulations with online processing measures and direct revision-qual­ ity coding. The findings are implementation- and context-specific. Feedback was generated using GPT-4o through the ChatGPT web interface with platform-default generation settings, condition-specific prompt templates, and the quality-control procedure described above. Different models, interface configurations, prompts, or screening pro­ cedures can produce different feedback. Participants were second-year Economics majors at one institution, and the intervention occurred during tightly timed source-based argumentation revision. Replication across disci­ plines, proficiency levels, institutions, languages, models, and longer drafting cycles is required before broader conclusions are drawn.
Broader instructional considerations

The active comparison condition shows that structured criterion exposure and revision planning can be imple­ mented without individualized AI diagnosis. Within this study, rubric-aligned LLM organization can therefore be viewed as one design option for making assessment criteria and revision targets more visible during formative revision. The present evidence does not establish that this option should replace teacher, peer, or checklist-based feedback, and its value should be tested against other structured feedback formats. AI-supported formative feedback also raises questions of transparency and authorship. Requiring students to retain drafts and document criterion-referenced revision decisions can help make the revision process visible while preserving attention to student responsibility for the final text. These practices are relevant beyond LLM feedback because similar organizational structures can be used in teacher and peer feedback.
Conclusion

This study provides descriptive, design-relevant evidence concerning a rubric-anchored GPT-4o feedback implementation used during time-limited source-based academic argumentation revision. Descriptive covariate- adjusted posttest means were highest under RA, followed by NA and the active self-revision comparison. The naive individual-level ANCOVA did not yield a statistically significant Condition term. At the dimension level, the largest descriptive separation occurred for Reasoning, with smaller differences on Claim, Evidence, and Counterargument. Task-specific revision-activity summaries showed more extensive textual change under RA on several indicators across both practice tasks, and the exploratory uptake subsample showed a higher proportion of fully adopted suggestions targeting Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, or Counterargument and somewhat fewer ignored or misinterpreted suggestions under RA than under NA. Taken together, these patterns suggest that rubric-aligned organization warrants further investigation as a fea­ ture of classroom feedback design. The findings concern the GPT-4o implementation conducted through the ChatGPT web interface, the specific prompt templates and quality-control procedure used in this study, and the six rubric dimensions assessed in the present source-based argumentation tasks. They do not isolate the influence of rubric anchoring from class-level differences or substantive variation arising from condition-specific prompts, do not establish reduced decision overhead, and do not demonstrate transfer to broader academic writing ability or other LLM implementations. Replication across models, prompt designs, student populations, and indepen­ dently assigned classes is needed to determine the robustness and generalizability of these patterns.

articles.title: Depleted inventories leave oil markets exposed to further supply disruptions
paragraphs: Depleted inventories leave oil markets exposed to further supply disruptions

This blog post is part of a special series based on the October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook, a report published by the World Bank Group. This series features concise summaries of commodity-specific sections extracted from the report. Explore the full report here .

Front-month Brent crude futures climbed above $115 per barrel (bbl) in late October, then eased to nearly $95/bbl in the first week of November as renewed near-term active conflict in the Middle East appeared less likely. After the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States failed to reach a follow-on agreement to their June memorandum of understanding, Brent fluctuated between $75/bbl and $100/bbl and then stayed above $100/bbl in September and October. Oil product markets also tightened sharply. The European diesel premium over Brent averaged about $91/bbl in September, a record high, and U.S. retail diesel prices averaged nearly $6.20 per gallon in October.

Middle Eastern crude exports have rebounded, yet the declines in global supply and demand remain historically large. By early October, Middle Eastern oil exports were near 2025 levels, supported by ship-to-ship transfers, untracked shipments, and pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Refinery damage delayed the recovery in refined-product exports, including diesel. Global output fell about 9 million barrels per day (mb/d) (8.5 percent) year-on-year in 2026Q2 and 7 mb/d in Q3, largely in Saudi Arabia and Iraq. Gains in six major producers—including Brazil, Kazakhstan, and the United States—offset just 18 percent of gross losses. Supply is projected to fall 5.5 mb/d (5.2 percent) in 2026, the steepest annual decline in over four decades apart from 2020. Consumption fell 5.0 mb/d (4.8 percent year-on-year) in 2026Q2 and 3.7 mb/d (3.4 percent) in Q3, mainly in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). China contributed about 35 percent of the decline in EMDE oil consumption, partly as electric vehicles displaced oil. Global demand is projected to shrink 2.6 mb/d (2.5 percent) for the year, a decline surpassed only in 1980 and 2020.

Lower inventories have left oil markets more exposed to further supply disruptions. As supply losses outpaced the decline in demand, the implied market deficit widened to 2.9 mb/d in 2026Q2 before easing in Q3. Observed global inventories declined at an average rate of about 2.4 mb/d from March to September, dropping from near the top of their 2021–25 range at the year’s start to near the bottom by end-September. Although stocks totaled about 7.8 billion barrels, much of the oil was in transit, needed for operations, or otherwise not readily available. OECD government stocks reached their lowest level in over three decades; U.S. strategic reserves remained at their lowest since 1982. In early October, International Energy Agency members agreed to accelerate the release of 100 million barrels of emergency stocks through January 2027, initially prioritizing diesel.

Oil prices are projected to ease gradually as supply rebounds and the market shifts into surplus. Brent is forecast to average nearly $100/bbl in 2026Q4 and $91/bbl for 2026 as a whole, before falling to $79/bbl in 2027 and $70/bbl in 2028. This outlook assumes a sustained recovery in Middle Eastern crude shipments, a return of Gulf refinery throughput to pre-conflict levels by 2027Q2, and a rebound in Russian crude output. Consumption is expected to recover in 2027 but remain about 0.5 mb/d below 2025 levels. Global supply would return to about 106 mb/d in 2027, near its 2025 level. The market would enter surplus conditions in 2027Q2, enabling inventories to recover about 80 percent of their 2026 drawdown by end-2027.

Near-term risks to oil prices remain tilted to the upside. Renewed hostilities could reverse the recent recovery in shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, while attacks on Gulf pipelines, Red Sea shipping, or Russian oil infrastructure could exacerbate shortages of crude oil and refined products. With inventories already depleted, even modest additional supply losses could trigger sharp price increases. In an adverse scenario in which Gulf production falls by about 5 mb/d in the first half of 2027 and Russian exports remain constrained, Brent would average $105/bbl in 2027—about 33 percent above the baseline forecast. A more restrictive OPEC+ production policy poses an additional upside risk. Downside risks become more prominent later in the forecast horizon: a durable resolution of the conflict, stronger-than-expected growth in supply from countries outside of OPEC+, and faster adoption of electric vehicles could put downward pressure on prices.
