articles.title: How markets react when hidden debt comes to light
paragraphs: How markets react when hidden debt comes to light

Governments sometimes borrow more than they publicly admit. Loans taken out by state-owned companies, debts guaranteed behind closed doors, payments owed to contractors but never recorded — these liabilities can accumulate for years without appearing in any official figure. To outside observers — investors, credit rating agencies, international lenders — the public balance sheet can therefore look stronger than it really is. Then, suddenly, that picture changes.

Recent research has shown that such “hidden debt” can be large. It tends to come to light in one of three ways: an incoming government inherits the books and discloses what it finds; an international audit or IMF review uncovers discrepancies; or a financial crisis forces a full accounting of what the state actually owes. When that moment arrives, the numbers can be startling — in some countries, reported public debt burden has been revised upward by billions of dollars. But the revelation itself is only the beginning. What happens next — to borrowing costs, to investor confidence, and to a country's ability to access financing — is less well understood. Do markets react immediately or gradually? Do reactions differ depending on how the government responds? And how persistent are the effects?

To answer these questions, we examined seven well-documented episodes of hidden debt coming to light between 2005 and 2025 in the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Mozambique, Pakistan, Senegal, Türkiye, and Zambia tracking daily borrowing costs and stripping out global market swings to isolate each country's specific experience. The results highlight important differences in how markets respond to hidden-debt revelations — and offer clear lessons for governments navigating the aftermath.
1. Borrowing costs rise steadily, and the reaction builds for weeks

Markets do not anticipate revelations — borrowing costs are broadly unchanged in the 10 days leading up to these events. Once the information becomes public, however, the cost of borrowing rises sharply and persistently. On average, spreads widen by about 80 basis points within 10 days and by about 150 basis points by day 20, peaking at nearly 250 basis points around day 50 (Figure 1). Strikingly, the adjustment is gradual. By day 10, less than half of the eventual two-month repricing has occurred, and spreads stay elevated well into the second month. Investors appear to spend weeks reassessing not only the larger debt burden but also how promptly the country's fiscal reporting is revised.

Sources: Authors’ calculations based on J.P.Morgan EMBI Global spreads. Note: The line shows the pooled mean of country-specific spreads across the seven episodes, normalized to the pre-event baseline (day 0 = revelation). Shaded band shows the 90 percent confidence interval.
2. The size of the hidden debt is not the whole story

It is tempting to assume that the larger the concealed liability, the larger the market reaction. But in our sample, the link between the size of the revealed debt and the spread response is weak. The two extremes make the point: Senegal had the largest revision in our sample, yet its market reaction was far from the worst.  Mozambique’s “tuna bond” revelation involved a more modest revision but triggered the sharpest repricing of any episode, with spreads jumping by roughly 700 basis points within three months (Figure 2). Mozambique's case stands out because the borrowing appeared deliberate and covert — when the loans came to light, the IMF suspended its program and donor support collapsed, compounding the market shock well beyond what the debt figures alone would have warranted.

How governments handle hidden debt after it is revealed matters as much as the revelation itself. We split the episodes into two groups: those where authorities promptly reconciled the newly revealed liabilities, with independent validation within a year (Dominican Republic, Türkiye, Ecuador, and Pakistan), and those where the true debt picture remained contested or the audit process dragged on (Zambia, Mozambique, and Senegal).

The difference is stark. Where reconciliation was prompt, spreads rose about 123 basis points after 60 days, and much of the initial increase later reversed. Where it was delayed or contested, spreads climbed about 324 basis points and remained elevated for longer (Figure 3). Markets price not only the debt they see but also the uncertainty about what else might still be hidden. Prompt, verifiable disclosure helps close that uncertainty; delay keeps it alive and costly.

With only seven episodes, the evidence on the role of reconciliation should be viewed as suggestive. But the pattern points to an important policy implication. Hidden debt is costly the moment it surfaces, but those costs are not sealed at the point of revelation — what governments do in the days and weeks that follow also matters. Markets are not simply pricing a larger debt stock; their response may also depend on how much they trust the numbers still on the page. A government that moves quickly and invites independent verification can help limit the increase in borrowing costs, while one that delays faces more persistent market repricing. The lesson is not only that transparency can reduce the risks associated with hidden debt — it may also help contain the costs once hidden liabilities come to light.
For further details, please see Sovereign Risk Repricing after Hidden-Debt Revelations .

articles.title: Making Student Reflection More Meaningful
paragraphs: Exit tickets, learning journals, and self-assessments have become familiar classroom practices, but how often do students have opportunities to use what they’ve learned from those tools in a meaningful way? We ask students to identify what went well, where they struggled, and what they might do differently, but recognizing these things doesn’t necessarily mean students know how to apply that information to future learning.

A student might recognize that a particular approach didn’t work but not understand why, or identify a successful strategy without recognizing when to use it again. Working to help students develop metacognitive skills requires us to move beyond reflection and help learners understand their own thinking, evaluate the strategies they’ve used, and make informed decisions when they encounter new challenges.

From my experience implementing these strategies with students and supporting teachers in using them in their own classrooms, I’ve found that the following four approaches can help develop metacognitive skills as part of everyday instruction, without adding lengthy reflection activities.
1. Help Students Notice What’s Happening in Their Thinking

Before students can make decisions about their learning, they need opportunities to recognize what’s happening as they work. Encourage your students to notice moments of confusion or changes in their understanding while they’re still engaged in a task.

For example, during a reading lesson, ask students to mark a passage where they lost track of the author’s argument. After reading, have them return to that section and consider what caused the confusion. Was the vocabulary unfamiliar? Did the author introduce a new idea? Did they make an assumption that turned out to be incorrect?

Once students identify the source of their confusion, teachers can help them consider which strategy might address it. For example, a student might realize that they understand the individual points an author makes but struggle to see how those ideas connect. Rather than simply rereading the passage, the student might map the relationship between the ideas or examine how the author’s reasoning develops across the text.

The ultimate goal is for students to develop the metacognitive skills to recognize when they’re confused, understand what’s causing the difficulty, and decide how to use that information to move forward .
2. Ask Students to Explain the Decisions They Made While Learning

Occasionally, students will be successful at a task but not understand why. If we ask those students to explain the strategies they used and how those decisions affected their work, it can help them recognize if their approach was worthwhile and when they might want to try something different in the future.

For example, in math, students might compare two ways of solving a problem and explain why they chose one approach over the other, and then say if their choice helped them solve the problem effectively.

Teachers can also help support this process by modeling their own thinking. When working through a difficult problem, a teacher can explain why they’re choosing a particular approach, how they’re determining whether it’s working, and what they might try if they become stuck. Hearing these decisions modeled can help students understand how experienced learners evaluate their progress and adjust their approach when needed.
3. Give students evidence to evaluate their understanding

Students sometimes feel confident about what they’ve learned but struggle to demonstrate that understanding independently. Helping students recognize the difference between knowledge and understanding gives them a more accurate picture of what they know and where they need additional support.

One approach is to ask students to predict how well they’ll do on a brief task before completing it independently. For example, in a writing assignment, students might predict how well a drafted paragraph meets two or three criteria before reviewing it against a rubric or checklist. Comparing their initial judgments with the evidence in their work helps them identify strengths, recognize gaps, and decide what needs further attention.

The initial prediction can take less than a minute, with students rating how well they think they’ll meet a few criteria. After completing the task, they can spend another minute or two comparing their prediction with their actual work and considering what they learned about their understanding.
This type of brief check helps students move from how well they think they understand something to using evidence from their own work to evaluate their learning.
4. Help students turn reflection into a specific next step

Recognizing what went well or where they struggled is only useful if students learn to apply that information the next time they do a task. Teachers can help by asking students to identify one specific change they’ll make the next time they encounter a similar task.

Instead of having students complete a reflection after every assignment, consider asking them to look at an earlier reflection before beginning a similar task. For example, before starting a new writing assignment, students could review feedback and reflections from their previous work, select one piece of feedback and decide how they want to approach the new assignment differently, and explain why. After completing the new assignment, they could compare the two pieces to determine whether that change made a difference.

Teachers might also periodically ask students to review several reflections or exit tickets from different assignments and look for patterns in their own understanding. A student who repeatedly struggles to support an argument with evidence, for example, might recognize that the difficulty isn’t limited to one assignment. Rather than students seeing this as something they’re simply not good at, teachers can help them look more closely at their work to figure out where they’re getting stuck. They might notice that they’re choosing evidence that doesn’t quite support their argument or that they need to work on explaining the connection between their evidence and their claims. This gives students something specific to work on rather than leaving them feeling that they’re just not good at writing.

Reflection gives students an opportunity to consider what happened during learning, but it shouldn’t end with identifying what went well or what was difficult. Students also need opportunities to use those insights to make decisions about how to approach similar challenges. This doesn’t require lengthy activities or separate lessons, as even brief conversations with the whole class, a partner, or a teacher can help students consider what they’ve learned about their thinking and how they might use that understanding in the future.

articles.title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
paragraphs: 01 Science funders and societies

We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program , which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.

We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)

Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute , a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.

AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:
The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.

Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.

Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.

The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.

CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.

Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:

Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.

Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.

EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.

Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.
Research projects and initiatives

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:

FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.

LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.

AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.

gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.

Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.

As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

articles.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
paragraphs: Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren, Alex Tamkin

When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call.

We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded.

Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead.

Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed.

Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment.

We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. Real agents will sometimes lean one way or another—with no lean assigned, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 out of 123 runs—but in this case we strengthened their preferences on purpose to measure their effect. When agents aren’t given clear preferences and instructions to voice them, the effect might be smaller.

This isn’t a simple cautionary tale against working with AI. Analysts who used the agent finished the task faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who chose to work without it, although the latter group was small and less experienced, so we are wary of reading too much into it. But as AI takes over more of the hands-on work, decisions like these are increasingly where human judgment and values will affect the result. If experts defer to agents without realizing it, the agents’ preferences—which could be arbitrary or misaligned—could shape important decisions about policy proposals or research directions without anyone having chosen those preferences. This is particularly important for research into keeping AI safe. Researchers have begun using agents to run and analyze experiments and a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own.

We recruited 61 analysts for a randomized controlled trial. All came from a pre-screened pool of professionals who had passed a causal-inference knowledge check, used the programming languages Python or R regularly, and had hands-on experience with observational causal analysis, which means studying cause and effect using real-world data rather than a controlled experiment.

The task was set at a fictional organization, the Greenfields Farming Cooperative, which runs an (equally fictitious) voluntary, paid advisory program to help its member farms improve their crop yields. About 40% of members have enrolled. The co-op’s board must decide whether to subsidize and expand the program, or discontinue it. The board will expand the program only if it improves farms’ productivity by a set margin, roughly 3–4%, but it doesn’t say exactly how productivity should be measured.
We deliberately left four analytical decisions open, each with two reasonable options:
Outcome : measure productivity as crop yield per hectare, or as yield per unit of operating cost?

Comparison method : look at how enrolled farms’ yields changed after joining compared with how other farms’ yields changed over the same period (a “difference-in-differences” design), or compare yields directly while adjusting statistically for differences between the farms?
Which farms the assessment covers : measure the effect only in the enrolled farms, or across the cooperative’s entire membership?
Weighting : count every farm equally, or give larger producers more weight?
These four choices led into a final recommendation: whether to roll out the program to everyone, or to discontinue it. Analysts and agents could also propose a one-year extension.
Each of the analytical decisions could move the estimated productivity gain by several percentage points, which is important when the board’s threshold is 3–4%.

For each of the five decisions presented to each analyst, the agent’s lean was set by a coin flip. We gave the agent its leans in hidden instructions (a system prompt) that told it to hold each lean as its own view, to raise it when the decision came up, and to make the strongest case for it that the data allowed. The same instructions told it to change its mind if the evidence turned decisively against it, and never to misrepresent results, hide data, or make an argument the numbers didn’t support.

Out of 61 participants, 11 chose not to use the agent and are left out of the analysis unless noted. Among the remaining 50, 65% held a master’s or doctorate or had six or more years of experience, and 90% rated themselves proficient or expert in observational causal inference (of the 48 who answered the survey). The median time on the task was 65 minutes, and half of the analysts took between 50 and 79 minutes. They worked in a web-based version of the VS Code editor with Claude Code built in, running Claude Opus 4.8 at High effort.

When they finished, analysts submitted their four analytical choices and their final recommendation alongside an estimate of the program’s effect on productivity, with a confidence interval. They then completed a post-task survey. A separate AI model read each submission and its code to record which option the analyst had chosen on each decision. Where its reading disagreed with the analyst’s own survey answer, we made the final call.

Analysts mostly went with their agents’ lean. On each of the four analytical decisions, analysts’ choices matched their agents’ lean the large majority of the time: 92% for the outcome measure, 82% for the comparison method, 81% for which farms the estimate covered, and 90% for weighting. Across all four combined, the result was 86%. Figure 2 shows how much the agents’ lean shifted analysts’ choices on each decision, including the final recommendation.

Agents’ lean had a weaker effect on the final recommendation, but its earlier input still shaped the result. When the agent leaned toward rolling out the program, 54% of analysts recommended it, compared with 36% when it leaned the other way. (A one-year extension counts as not rolling out.) We think the effect was weaker because, once the analysts had their estimate, the recommendation largely followed from whether it cleared the board’s 3–4% threshold, which left less room for judgment. But by then, an agent’s lean on the analytical decisions had already shaped the estimate itself. Using only those four leans, a statistical model correctly predicted 82% of the analysts’ recommendations, compared with 61% for always guessing the most common recommendation. (This excludes analysts who proposed an extension.) So we could largely predict what an analyst would recommend from the coin flips alone, before they had even started the task.

Analysts who had already picked an option often switched when their agent disagreed. In 38 cases, an analyst had expressed a preference on one of the analytical decisions before the agent expressed its lean. When the lean went against their choice, they switched 60% of the time, compared with 6% when it agreed with their choice. That’s a gap of 54 percentage points, but because this rests on only 38 cases, the estimate is imprecise, and the 95% confidence interval runs from 24 to 82 percentage points. We also can’t be sure that the difference is caused by the AI’s influence: the analysts who expressed a preference may have been systematically different in some way from those who didn’t.

Experience and expertise did not predict who deferred. In an exploratory analysis, we checked whether any of 10 characteristics predicted how often analysts’ decisions followed their agents’ lean: years of experience, self-rated expertise in causal inference, education, score on a causal-inference quiz, trust in AI, how often they used AI, “need for cognition” (a measure of how much people enjoy effortful thinking), open-mindedness, gender, and age. Only age showed a statistically significant link, with older analysts following the lean more often. But we don’t read very much into that: if you test many different things, you’re more likely to get one positive result just by chance, and when we adjusted for that the result disappeared. Because most analysts followed their agent on most decisions, there was little variation to explain anyway, so even real differences would have been hard to detect.

Analysts who followed their agent’s lean still called the recommendation their own. On the post-task survey, 52% of analysts rated the final recommendation as more their own than their agent’s. The rest said it was more the agent’s recommendation. But both groups were roughly equally influenced by their agents: the former’s choices shifted about 65 percentage points toward their agents’ lean, on average, compared to 79 percentage points for the latter, a difference within the margin of error. Analysts’ confidence in their own recommendation showed a similar pattern. They were asked to rate their confidence from 0 (“it’s a coin flip”) to 100 (“I’d stake my professional reputation on it”). Those who followed the lean on all four analytical decisions averaged 71, compared to 73 for the rest.

Analysts explained their choices in their agent’s words. After the task, the survey asked about each decision: “Briefly, why that choice rather than the alternative? If it wasn’t an active choice, just say so.” Analysts couldn’t look back at their conversations with the agent while answering. Even so, 77% repeated their agent’s argument in at least one answer, sometimes word for word, and only 15% credited the agent anywhere.

When explicitly asked what they thought the study was about, six of the 48 correctly guessed that it was about the AI’s influence on their choices, but none suspected that the AI’s own preferences had been manipulated.

Analysts who worked without AI made more serious errors and took longer. Of the 11 participants who chose not to use the agent, six (55%) made serious methodological errors that invalidated their results, compared with three of the 50 (6%) who did use it. Two AI models flagged the errors, and one of the study’s authors checked each one without knowing which group the analyst was in. The analysts who worked without an agent also took longer, with a median time of 90 minutes, compared to 65 for the others.

The two groups were not directly comparable, so we can’t be sure whether the different outcomes were caused by the decision to use or not use AI. Those who worked without AI were less experienced on average: fewer held a master’s degree or a doctorate (four out of 11, compared to 24 out of 46 who used the agent), more had two years or less in analysis roles (six out of 11, compared to 15 out of 48), and fewer rated themselves proficient or expert in causal inference (eight of 11, compared to 43 out of 48).

We deliberately strengthened the agents’ lean. Our instructions made the agent hold and voice a preference reliably, so that we could measure its effect. The rates we report show what happens when an agent leans one way and says so, but how much that applies to real-world work will depend on how strong the expert’s own views are, how clearly the decisions involved are defined, and how the model behaves, including whether it has a preference and whether it volunteers it.

We studied one task, in one field, with one model. The task took about an hour, it was specifically about farming, and the agent ran on Claude Opus 4.8. The analysts were experts in causal inference but new to farming. In real work, they would know the field better, and probably have stronger views of their own. They could also interview relevant people, talk to the board, and in other ways narrow down the reasonable options, which might reduce the agent’s influence.

Our estimates are averages across analysts. Because the coin flips differed between analysts, comparing analysts whose agents leaned in opposite ways tells us the lean’s average effect. We didn’t record each participant’s own view before the agent voiced its lean, so we can’t say how much any single participant was influenced.

We recorded which option analysts chose, but not how strongly they preferred it. One possible explanation for deferring is that the expert didn’t have strong opinions of their own. We measured only whether analysts’ choices shifted, not how confident they were in their choice.

One reason analysts deferred so readily may be that experts don’t always arrive with their views fully formed. They often work out, or even discover , what they think while weighing the options. The agents in our study were told not to mislead, and they were often open about how the results would change under each option. But they rarely made a strong case for why an expert might prefer the other option, which might have helped analysts make a better-informed choice. With only one side argued well, the analysts could adopt the agent’s assumptions without working out their own.

For individual experts, this could mean losing agency over their own work, a form of what researchers call disempowerment . The work still goes out under the expert’s name, but the decisions that most depend on their judgment are in reality settled by the agent’s prior beliefs.

The stakes extend beyond individuals, though, because so much of science and policy rests on judgment calls like these. When separate research teams reach the same result, we trust it more, because we assume each team reached it independently. If those teams all defer to models with the same preferences, their agreement may no longer be independent . An apparent consensus might reflect one model’s preferences, and if those preferences are arbitrary or misaligned, the same bias would shape many results at once.

The same problem applies to AI safety research. Researchers have begun to use AI agents to run and analyze experiments, in part because there is more work than human staff can keep up with. Keeping a human in the loop assumes that the human’s judgment provides an independent check. But in our study, analysts signed off on work in which judgment calls had largely been settled by the agent’s randomly assigned preferences. Our full paper also shows that agents without an assigned lean have weaker preferences of their own, and sometimes push back against users.

Deferral of this kind is hard to detect. Checking AI-assisted work for errors, or against a reference answer, assumes there is a correct answer. But where there isn’t one, as in judgment calls, the work can look sound whichever option is chosen. Asking experts afterward may not help either, because they may not notice the agent’s influence.
This isn’t an argument for using AI less. Used well, AI could expand people’s agency rather than eroding it. We suggest three areas for future study:

Measuring deferral. We could measure deferral in our study because we randomized the agent’s lean, which is rarely possible in real work, and our results suggest that people may not be able to report it accurately themselves. We need ways to measure it in everyday settings, and recent work that estimates how someone would have carried out a task without AI is a good start. We also need a better picture of models’ default preferences and how they express them, so that people can engage with models in a more informed way.

Designing agents differently. Agents could make the best case for each option, or ask experts for their own view before offering one. But this could quickly become overwhelming for users. A single analysis can involve many open decisions, and much of the value of AI is that people don’t have to think through each one. Agents would need to raise only the decisions that matter most, but picking those is itself a judgment call. How a model speaks probably matters too, since confidence and fluency can sway people. A model that sounds very sure of itself might tilt people more than is warranted, but a mealy-mouthed model will just irritate the people who try to use it.

Changing institutions. Institutions often treat an expert’s sign-off as evidence of independent judgment. As AI does more of the work, that assumption becomes shakier. Organizations will need to decide deliberately which decisions need a person’s own informed judgment, and give people the time and resources to form one. Judgment also depends on skill, and people who stop making these decisions may lose the ability to make them. As models become more capable, institutions will need an explicit strategy for establishing the role of humans and the development of their skills . Even with extremely capable AI systems, institutions may want to protect human skills and oversight for reasons of safety or resilience, or because they value them for their own sake.

There may be no single right division of labor between people and AI. Some decisions may be fine to hand over, and others worth keeping. With the right tools, that split can be something we choose, instead of something we drift into.
This project was led by Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren, and Alex Tamkin. Editorial support for this blog post was provided by Tom Chivers and Arjun Panickssery.

We would like to thank Joe Benton, Mojmir Stehlik, and Avery Griffin for making this project possible through the Anthropic Fellows Program. We would also like to thank Matthew Jörke, Onur Altındağ, and Vishakh Padmakumar for experimental design feedback.

World Bank Group Helps Improve Pre-primary and Primary Education in Bangladesh
https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/11/06/world-bank-group-helps-improve-pre-primary-and-primary-education-in-bangladesh

WASHINGTON, November 6, 2026 — The World Bank Group’s Board of Executive Directors today approved $300 million in financing to improve learning outcomes for 26 million children studying in pre-primary level to grade 5 in Bangladesh.

The Learning Enhancement and Acceleration in Primary Education Program will help Bangladesh improve its pre-primary and primary education system. It will help children acquire essential skills in reading, writing, and mathematics as per their grade level. The program will support implementation of the government’s Fifth Primary Education Development Program.

While Bangladesh achieved near-universal access to primary schooling, quality of education remains a significant challenge. About 50 percent of 10-year-olds are unable to read and understand a simple, age-appropriate text, as compared to upper-middle-income countries, such as Malaysia at 42 percent and Brazil at 47 percent.

“Quality primary education is one of the building blocks for a globally competitive workforce,” said Jean Pesme, World Bank Division Director for Bangladesh and Bhutan . ‘For the last two decades, the World Bank Group helped Bangladesh bring nearly all children to school. This financing will help children to learn better and stay at the school, creating the foundation for getting better jobs later in their lives.”

The primary education system in Bangladesh is one of the largest in the world with more than 20 million children in government schools, NGO schools, kindergartens and madrasas. The program will roll out a foundational literacy and numeracy package, with teaching materials, structured lesson plans and teacher training. The program will also support leadership training for headteachers in 90% government primary schools and strengthen school management systems.

“Strong foundational learning is a critical step towards the accumulation of skills for better jobs. To ensure that no children are left behind, the program will support remedial learning for children who are falling behind, with a focus on districts that lag the furthest,” said Tashmina Rahman, World Bank Senior Education Specialist and Team Leader for the program . ‘It will also support better teacher and school leadership, more accountable use of budgets and stronger use of data to guide decisions.”

The program will provide training and support to primary teachers to deliver better foundational literacy and numeracy lessons in the classrooms of in government schools. It is expected to improve the quality of pre-primary education in government primary schools to ensure children have a strong start in learning and improved school readiness. It is envisaged that this program will generate 843,000 more and better-paid jobs in government primary schools.

The program received financing from the International Development Association (IDA), part of the World Bank Group that helps lower-income countries and has a has a 25-year term, including a five-year grace period.

paragraphs: International community calls for increased and sustainable financing for education

On 29 October 2026, UNESCO New York participated in the interactive dialogue with Farida Shaheed, Special Rapporteur on the right to education, following the presentation of her report titled Obstacles to realizing the right to education under the international financial architecture .
Interactive Dialogue on global financial architecture and education as a public good

The Special Rapporteur emphasized that sustained public financing is essential to realizing the right to education. Drawing on UNESCO ’s and UNCTAD ’s analysis, the Special Rapporteur described the current debt crisis as “one of the most significant barriers to adequate education financing” highlighting how debt servicing, austerity frameworks and unequal tax governance constrain countries’ fiscal space to invest in education. According to UNESCO, additional US$97 billion are needed annually to achieve national SDG 4 targets in low- and lower-middle-income countries. This deficit would require greater public investment in education, including through stronger domestic resource mobilization, fairer taxation, international cooperation and debt relief.

During the interactive dialogue, Lily Gray, UNESCO Senior Liaison Officer, welcomed the report as an important basis for collective action and reaffirmed education financing as a central priority for UNESCO. Her intervention underscored UNESCO’s support to governments through policy advice, technical assistance and practical tools, as well as through targeted advocacy for sustained public investment in education.  While recognizing that debt swaps cannot replace comprehensive debt relief or concessional financing, UNESCO also provides policy guidance on debt-for-education swaps that helps governments assess opportunities to fund national education priorities. In this context, UNESCO will continue working with the Special Rapporteur and partners to align financing and debt solutions with nationally defined development strategies and build wider ownership of the report’s recommendations among those shaping fiscal and financing policy.

Looking ahead, UNESCO’s representative highlighted the forthcoming Global Education Meeting in Bangkok, from 31 March to 2 April 2027 , as an important opportunity to carry forward this partnership and strengthen collective action on education financing.

In her response, the Special Rapporteur called for stronger coordination between financial institutions and education actors to ensure that decisions affecting public sector employment are informed by the data from by UNESCO and ministries of education on critical teacher shortages . Globally, an 44 million teachers will be needed by 2030 .  She further noted that the IMF and World Bank increasingly recognise the need to protect education and social spending although that has yet to be consistently reflected in financing negotiations and policies at the country level.
UNESCO and global financing architecture for education

UNESCO is at the forefront of global efforts to strengthen education financing, supporting countries through research, policy advise and monitoring to ensure education resources are mobilized and used more sustainably and equitably.   At a time when many education systems face mounting fiscal constraints, the organization is advocating for greater investment in public education and more coherent financing policies. The importance of this agenda is reflected in SDG 4 High-Level Steering Committee 2026–2027 priorities, which place resilient and well-financed education systems at the centre of efforts to achieve quality education for all.

paragraphs: Accelerating engineering for the physical world

Today, we’re sharing advances in how OpenAI models help engineers design, simulate, and build physical products. These capabilities span mechanical and electrical engineering and end-to-end system design, and are already helping our internal teams test ideas and iterate faster.

Across these projects, engineers need to bring together mechanical designs, electronics, software, and manufacturing requirements using specialized tools. We’re teaching models to support that work, from preparing drawings and setting up simulations to coordinating changes across disciplines. Our goal is to give engineers more time to explore ideas and improve designs.

Over the past year, improved frontier model capabilities have helped our internal teams test new ideas and iterate faster, and we are seeing early evidence of these capabilities improving professional workflows in industry as well. We’re working with collaborators to understand where these capabilities can make the biggest difference and what needs to improve. If you’re an engineer, engineering firm, or software vendor involved in the design, simulation, manufacturing, or production of complex physical products, we’d love to work with you to shape this effort around the tools you use and the problems you need to solve.

We tested Astra’s state-of-the-art performance ⁠ in multimodal and computer use workflows by seeing if we can create a device without any direct human edits. To do this, we used GPT‑6 to define the functional requirements and design the enclosure, printed circuit board (PCB), and software integrations needed to create a device users can use to talk to Codex.
Aesthetics and design: Astra developed the look of the device, drawing on our recent Work Louder ⁠ (opens in a new window) collaboration and references from games and toys.
Aesthetics and design: Astra developed the look of the device, drawing on our recent Work Louder ⁠ (opens in a new window) collaboration and references from games and toys.
Mechanical design: Astra designed the enclosure ⁠ (opens in a new window) and the internal structures that hold the components in place.
Mechanical design: Astra designed the enclosure ⁠ (opens in a new window) and the internal structures that hold the components in place.
Electrical design: Astra selected the electrical components and designed the printed circuit board (PCB), including component placement and connections, to fit within the enclosure.
Electrical design: Astra selected the electrical components and designed the printed circuit board (PCB), including component placement and connections, to fit within the enclosure.
UI/UX and software: Astra designed the user interface and generated the firmware and software integrations needed to connect the device to Codex.
UI/UX and software: Astra designed the user interface and generated the firmware and software integrations needed to connect the device to Codex.
Two team members designed this test device with Astra in under a week while working on it as a side project. A contract manufacturer built a small batch of prototypes in under a month.

Getting the device ready for manufacturing still required several rounds of review and iteration. Astra did not consistently account for the manufacturer’s production limits, tolerances, or details required for assembly. These gaps are helping us identify what future models need to do better.
Accelerating OpenAI hardware teams

OpenAI’s hardware and infrastructure teams use Codex and ChatGPT to create and revise computer-aided design (CAD) models, prepare manufacturing drawings, set up simulations, and review designs. This work spans robotics and compute infrastructure. Since February, model usage across our hardware teams, measured in tokens, has grown 23-fold.
— Grace Lam, Forward Deployed Engineer at OpenAI
— Qiong Wang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI
— Jackie Lee, Member of Infrastructure Staff at OpenAI
— Grace Lam, Forward Deployed Engineer at OpenAI
— Qiong Wang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI
— Jackie Lee, Member of Infrastructure Staff at OpenAI
Measuring progress on engineering tasks

We’re also measuring progress in newer models on tasks that combine coding with engineering knowledge. BenchCAD 2.0 tests whether models can reconstruct 3D parts and assemblies and identify connections in circuit boards. A newer internal model achieved an average score of 0.875, compared with 0.594 for GPT‑6 Astra at its highest reasoning setting. While the engineering lifecycle includes many other elements beyond design, we view improvements in capability here as early evidence of the ability of AI models to positively impact iteration speed for professional workflows.
Safely deploying with industry collaborators

We’re working with a small group of industry collaborators to test these capabilities on real engineering problems. Their engineers review model outputs for accuracy and practical use, helping us understand which tasks models can support today and what needs to be improved for safe and reliable use.

We’re expanding our collaboration with Chip Ganassi Racing (CGR) to explore how OpenAI models can accelerate engineering and prototyping. Working with its R&D team, we’re testing workflows that turn 3D scans of existing parts into editable CAD models and 2D manufacturing drawings. This is particularly useful when the original design files are unavailable.
CGR engineers review the models and drawings for accuracy and manufacturability. Their feedback helps us identify where models can reduce manual work and where further improvements are needed.

We’re also announcing a new research collaboration with Mazda. Our research and Forward Deployed Engineering teams are working with Mazda’s aerodynamics and crash-safety engineers to explore how OpenAI models can help develop and evaluate new vehicle designs.
The work uses simulations of airflow and structural behavior to explore improvements in performance while accounting for styling and cost. We’ll share more progress and results in the coming months.

GPT‑6 Astra helps Mazda’s aerodynamics engineers explore ways to reduce vehicle drag by modeling new nose shapes, simulating airflow, and refining the most promising designs. Agreement for use has been obtained from Mazda Motor Corporation. Any republication or reuse elsewhere is strictly prohibited.
Help shape AI for engineering and manufacturing

We have been working closely with industry partners and early adopters to push the bounds of what we can do with AI agents in hardware and manufacturing. These early results have shown exciting promise, and we’re now looking for collaborators to accelerate these capability improvements and ensure we deploy these safely into industry.

articles.title: Comparing self-regulation, anxiety, and willingness to communicate across blended, face-to-face, and online instruction in female EFL learners
paragraphs: Comparing self-regulation, anxiety, and willingness to communicate across blended, face-to-face, and online instruction in female EFL learners
Haige Shi · Vida Salimi · Siros Izadpanah
Received: 19 September 2025 / Accepted: 5 November 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Technology-enhanced language instruction has expanded the range of instructional options available to EFL learners, yet evidence comparing blended, online, and face-to-face modes across multiple cognitive and affec­ tive outcomes remains limited, particularly among advanced EFL learners. This study compared self-regulated learning strategies (SRLSs), foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA), and willingness to communicate (WTC) in English writing across these three instructional modes. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was conducted with 360 advanced female EFL learners in Iran (120 per group), selected through two-stage cluster sampling from language institutes. Learners participated in 10 instructional sessions delivered through blended, online, or face-to-face modes. Pre-test and post-test measures of SRLS, FLCA, and WTC were col­ lected using self-report questionnaires. One-way ANCOVAs were conducted for each outcome, controlling for the corresponding pre-test score, followed by Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. After adjustment for baseline scores, statistically significant between-group differences were observed for SRLS, FLCA, and WTC. The blended group had higher adjusted SRLS scores than the online and face-to-face groups (partial η² = 0.411) and higher adjusted WTC scores in English writing (partial η² = 0.266), but lower adjusted FLCA scores than both comparison groups (partial η² = 0.136). No statistically significant differences were observed between the online and face-to-face groups for any outcome. These findings identify a consistent pattern of adjusted between-group differences associated with instructional mode among advanced female Iranian EFL learners. They do not establish comparative efficacy or causal superiority of blended instruction. Pending replication using randomized designs, objective measures, and more diverse samples, the findings may inform further investigation of blended instructional arrangements and the specific pedagogical features associated with learner outcomes.

Keywords Blended learning · EFL learners · Face-to-face instruction · Foreign language classroom anxiety · Online learning · Self-regulated learning strategies · Willingness to communicate · Writing skills
