Introduction

Writing plays a central role in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning because it is essential for academic achievement and participation in global knowledge communities1–3. Developing effective EFL writing extends beyond linguistic competence and relies heavily on psychological and affective processes such as motivation, emotion regulation, and engagement. These demands are intensified in EFL contexts, where writing tasks can heighten anxiety and reduce learners’ confidence in communicating their ideas. At the same time, advances in information and communication technologies (ICT) have reshaped writing instruction, with blended and online environments becoming increasingly common in higher education worldwide4,5. Blended learning, in particular, integrates face-to-face and digital components to enhance flexibil­ ity and interaction6. Despite growing interest in these instructional modes, limited research has examined their differential impact on key psychological constructs linked to EFL writing, self-regulated learning strategies7, foreign language class­ room anxiety8, and willingness to communicate9. To address this gap, the present study adopts an integrative conceptual framework that connects these constructs with the affordances and demands of different instructional contexts. Connectivism provides the first pillar of this framework by conceptualizing online and blended environments as digital learning ecologies in which learners access distributed knowledge, interact through networks, and learn by forming connections10. Sociocultural Theory complements this view by emphasizing how writing develop­ ment is mediated through interaction, feedback, and scaffolded support within instructional settings11. Within these social and digital contexts, Self-Regulated Learning Theory explains how learners manage writing pro­ cesses through planning, monitoring, and revising7. Self-Determination Theory further clarifies how autonomy- supportive conditions shape motivation, anxiety, and sustained engagement in writing tasks12. Taken together, these perspectives form a coherent conceptual model in which instructional context, interactional processes, and learner psychology jointly influence EFL writing performance. This study treats face-to-face (FTF), blended (BL), and online modes as delivery systems rather than fixed pedagogical approaches, as each can accommodate diverse instructional orientations. Their distinction lies pri­ marily in the modality and quantity of learner–teacher and learner–peer interaction4, making them suitable con­ texts for examining how learning environments shape SRLS, FLCA, and WTC in writing. Because concurrent multi-group comparisons across cognitive and affective dimensions remain sparse among advanced female EFL learners, this study seeks to offer incremental empirical insights into how these delivery environments associate with learners’ self-regulation, writing anxiety, and willingness to communicate in writing.
Literature review
Blended learning

Blended instruction combined physical and digital modalities to operationalize constructivist interaction and con­ nectivist resource networking within the specific design rather than claiming theoretical universality13. Research shows that social interaction in FTF classes promotes motivation and engagement, while digital elements offer flexibility14. These psychological constructs play a central role in learner success. Theoretical perspectives such as connectivism and sociocultural frameworks highlight how these factors function in blended settings15,16. Despite extensive research on these constructs individually, few studies have examined how their interrelations vary across learning modes. Some findings remain inconclusive: while17 reported improved engagement and lower anxiety in blended contexts18, observed high dropout rates when digital and in-person components were
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z Article in Press
poorly aligned. These inconsistencies underscore the need to evaluate BL not as a uniform innovation but as a complex system shaped by design quality, learner agency, and contextual support.
Online learning

Online learning delivers instruction entirely through digital platforms without FTF contact19. It offers flexibility through LMSs and video conferencing but may heighten anxiety and lower WTC because of reduced immediate interaction20. Dependence on self-reports and short-term studies limits understanding of how psychological fac­ tors evolve in online environments. Moreover, online learning is often treated as a uniform experience, overlook­ ing how learner proficiency, cultural background, and gender shape experiences and outcomes. Contradictory findings illustrate this complexity: while20 found that online environments enhance self-regulation21, reported heightened anxiety and reduced motivation among EFL learners in purely virtual settings. These divergent results highlight the importance of hybrid approaches that balance flexibility with social presence.
Face-to-face learning

Face-to-face (FTF) instruction involves direct teacher–student interaction22,23 and, in EFL contexts, is informed by Communicative Language Teaching and Sociocultural Theory, emphasizing authentic, socially mediated learn­ ing21,24. Face-to-face sessions, principles analogous to Communicative Language Teaching and Sociocultural mediation guided interaction, though these approaches were not assumed to underpin all FTF practices gener­ ally. Since the 1970s, communicative approaches have positioned teachers as facilitators who provide immedi­ ate feedback and promote peer collaboration25. While FTF enhances social engagement, it lacks flexibility and scalability, prompting BL, which integrates FTF interaction with digital platforms to support student-centered, autonomous learning. Grounded in constructivist principles, BL fosters active, collaborative learning, though implementation often suffers from limited planning, governance, and faculty development26.
Self-regulated learning strategies

Self-regulated learning strategies (SRLSs) involve managing cognition, motivation, and behavior to achieve academic goals7, encompassing metacognition, motivation, and strategic action27. By identifying strengths, addressing weaknesses, and adapting strategies, learners progress from teacher-directed to autonomous, lifelong learning28,29. SRL is especially important in blended and online settings, where students must self-manage time and motivation. It predicts online achievement30, supports MOOC success through goal setting and effort regu­ lation31, and mediates motivation–outcome links32. This study examines SRL across blended, FTF, and online modes to clarify its role in autonomy and engagement.
Willingness to communicate

Willingness to communicate (WTC) reflects a learner’s readiness to engage in second-language interaction21 and influences both comprehensible input33 and output34. WTC is a strong predictor of language learning success35. E-learning shows mixed effects on WTC, self-regulation, and anxiety36. BL often enhances self-regulation, reduces anxiety, and fosters WTC37. Few studies have directly compared blended, online, and FTF instruction regarding WTC in EFL writing.
Foreign language classroom anxiety

Foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA) refers to the fear and negative emotions associated with learning or using a foreign language8,38. It affects learners’ attitudes, emotions, and behaviors and is a well-known barrier
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z

to language acquisition39. Reducing FLCA is crucial for fostering willingness to communicate, yet strategies to address it across instructional contexts remain underexplored. In line with the principles of Social Constructiv­ ism40 and Self-Determination Theory12, this study views SRLSs, FLCA, and WTC as theoretically related con­ structs shaped by social interaction and individual motivation. In this design, however, they were analyzed as separate outcomes; no mediation, moderation, or structural models were conducted. From a social constructivist perspective, BL facilitates collaborative knowledge construction and scaffolding, enhancing communicative con­ fidence and autonomy. Self-Determination Theory further explains how blended environments satisfy learners’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, thereby reducing anxiety and increasing engagement. This integrative theoretical framework illustrates how blended learning (BL) was associated with higher SRLS scores, lower reported FLCA levels, and greater WTC in English writing. As illustrated in Fig. 1, instructional modes provide distinct learning environments characterized by differing interactional opportunities, access to networked resources, motivational affordances, and strategic self-management processes.
Interrelationships among self-regulation, anxiety, and willingness to communicate in writing

The focal constructs represent complementary cognitive, affective, and communicative dimensions of language learning. Effective self-regulation (SRLS) enables learners to plan, monitor, and manage cognitive resources dur­ ing complex tasks7, which can alleviate classroom anxiety8. Reduced anxiety, in turn, fosters higher perceived communicative competence and situational readiness to engage in target-language interaction9. Conversely, heightened anxiety may deplete regulatory bandwidth and suppress communicative participation. Instructional delivery modes provide distinct affordances and constraints for these dynamic processes. While blended and online environments offer autonomy, asynchronous reflection, and digital connectivity (Connectivism), face-to- face settings provide immediate social scaffolding and direct interpersonal feedback (Sociocultural Theory11.
Fig. 1 Integrative theoretical framework.
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z Article in Press

Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000), these three constructs are examined as conceptu­ ally related yet analytically distinct outcomes across delivery configurations. Although self-regulated learning, foreign language anxiety, and willingness to communicate have been stud­ ied separately, few studies explore their interaction in EFL writing across instructional modes. With the rise of blended and online learning, understanding how these environments affect learners’ psychological engagement is crucial. This study examines these constructs together across face-to-face, blended, and online contexts to provide an integrated view of how instructional modes shape key psychological factors in EFL writing. Based on these gaps, this study seeks to answer the following research questions:
Research questions

RQ1. Are there significant differences in self-regulated learning strategies among advanced female EFL learners receiving blended, face-to-face, and online instruction, after controlling for pretest scores? RQ2. Are there significant differences in foreign language classroom anxiety among advanced female EFL learners receiving blended, face-to-face, and online instruction, after controlling for pretest scores? RQ3. Are there significant differences in willingness to communicate in English writing among advanced female EFL learners receiving blended, face-to-face, and online instruction, after controlling for pretest scores?
Methods
Participants and research design

The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group. Participants were selected using a two-stage cluster sampling method. The selected classes were assigned to blended, face-to-face, or online instruction based on institutional schedules and available facilities rather than individual randomization, preserving ecological validity. Equivalence in proficiency was confirmed with the Oxford Placement Test (OPT), ensuring comparable initial ability across groups. According to Morgan’s sample size table, a minimum sample of 360 participants was required for a population of approximately 6,700 individuals. A two-stage cluster sampling procedure was employed. In the first stage, five institutions were randomly selected from 25 language institutes in Zanjan city. In the second stage, three intact classes were selected from each participating institution. Given an average of approximately 30 students per class, approximately 450 learners were initially identified. All eligible learners completed the Oxford Placement Test (OPT), and those who did not meet the predefined proficiency criterion were excluded. The final sample comprised 360 advanced female EFL learners, with 120 learners in each instructional condition. English profi­ ciency was assessed using the Oxford Placement Test (OPT)41. The study included female learners enrolled in the participating language institutes. Because the sample was restricted to female learners, the generalizability of the findings to male and mixed-gender populations may be limited. We also clarify that the study used intact classes without individual randomization and was therefore appropriately treated as a quasi-experimental study.
Instruments
Oxford placement test (OPT)

The Oxford Placement Test (OPT) was administered before the intervention as a screening instrument to assess participants’ English proficiency and determine their eligibility for inclusion in the study. The OPT was not used as an outcome measure; therefore, it was administered only once, before the intervention, and no post-test admin­ istration was required. The version used in the present study consisted of 60 multiple-choice items assessing
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z

general English proficiency, including grammar, vocabulary, reading, and listening. Each item was scored dichot­ omously as correct or incorrect, yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating higher proficiency. Because the study targeted advanced EFL learners, item-level characteristics of the OPT were examined in the present sample. Item facility (IF), defined as the proportion of participants answering an item correctly, ranged from 0.28 to 0.72, with a mean of 0.54, indicating a moderate distribution of item difficulty and reducing the likelihood of a substantial ceiling effect. Item discrimination (ID) was also examined to assess the ability of individual items to distinguish between participants with relatively higher and lower overall proficiency. The ID values ranged from 0.30 to 0.39, indicating acceptable item discrimination across the test items. The items were scored dichotomously; internal consistency was assessed using the Kuder–Richardson For­ mula 20 (KR-20). The obtained coefficient was 0.81, indicating satisfactory internal consistency for the present sample. The OPT was therefore used exclusively for pre-intervention proficiency screening and participant selection. Learners who met the predefined criterion for the advanced proficiency level were eligible to participate in the study. The proficiency test was not repeated after the intervention because its purpose was to establish eligibility at baseline rather than to measure instructional change.
Pre-tests
Pretests were administered to establish a baseline before the treatment. The participants in three groups were given 45 min to complete the three questionnaires (SRLS, FLCA, WTC) as the pre-test.
Post-tests
After the completion of the 10 teaching sessions, all three groups of students were asked to complete the three questionnaires again as post-tests.
Data collection
Data from the OPT, SRLSQ, WTC, and FLCA were collected at the pre- and post-tests.
Self-regulation

Self-regulation was assessed using the Academic Self-Regulated Learning Scale (ASRLS)42, comprising 55 items across seven domains: memory strategy (14), goal setting (5), self-evaluation (12), seeking assistance (8), environmental structuring (4), learning responsibility (5), and planning/organizing (6). Sample items include: “I make a detailed schedule of my daily activities,” “If I am having difficulty, I seek help from an expert,” and “I use a variety of sources in making my research papers.” Responses were rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 4 = strongly agree). In the present study, the reliability of the Self-Regulated Learning Strategies (SRLS) scale and its subcomponents was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficients. At pretest, the scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency, with alpha coefficients of 0.84 for Memory Strategies, 0.83 for Self-Evaluation, 0.80 for Responsibility, 0.78 for Environmental Structuring, 0.77 for Seeking Assistance, 0.76 for Organizing, and 0.75 for Goal Setting. The 55-item total scale yielded a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.77. At posttest, the total scale demonstrated good internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.81.
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z Article in Press
Foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA)

Foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA) was assessed with an 8-item questionnaire on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree), measuring physical anxiety and feelings of confidence or nervousness in class. Two negatively worded items were reverse-scored, with higher scores indicating greater anxiety. The scale demonstrated strong internal consistency for FTF (α = 0.89) and online instruction (α = 0.85), with overall Cronbach’s α values ranging from 0.72 to 0.89 across contexts, indicating acceptable to high reliability8. In a study conducted by Yamini, the Persian version of the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (FLCAS) demonstrated high internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of.9343. In the present study, the Foreign Lan­ guage Classroom Anxiety (FLCA) scale demonstrated good internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha coef­ ficients of 0.89 at pretest and 0.79 at posttest.
The L2 willingness to communicate questionnaire (WTC)

The study used a 25-item L2 Willingness to Communicate (WTC) questionnaire assessing learners’ willing­ ness to engage in written English communication. The questionnaire was not newly developed for the present study. Seventeen items were drawn from44 classroom-based measure of L2 willingness to communicate, and the remaining eight writing-task items (Items 18–25) were taken from the questionnaire used by45 in their study of tertiary-level EFL learners’ willingness to communicate in English. The questionnaire therefore consisted entirely of previously published writing-task items. In the present study, responses were recorded on a five-point scale ranging from “Not true at all” (1) to “Very much” (5), with higher scores indicating greater willingness to engage in the specified writing activities. Content relevance was assessed through expert review, yielding a content validity ratio (CVR) of 0.99. A con­ firmatory factor analysis (CFA) was subsequently conducted to examine the hypothesized five-factor structure of the 25-item questionnaire. The CFA yielded χ²(236) = 691.07, p < .001, RMSEA = 0.073, CFI = 0.82, and GFI = 0.87. These findings indicated acceptable approximate fit according to the RMSEA, but weaker fit according to the CFI and GFI; therefore, the results were interpreted as providing partial rather than unequivocal support for the proposed five-factor structure. Given the only partial support for the hypothesized factor structure and the absence of formal measurement-invariance testing across the three instructional groups, the WTC scores were treated as an exploratory outcome measure. Accordingly, the results involving WTC were interpreted cautiously and were not taken as evidence that the questionnaire measured an equivalent latent construct across the three instructional modes. The 25-item WTC questionnaire demonstrated acceptable internal consistency at pretest (Cronbach’s α = 0.731, N = 360) and good internal consistency at posttest (Cronbach’s α = 0.830). At pretest, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficients were 0.739 for the blended-learning group, 0.715 for the online group, and 0.733 for the face-to-face group.
Procedure

All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations (Declaration of Hel­ sinki). The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Islamic Azad University of Zanjan, Iran (Approval Code: IR.IAU.Z.REC.1402.089). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their involvement in the study. Learners first completed the Oxford Placement Test (OPT), after which they par­ ticipated in three instructional conditions: face-to-face (FTF), blended, and online. The instructional intervention lasted 10 weeks and comprised 10 instructional sessions, with one session per week. Each session lasted 60 min. All three conditions covered Units 1 and 2 of Collins Writing for IELTS, while the mode of instructional delivery differed across conditions. The FTF group received all instruction in a conventional classroom setting through teacher-led instruc­ tion, guided writing practice, collaborative activities, and classroom interaction. The online group received all
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z

instructional content and learning activities through VADANA, with no face-to-face instruction. The blended group combined face-to-face classroom instruction with online learning activities delivered through VADANA. The instructional time in the blended condition was equally divided between the two modes, with 50% delivered face-to-face and 50% online. The online component included digital writing practice, asynchronous discussion, and the exchange of written work, whereas the face-to-face component involved teacher scaffolding, collabora­ tive activities, and guided writing practice. These delivery arrangements were maintained consistently across the 10-week intervention. In the blended condition, selected theory-informed features were incorporated into the instructional activities. Connectivist principles were reflected in asynchronous discussion boards and digital writing exchanges, which provided opportunities for learners to share drafts and exchange peer feedback. Face-to-face sessions incorpo­ rated collaborative group tasks, teacher scaffolding, and dialogic interaction. To support self-regulated learning, learners completed reflective logs and structured goal-setting activities after each session. These activities pro­ vided opportunities for learners to monitor their learning, reflect on their performance, and formulate goals for subsequent learning activities. Before and after the intervention, participants completed the self-regulated learning strategies questionnaire (SRLSQ), willingness-to-communicate (WTC) questionnaire, and foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA) measure. Paper-based questionnaires were administered in the FTF and blended conditions, whereas electronic questionnaires were administered in the online condition. Participation was voluntary, and confidentiality and anonymity were maintained throughout the data-collection process.
Data analysis

Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26. Descriptive statistics, including means and standard deviations, were calculated for the pre-test and post-test scores of self-regulated learning strategies (SRLSs), for­ eign language classroom anxiety (FLCA), and willingness to communicate (WTC) in English writing. One-way analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were initially conducted to examine unadjusted differences among the blended, online, and face-to-face groups at the pre-test and post-test stages. Prior to the main analyses, the assumptions underlying the statistical procedures were examined. The distri­ butions of the outcome variables were assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and inspection of the data distribution. Homogeneity of variances across the three instructional groups was evaluated using Levene’s test. The assumption of homogeneity of regression slopes was assessed by testing the interaction between the instruc­ tional group and each corresponding pre-test covariate. These assumption checks did not indicate statistically significant violations (p > .05). The primary analyses were conducted using one-way analyses of covariance (ANCOVAs), with post-test SRLSs, FLCA, and WTC scores as the dependent variables and their corresponding pre-test scores as covariates. A separate ANCOVA was performed for each outcome to compare the three instructional groups while adjusting for baseline scores. Adjusted marginal means, standard errors (SEs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated at the overall mean of the corresponding pre-test score. When the omnibus group effect was statis­ tically significant, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons were conducted to identify differences between instructional groups. Partial eta squared (ηp²) was reported as an effect-size measure for the ANCOVA effects. Statistical significance was evaluated at p < .05, with Bonferroni adjustment applied to pairwise comparisons. Because intact classes were used and learners were nested within delivery modes, the reported standard errors and significance tests should be treated as preliminary.

Results
Descriptive findings

The demographic statistics of the variables are shown in Table 1. The baseline characteristics of the three instructional groups are presented in Table 1. The mean age was 25.54 (SD = 3.12) years in the blended-learning group, 25.02 (SD = 3.43) years in the online group, and 24.85 (SD = 3.34) years in the face-to-face group. There was no statistically significant difference in age across the groups (p=.270). The corresponding pairwise standardized mean differences were small. Baseline language proficiency was similarly distributed across the groups, with mean scores of 51.06 (SD = 2.11), 50.91 (SD = 1.98), and 51.01 (SD = 2.07) for the blended-learning, online, and face-to-face groups, respectively. The overall difference was not statistically significant (p = .881), and all pairwise SMDs were neg­ ligible. Thus, the three groups showed comparable baseline distributions for age and language proficiency prior to the instructional intervention (Table 1).
Self-regulated learning (SRL) scores

Descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA results for self-regulated learning (SRL) scores are presented in Table 2. At pre-test, the mean SRL scores were 162.68 (SD = 10.61) in the blended group, 163.98 (SD = 13.70) in the online group, and 163.82 (SD = 13.89) in the face-to-face group. The one-way ANOVA showed no statistically significant difference in pre-test SRL scores across the three groups (F = 0.36, p = .696). At post-test, the mean SRL scores were 168.71 (SD = 11.36) in the blended group, 165.13 (SD = 13.18) in the online group, and 164.21 (SD = 13.86) in the face-to-face group. The post-test ANOVA indicated a statistically significant difference in SRL scores across the three instructional groups (F = 4.11, p = .017; Table 2). After controlling for pre-test self-regulated learning scores, a statistically significant difference in post-test SRL scores was observed across the three instructional groups, F(2,356) = 124.41, p < .001, partial η² = 0.411. Foreign language classroom anxiety

For foreign language classroom anxiety, the one-way ANOVA showed no statistically significant difference in pre-test scores across the blended, online, and face-to-face groups, F(2,357) = 1.26, p = .283. At post-test, the unadjusted group comparison was statistically significant, F(2,357) = 4.82, p = .009 (Table 4). A one-way ANCOVA was subsequently conducted to compare post-test FLCA scores across the three instructional groups while controlling for pre-test FLCA scores. The overall model was statistically significant, F(3,356) = 253.27, p < .001, R² = 0.68. Pre-test FLCA scores were significantly associated with post-test scores, F(1,356) = 730.45, p < .001, partial η² = 0.67. After controlling for pre-test FLCA scores, a statistically significant difference in post-test FLCA scores was observed across the three instructional groups, F(2,356) = 28.10, p < .001, partial η² = 0.136 The adjusted post-test mean FLCA score was 19.17 (SE = 0.22, 95% CI: 18.74–19.61) in the blended group, compared with 21.01 (SE = 0.22, 95% CI: 20.58–21.45) in the online group and 21.36 (SE = 0.22, 95% CI: 20.92–21.79) in the face-to-face group. Discussion

The present study compared self-regulated learning strategies (SRLSs), foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA), and willingness to communicate (WTC) in English writing among advanced female EFL learners receiv­ ing blended, online, or face-to-face instruction. After adjustment for the corresponding pre-test scores, statisti­ cally significant between-group differences were observed for all three outcomes. The blended group had higher adjusted SRLS and WTC scores and a lower adjusted FLCA score than both the online and face-to-face groups, whereas no statistically significant differences were observed between the latter two groups. Although this pattern was consistent across the three outcomes, the magnitude of the group differences varied, with partial η² values of 0.411 for SRLS, 0.136 for FLCA, and 0.266 for WTC. These findings should be interpreted as adjusted between- group differences rather than evidence of comparative efficacy or causal effects of one instructional mode over another, particularly given the quasi-experimental design and the use of self-report outcome measures.
Self-regulated learning

In relation to the first research question, the blended group had a higher adjusted post-test SRLS score than both the online and face-to-face groups, while the difference between the online and face-to-face groups was not sta­ tistically significant. This pattern is broadly consistent with studies emphasizing the role of instructor presence, structured learning activities, and the integration of digital resources in supporting self-regulatory processes in EFL contexts46,47,48. The finding also corresponds with literature suggesting that blended environments can pro­ vide opportunities for goal setting, time management, self-monitoring, and reflection while retaining elements of teacher guidance and interaction (Zhao & Chen, 2016). However, the present results differ from reports of moderate or non-significant differences associated with online learning ;. Such variation may reflect differences in instructional design, learner characteristics, technological conditions, or the extent of teacher support rather than an inherent advantage of one delivery mode. Thus, the present study suggests that, within this sample, the blended group reported higher levels of self-regulated learning than the two comparison groups, but it does not establish that blended instruction itself produced these differences.
Foreign language classroom anxiety

Regarding the second research question, the blended group had a lower adjusted FLCA score than both the online and face-to-face groups, whereas the online and face-to-face groups did not differ significantly. This finding is consistent with theoretical accounts emphasizing the role of the learning environment in learners’ affective expe­ riences8 and with studies reporting potential benefits of flexibility, learner autonomy, and supportive instructional arrangements for learners’ experiences of anxiety25. It also corresponds with findings that learners may experience anxiety in fully online or emergency remote learning environments when instructional organization and support are inadequate49. At the same time, the literature is not uniform18. and studies of hybrid learning preferences50,51 suggest that the combination of online flexibility and face-to-face interaction may be experienced positively, whereas other evidence indicates that anxiety outcomes depend substantially on contextual and instructional conditions21,38. The present findings therefore support an association between instructional mode and FLCA dif­ ferences in this sample, while leaving the specific processes underlying these differences unresolved.
Willingness to communicate

For the third research question, the blended group had a higher adjusted WTC score in English writing than both the online and face-to-face groups, while the latter two groups did not differ significantly. This finding is con­ sistent with research emphasizing the relevance of interaction, social presence, learner autonomy, and teaching support to communicative engagement52,53. It is also compatible with evidence that digitally supported writing
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z Article in Press

activities, including online peer review, may provide opportunities for written interaction22. Similarly25, reported positive learner attitudes toward computer-assisted writing, while21 highlighted the relevance of self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and teaching presence to engagement. Nevertheless, the present findings should be dis­ tinguished from studies reporting no clear differences between online and face-to-face learning, such as54, and from evidence identifying access and digital-literacy challenges in online learning55. These contrasts reinforce the importance of instructional and contextual conditions when interpreting differences across delivery modes. The pattern across the three outcomes also provides a useful basis for theoretical interpretation, although the underlying relationships were not directly tested in the present study. Previous research has reported associations among self-regulation, anxiety, and L2 communication56 has emphasized the role of self-regulatory processes in sustaining motivational and communicative behavior. The present finding that the blended group simultane­ ously showed higher adjusted SRLS and WTC scores and lower FLCA scores is compatible with these perspec­ tives. However, it would be inappropriate to infer from the current data that higher self-regulation mediated the relationship between instructional mode and WTC or FLCA. No mediation or path analysis was conducted, and the temporal and causal relationships among these constructs therefore remain uncertain. Future longitudinal studies using path or mediation models could examine whether the observed outcomes are linked through such mechanisms. Taken together, the findings suggest that, among the advanced female Iranian EFL learners included in this study, the blended group differed from the online and face-to-face groups across all three examined outcomes after adjustment for baseline scores. The convergence of the findings across SRLS, FLCA, and WTC is note­ worthy, but it should not be interpreted as evidence that blended instruction is generally superior to alternative instructional modes. Differences in instructional implementation, learner characteristics, institutional context, and measurement approach may contribute to the observed pattern. In particular, the outcomes in this study were assessed using learner-reported measures, and the study did not directly measure the proposed learning-environ­ ment mechanisms. Accordingly, the findings provide a basis for further investigation rather than a basis for broad policy or pedagogical claims about the comparative effectiveness of blended learning.
Conclusion

This study compared self-regulated learning strategies (SRLSs), foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA), and willingness to communicate (WTC) in English writing among advanced female Iranian EFL learners receiving blended, online, or face-to-face instruction. After adjustment for the corresponding pre-test scores, the blended group had higher adjusted SRLS and WTC scores and lower adjusted FLCA scores than both the online and face-to-face groups, whereas the online and face-to-face groups did not differ significantly on any of the three outcomes. These findings indicate a consistent pattern of between-group differences associated with instructional mode in this study population. However, they do not establish the comparative efficacy or causal superiority of blended instruction over online or face-to-face instruction. Given the quasi-experimental design, class-level allocation, clustering of learners within classrooms, and reliance on self-report measures, the findings should be interpreted as context-specific evidence requiring replication.
Implications, limitations, and future directions
Implications

Pending replication with randomized designs, objective outcome measures, and larger numbers of classroom- level clusters, the observed pattern may have relevance for the design of blended EFL instruction for advanced female learners in comparable Iranian contexts. In particular, the findings suggest that combining structured
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80272-z

face-to-face interaction with digitally supported learning activities warrants further investigation as a potential instructional arrangement associated with differences in self-regulated learning, classroom anxiety, and willing­ ness to communicate. These findings should not, however, be interpreted as a basis for recommending blended instruction over online or face-to-face instruction more broadly. Future implementation studies should examine which specific features of blended courses, such as instructional structure, teacher interaction, feedback, and opportunities for learner autonomy, are associated with learner outcomes.
Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, all three outcomes were assessed using self-report questionnaires, which may reflect perceived rather than objectively observed learning or com­ munication behavior and may be subject to reporting and common-method biases. Objective indicators, such as observed writing performance, behavioral measures of communication, or learning-platform records, were not incorporated. Second, the study used intact classrooms rather than individual randomization. Although class­ room-level allocation preserved the natural instructional setting and reduced potential contamination between conditions, learners were nested within classrooms, and their observations may therefore have been correlated. The relatively small number of classroom-level clusters limited the reliability of estimating between-classroom variability and the use of more robust multilevel approaches. Consequently, because standard errors may be underestimated due to clustering, the reported standard errors and significance tests should be treated as prelimi­ nary and interpreted with caution, pending future confirmation via multilevel modeling or cluster-randomized trials. Third, blended instruction was examined as a single instructional condition; differences in teacher support, feedback, interaction, task structure, and the proportion of online and face-to-face activities were not separately examined. Fourth, the sample consisted exclusively of advanced female EFL learners in Iran, limiting the extent to which the findings can be generalized to male learners, other proficiency levels, other regions, or different educational and cultural contexts. The study was not designed to test mediation or other structural relation­ ships among SRLS, FLCA, and WTC. Consequently, the observed pattern across these outcomes should not be interpreted as evidence of causal pathways among the constructs. Finally, the WTC measure showed moderate internal consistency and only partial support for its hypothesized five-factor structure. Because measurement invariance and convergent/discriminant validity were not established, WTC was treated as an exploratory out­ come, and between-group differences should therefore be interpreted cautiously. Future studies should further validate the measure and test its cross-group invariance. LMS usage data were not collected in the present study. Therefore, the study did not use platform-based engagement indicators as outcome measures. Future research could complement questionnaire-based outcomes with objective performance measures, such as writing scores and examiner ratings, together with LMS analytics to provide a more comprehensive assessment of learners’ engagement and progress.
Future directions

Future research should replicate these findings using randomized designs, preferably with a larger number of classroom-level clusters to account for the hierarchical structure of EFL data. Studies incorporating objective measures of writing performance, observed communicative behavior, and learning-platform data could comple­ ment self-report assessments. Replication across genders, proficiency levels, regions, and educational settings would help determine the extent to which the observed pattern is context-specific. Longitudinal research could further examine whether differences in SRLS, FLCA, and WTC persist over time. Future studies should also investigate whether specific components of blended instruction, including teacher presence, feedback, interac­ tion, task structure, and learner autonomy, are associated with particular outcomes. Finally, validated measures

and, where appropriate, measurement-invariance testing should be considered when comparing these constructs across instructional groups and populations.

articles.title: Structural model between financial literacy, artificial intelligence, and decision-making among business sciences university students
paragraphs: Structural model between financial literacy, artificial intelligence, and decision-making among business sciences university students
M E Melina Elizabeth Chávez-Choque *
Melina Elizabeth Chávez-Choque *
D E Dilma Erveni Portugal-Portales
G L Guillermo Leonardo Aguilar-García
Guillermo Leonardo Aguilar-García
L A Luis Alberto Zeballos-Valdivia
Facultad de Ciencias Sociales, Universidad Nacional de Moquegua, Moquegua, Perú
Facultad de Ciencias Sociales, Universidad Nacional de Moquegua, Moquegua, Perú

In the context of digital transformation and the growing complexity of economic environments, decision-making among university students has emerged as a key competency influenced by both financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence. Within this framework, the objective of the study was to analyze the structural effect of financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence as predictive factors of decision-making among students at the National University of Moquegua.

A quantitative approach was adopted using a non-experimental, cross-sectional, and explanatory-predictive design. The sample consisted of 259 university students selected through non-probabilistic sampling. A 21-item Likert-type questionnaire was administered, structured into three dimensions: financial literacy, use of artificial intelligence, and decision-making. Reliability was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, obtaining values above 0.80. Data analysis was conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics and AMOS through structural equation modeling techniques.

The findings demonstrated an adequate model fit (CFI = 0.95; RMSEA = 0.06; SRMR = 0.057), confirming consistency between the theoretical model and the empirical data. In the structural analysis, financial literacy showed a positive, significant, and stronger effect on decision-making ( β = 0.424; p < 0.001), highlighting its central role in shaping economic behavior. Likewise, the use of artificial intelligence presented a moderate positive effect ( β = 0.235; p < 0.001), indicating a relevant contribution, although subordinate to cognitive competencies. In addition, a positive relationship was identified between financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence, suggesting that higher levels of financial knowledge favor technological adoption. The model explained 36.2% of the variance in decision-making, reflecting an acceptable explanatory capacity in complex educational contexts.

The study confirms that financial literacy constitutes the main predictor of decision-making among university students, whereas artificial intelligence acts as a complementary factor that enhances, but does not replace, financial knowledge.

In the current context marked by the digital transformation of financial systems and the increasing complexity of markets, economic decision-making has become an essential competency in higher education ( Akour and Alenezi, 2022 ; Baque-Cantos et al., 2023 ; Brunetti et al., 2020 ; Mohamed et al., 2022 ; Moreira-Choez et al., 2023). Financial literacy, understood as the set of knowledge, skills, and attitudes required to manage economic resources, plays a central role in this process ( Dewi et al., 2020 ; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014 ). Various studies have shown that financial literacy significantly influences the quality of economic decisions ( Bastidas-Guerrón et al., 2025 ), implying that individuals with greater conceptual mastery possess better tools to evaluate alternatives and minimize risks. Therefore, financial literacy not only functions as technical knowledge but also as a behavioral determinant that guides rational decision-making in uncertain environments.

In the educational field, the literature has extensively analyzed the relationship between financial education and decision-making, highlighting the mediating role of financial literacy in the development of decision-making competencies ( Bai, 2023 ; Hidayat-ur-Rehman, 2025 ; Kumar et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2025 ). It has been demonstrated that economic education positively influences the development of decision-making skills and entrepreneurial behavior ( Pashaei et al., 2024 ), evidencing that the acquisition of financial knowledge strengthens students’ capacity to interpret complex economic scenarios. This finding suggests that academic training not only transmits information but also shapes cognitive structures that facilitate informed decisions, particularly in contexts characterized by high uncertainty.

Likewise, recent studies have validated empirical models explaining the influence of educational variables on financial literacy through multivariate techniques ( Bajaj and Kaur, 2022 ; Pérez-Campdesuñer et al., 2025 ; Raut, 2020 ). Evidence has shown that educational level exerts a significant effect on financial literacy, validating dimensions such as technical knowledge and financial self-management ( Bastidas-Guerrón et al., 2025 ), suggesting that financial literacy develops progressively and cumulatively according to academic training. Consequently, these findings reinforce the relevance of using structural equation modeling to analyze complex relationships among latent variables in educational contexts.

However, empirical evidence has also identified limitations in the relationship between financial knowledge and decision-making, especially when behavioral factors intervene ( Merter and Balcıoğlu, 2025 ; Rasool and Ullah, 2020 ; Ventre et al., 2024 ). Research has demonstrated that financial knowledge does not always translate into appropriate behaviors due to the influence of cognitive biases and subjective perceptions ( Ahmad and Shah, 2022 ; Carpena et al., 2019 ; Mandić et al., 2026 ), indicating that individuals may behave irrationally even when they possess sufficient information. This phenomenon highlights the need to integrate psychological and behavioral variables into explanatory models, moving beyond exclusively rational approaches in the analysis of decision-making.

Within this same framework, the incorporation of artificial intelligence into financial and educational environments has introduced new dynamics into analysis and decision-making processes ( Alex Avelar and Jordão, 2025 ; Han et al., 2024 ; Wang, 2021 ). It has been noted that artificial intelligence improves efficiency in information processing, although its impact depends largely on users’ trust in technology ( Hanson and Ott, 2026 ), implying that technological adoption does not automatically guarantee more accurate decisions. In this sense, artificial intelligence should be understood as a mediating tool whose effect depends on cognitive and attitudinal factors, thereby increasing the complexity of its integration into behavioral explanatory models.

Similarly, recent research has emphasized that the integration of artificial intelligence into financial education offers potential benefits in terms of personalization and learning enhancement, although evidence regarding sustained behavioral changes remains limited ( Hesami, 2025 ; Leal and Oliveira, 2024 ; Paramesha et al., 2024 ). Although AI enhances the understanding of financial content, its long-term effects on decision-making continue to be constrained ( Asemi et al., 2025 ; Balcazar-Paiva et al., 2026 ), suggesting that technology alone is insufficient to modify behavioral patterns. This finding reinforces the need to integrate pedagogical and technological approaches in a coordinated manner.

Based on the foregoing, relevant gaps in the scientific literature can be identified. A conceptual fragmentation persists in the study of financial literacy and decision-making, particularly regarding the integration of technological and behavioral variables ( Ingale and Paluri, 2022 ; Mandić et al., 2026 ; Negi and Jaiswal, 2024 ; Yeo et al., 2024 ), which limits the construction of comprehensive explanatory models. Consequently, it is necessary to develop research that articulates these dimensions within a structural approach, enabling a more precise understanding of the interactions among knowledge, technology, and economic behavior ( Garay-Rondero et al., 2019 ; Iammarino and McCann, 2006 ; Magliocca et al., 2024 ).

The relevance of addressing this issue within the context of the National University of Moquegua lies in the need to train professionals capable of functioning in complex economic environments characterized by the digitalization of financial services and the growing interdependence between technology and decision-making. In this scenario, financial education emerges as a strategic component in the comprehensive training of university students, as it promotes competencies related to the efficient management of resources and the critical evaluation of economic alternatives. It has been noted that financial literacy constitutes a key element for economic well-being and social inclusion ( Marin and Notargiacomo, 2021 ), implying that its strengthening within academic environments not only improves the quality of individual decisions but also contributes to the formation of economically responsible and socially committed citizens. In the case of the UNAM, an institution that promotes education grounded in values, social responsibility, and sustainable development, the incorporation of financial and digital competencies becomes even more relevant, as it enables the integration of technical knowledge with ethical principles in decision-making. Furthermore, the profile of university students, increasingly exposed to digital tools and technology-mediated learning environments, requires the integration of artificial intelligence as an educational resource capable of enhancing analytical skills and the interpretation of financial information.

In line with the above, the present research raises the following research question: To what extent do financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence act as predictive factors of decision-making, and how are financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence associated, among business sciences students at the National University of Moquegua? In accordance with the theoretical framework and the proposed conceptual model, the following hypotheses are formulated:
H1: Financial literacy has a positive and significant effect on decision-making among business sciences university students.
H1: Financial literacy has a positive and significant effect on decision-making among business sciences university students.
H2: The use of artificial intelligence has a positive and significant effect on decision-making among business sciences university students.
H2: The use of artificial intelligence has a positive and significant effect on decision-making among business sciences university students.
H3: Financial literacy is positively associated with the use of artificial intelligence among business sciences university students.
H3: Financial literacy is positively associated with the use of artificial intelligence among business sciences university students.

Consequently, the objective of this study is to analyze the structural effect of financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence as predictive factors of decision-making among students at the National University of Moquegua through a structural equation model, in order to determine the magnitude and significance of the relationships among the variables, explain decision-making behavior in digitalized academic contexts, and generate empirical evidence supporting the design of educational strategies aimed at strengthening financial and digital competencies in higher education.

The study was conducted under a quantitative approach, as it was aimed at measuring and analyzing the relationships among variables through inferential statistical techniques. This approach made it possible to empirically evaluate the effect of financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence on decision-making, considering the measurable nature of the analyzed constructs. Likewise, an applied research type was adopted, since the results seek to contribute to solving specific problems within the university educational context, particularly in improving students’ financial and digital competencies.

The methodological design corresponded to a non-experimental cross-sectional design, insofar as the variables were not deliberately manipulated and data collection was carried out at a single point in time. This design allowed the observation and analysis of the existing relationships among the variables within their natural context, without researcher intervention. Regarding the research level, it was established as explanatory-predictive, because the study sought not only to describe the variables but also to explain causal relationships and estimate the predictive capacity of financial literacy and artificial intelligence on decision-making.

The population consisted of university students enrolled at the National University of Moquegua, belonging to academic programs in the field of business sciences. From this population, a non-probabilistic purposive sample was selected, composed of 259 students who voluntarily participated in the study. The sociodemographic characterization of the sample revealed diversity in terms of sex, age, level of study, and academic program, which enabled a comprehensive approach to the analyzed phenomenon. Accordingly, the analytical population was restricted to business sciences students (Business Administration and Accounting). The findings therefore refer to this disciplinary population and should not be generalized to university students from other fields without additional evidence.

To characterize the study sample and contextualize the obtained results, Table 1 presents the sociodemographic, academic, and technological distribution of the participants. This information makes it possible to identify relevant patterns in variables such as sex, age, level of study, academic program, and experience in the use of digital tools, as well as the frequency of artificial intelligence use in academic activities. The detailed description of these characteristics is essential for the appropriate interpretation of the findings of the structural model, since these factors may influence the development of financial competencies and decision-making processes within the university context.
Sociodemographic, academic, and technological characterization of the sample of students.

n = 259 university students. Percentages were calculated based on the total sample. The variable “experience in the use of digital tools” refers to the level of perceived proficiency reported by the participants, whereas “frequency of artificial intelligence use” corresponds to the reported use in academic activities. Prepared by the authors.

Table 1 shows a heterogeneous characterization of the sample, with a predominance of female participants (62.9%) compared to male participants (34.4%), suggesting greater participation of women in programs related to the field of study, an aspect considered relevant since the literature has identified gender differences in financial competencies. Regarding age, a concentration is observed within the range of 17 to 22 years (77.6%), indicating that most participants are in the early stages of university education, where financial and digital competencies are still under development. Concerning academic level, the presence of fourth-year or higher students (32.8%) stands out, allowing the inference of different levels of academic maturity within the sample, thereby favoring variability in the results. Likewise, the predominance of the Business Administration program (75.3%) over accounting (24.7%) suggests a disciplinary bias that could influence the reported level of financial literacy. In relation to digital experience, most students were classified at intermediate (51.4%) and basic (45.6%) levels, evidencing functional but not advanced technological competencies, which is consistent with the limited proportion reporting permanent use of artificial intelligence (6.2%). However, the fact that 83.4% reported using artificial intelligence “sometimes” or “frequently” indicates a progressive integration of these tools into the academic environment, reinforcing their relevance as an explanatory variable within the structural model.

Data collection was carried out through a structured self-administered questionnaire designed to measure the constructs of financial literacy, use of artificial intelligence, and decision-making among university students. The instrument was developed based on a review of specialized literature and adapted to the academic context, ensuring coherence with the proposed theoretical model. It was organized into three sections: the first included the informed consent form, which explained the voluntary nature of participation, the confidentiality of the information, and the exclusive use of the data for academic purposes; the second collected relevant sociodemographic information, such as sex, age, level of study, academic program, experience in the use of digital tools, and frequency of artificial intelligence use in academic activities; and the third corresponded to the measurement scale of the analyzed constructs. The scale was structured using a five-point Likert format (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) and included 21 items distributed across three dimensions: financial literacy, use of artificial intelligence, and decision-making. Each dimension incorporated indicators aimed at evaluating both cognitive and behavioral aspects, such as understanding financial concepts, risk analysis, use of artificial intelligence tools, and evaluation of alternatives in decision-making. Likewise, the instrument included reverse-worded items to reduce response bias, which were recoded prior to statistical analysis.

Likewise, the structural relationships between the exogenous variables and the endogenous variable are displayed in accordance with the proposed theoretical model. This graphical representation facilitates understanding of the organization of the instrument and the way in which the items operationalize each analyzed dimension, thereby supporting the interpretation of the results obtained through the structural equation model.

Figure 1 shows a measurement and structural model consistent with the theoretical framework of the study, in which financial literacy (F1) and the use of artificial intelligence (F2) are configured as exogenous variables influencing decision-making (F3) as the endogenous variable. It can be observed that each latent construct is adequately represented by multiple indicators, suggesting a robust operationalization of the variables and supporting the validity of the model. Likewise, the factor loadings reflected in the relationships between the items and their respective constructs demonstrate consistency in the measurement of the analyzed dimensions. In the structural component, the arrows directed from F1 and F2 toward F3 indicate the hypothesis of direct influence on decision-making, whereas the relationship between F1 and F2 suggests a possible association between financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence. This approach is theoretically consistent, since mastery of financial knowledge may facilitate the critical use of technological tools in academic contexts. Nevertheless, the structure of the model also allows the anticipation that the explanatory weight of each variable may differ, which will be empirically determined through standardized coefficients.

The reliability of the instrument was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficient, obtaining values of 0.836 for financial literacy, 0.819 for the use of artificial intelligence, and 0.820 for decision-making, indicating adequate internal consistency. Composite reliability (CR) was 0.812 for artificial intelligence and 0.785 for decision-making, whereas financial literacy yielded CR = 0.627, below the conventional threshold of 0.70. Average variance extracted (AVE) was 0.570 for artificial intelligence and 0.579 for decision-making, while financial literacy yielded AVE = 0.464, below the conventional threshold of 0.50. Therefore, convergent validity was supported for artificial intelligence and decision-making but was weaker for financial literacy. This measurement limitation was retained transparently and was considered when interpreting the structural effect of financial literacy.

Finally, data processing and analysis were conducted using specialized statistical software. In the first stage, the IBM SPSS Statistics program was employed for descriptive analysis and verification of statistical assumptions. Subsequently, the AMOS software was used for the estimation of the structural equation model (SEM), allowing the evaluation of model fit quality through indices such as CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR, as well as the estimation of structural relationships among the variables through standardized coefficients ( β ). This analytical approach enabled validation of the proposed theoretical model and determination of the significance of the relationships among financial literacy, artificial intelligence, and decision-making in university students.

This section presents and analyzes the results obtained from the application of the structural equation model, integrating the empirical evidence with the theoretical foundation of the study. First, the psychometric analyses of the instrument are presented, including indicators of reliability and validity of the constructs. Subsequently, the quality of fit of the structural model is examined, and the relationships among financial literacy, the use of artificial intelligence, and decision-making among university students are interpreted.

The results presented in Table 2 show adequate internal consistency for the three scales; however, convergent validity is not equally supported across all constructs. Financial literacy (F1) yielded CR = 0.627 and AVE = 0.464, below the conventional criteria of CR ≥ 0.70 and AVE ≥ 0.50. Consequently, F1 presents a measurement weakness and its structural effect should be interpreted cautiously because a comparatively large proportion of indicator variance may be attributable to measurement error. The retained indicators were preserved to maintain the theoretical content represented in the original instrument, but this decision does not eliminate the need for subsequent item-level refinement and independent validation. Cronbach’s alpha coefficients and item-total correlations suggest that the indicators consistently capture the dimensions of financial literacy, use of artificial intelligence, and decision-making. This behavior aligns with evidence recognizing financial literacy as a multidimensional competency articulated with technological and cognitive skills to address digitalized economic environments ( Hanson and Ott, 2026 ). In this sense, it is argued that the consistency observed in financial literacy reflects not only conceptual mastery but also the ability to apply knowledge in real-world contexts, thereby strengthening its role as a structural basis of decision-making behavior in academic settings.

Regarding the indicators of artificial intelligence use, although they present acceptable values, their behavior reveals relatively lower consolidation compared to financial literacy, suggesting that adoption is still incipient in terms of decision-making application. This result is consistent with findings indicating that, although students widely use artificial intelligence tools, their incorporation into financial decisions remains moderate and conditioned by factors such as trust, perceived usefulness, and system understanding ( Dutta, 2026 ). Complementarily, it has been demonstrated that artificial intelligence literacy maintains a positive relationship with financial behaviors, although its influence tends to be limited when analyzed alongside deeper cognitive variables ( Tembelo and Özyeşil, 2026 ). Under this logic, technology is understood as an enabler of the decision-making process, but not as a substitute for the cognitive foundation provided by financial literacy, which explains the variability observed in the technological indicators.

On the other hand, the relationship among the constructs makes it possible to identify that decision-making is more strongly associated with financial literacy than with the use of artificial intelligence, evidencing the predominance of cognitive and educational factors in economic behavior. This finding is consistent with studies highlighting the role of financial literacy as a direct predictor of rational and sustainable decisions, even in technology-mediated environments ( Dash and Mohanta, 2025 ). Likewise, recent research emphasizes that the integration of artificial intelligence into educational processes can strengthen financial literacy through personalized and adaptive systems, thereby contributing to improved long-term decision quality ( Maknuni, 2025 ). This demonstrates that university education should move toward an integrative approach in which financial literacy is consolidated as the central axis, while artificial intelligence functions as a complementary tool that amplifies analytical capacity, reduces uncertainty, and promotes more informed decisions in complex contexts.

Figure 2 shows that the results present a differentiated trend according to the level of experience in digital tools, revealing that students with an advanced level achieve higher values in decision-making and use of artificial intelligence, whereas the basic and intermediate levels exhibit greater dispersion and the presence of outliers. Specifically, the median of decision-making progressively increases from the basic to the advanced level, suggesting an improvement in analytical capacity as digital experience increases. This behavior is consistent with evidence indicating that artificial intelligence enhances decision-making processes by optimizing information analysis and reducing cognitive biases in financial contexts ( Bayakhmetova et al., 2025 ). Based on these results, it is argued that technological mastery not only increases access to tools but also strengthens analytical skills that are reflected in more consistent decisions.

Regarding financial literacy, the results show lower variability across experience levels, maintaining relatively stable values compared to the other constructs. However, lower median values were identified at the basic levels, indicating that limited digital experience could be associated with lower levels of applied financial understanding. This situation may be interpreted as an initial stage in the development of competencies, in which students have not yet fully integrated financial knowledge with technological tools. In this regard, it has been documented that the adoption of artificial intelligence in academic contexts requires progressive adaptation and training processes to significantly impact decision-making ( Chávez-Díaz et al., 2024 ). Therefore, the dispersion observed at intermediate levels reflects heterogeneity in the process of digital and financial learning.

On the other hand, the results demonstrate that, although the use of artificial intelligence increases at more advanced levels, its effect is not homogeneous, since outliers persist even within this group, indicating individual differences in technological appropriation. This finding reinforces the idea that technology alone does not guarantee optimal decisions, but rather requires a solid foundation of financial literacy for its proper interpretation. In fact, the literature has demonstrated that financial literacy significantly influences the quality of economic decisions by providing criteria for evaluating risks and opportunities ( Johri et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, it is also recognized that artificial intelligence may generate counterproductive effects if it reduces the perception of decision costs or automates processes without sufficient critical supervision ( De La Rosa and Bechler, 2024 ). This suggests that the observed behavior at advanced levels responds to the interaction between digital experience and financial competencies, enabling more informed decisions in complex environments.

On the other hand, the significant but lower magnitude effect of the use of artificial intelligence suggests that its influence is conditioned by factors related to technological acceptance and perceived usefulness. In this line, evidence has shown that the adoption of artificial intelligence-based tools depends mainly on ease of use, perceived usefulness, and user attitudes ( Szopiński et al., 2026 ). From this perspective, it can be inferred that artificial intelligence contributes to the decision-making process insofar as individuals are able to understand and trust its functionalities, which explains its moderate effect compared to more consolidated variables such as financial literacy. Complementarily, it has been documented that the integration of artificial intelligence into financial education promotes personalized learning and improves content comprehension, although its effects on behavior still present limitations ( Balcazar-Paiva et al., 2026 ). This finding suggests that the impact of artificial intelligence on decision-making is not immediate, but rather progressive and dependent on the educational context.

Finally, the results demonstrate that decision-making responds to the interaction between financial literacy and digital competencies rather than to the isolated use of technological tools. From this perspective, it has been proposed that artificial intelligence may influence the psychological processes involved in economic decisions, generating both improvements and risks associated with financial behavior ( De La Rosa and Bechler, 2024 ). This approach makes it possible to understand that the use of these technologies requires a critical framework that prevents impulsive or biased decisions. Likewise, it has been demonstrated that artificial intelligence-based tools can strengthen financial literacy through personalized learning strategies ( Rahman, 2024 ), reinforcing their potential as a complementary educational resource. However, gaps in digital financial literacy still persist, limiting their effective use ( Ntakirutimana et al., 2026 ), which implies the need for more comprehensive educational interventions. Consistent with this, it has been confirmed that financial and digital literacy explain a significant proportion of the variability in economic decision-making ( Mishra et al., 2024 ), reaffirming their role as structural determinants in contemporary financial contexts.

Table 3 presents an integrated evaluation of the structural model, including global fit indices and the estimation of the relationships among the analyzed constructs. It reports the main goodness-of-fit indicators, as well as the standardized coefficients of the structural paths, their significance levels, and confidence intervals. This information makes it possible to assess the adequacy of the proposed model and determine the predictive effect of financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence on decision-making among business sciences university students, providing an empirical basis for interpreting the results according to the theoretical framework.

Table 3 shows that the structural model presents an adequate overall fit, as evidenced by indicators such as CMIN/DF = 1.923, SRMR = 0.057, and PClose = 0.174, which meet the criteria of acceptability and excellence in structural equation models. Likewise, the CFI reaches 0.95 and the RMSEA stands at 0.06, suggesting a consistent empirical representation of the theoretical model. In this context, it has been documented that the integration of artificial intelligence into financial analysis models improves the precision of structural relationships and strengthens the quality of data-driven decisions ( Choowan and Daovisan, 2025 ). This finding supports the argument that an adequate model fit not only validates the statistical consistency of the model but also reflects the capacity to integrate technological variables within complex analytical frameworks, which is essential in digitalized financial environments.

Regarding the structural relationships, financial literacy had a positive and statistically significant effect on decision-making ( β = 0.424; p < 0.001; 95% CI [0.278, 0.570]), while the use of artificial intelligence also had a positive and statistically significant effect ( β = 0.235; p < 0.001; 95% CI [0.104, 0.366]). Financial literacy showed the larger standardized coefficient, supporting its comparatively stronger contribution within the estimated model. These results support H1 and H2 and indicate that financial knowledge and AI use contribute jointly, although with different magnitudes, to students’ self-reported decision-making capacity.

The significant but smaller coefficient for artificial intelligence indicates that its contribution is complementary to financial literacy. AI-based tools can facilitate access to information, comparison of alternatives, and analysis; however, their educational value depends on students’ ability to interpret and critically evaluate the information generated. Accordingly, the findings support an integrated approach in which financial knowledge provides the conceptual basis for decision-making, while artificial intelligence functions as a technological resource that can extend analytical support in digitally mediated financial contexts.

Figure 4 shows that the standardized residuals of the regression model present a distribution close to normality, as evidenced by the symmetric shape of the histogram and the alignment of the points in the P–P plot with the theoretical diagonal. This behavior indicates that there are no significant deviations compromising the statistical assumptions of the model, particularly the normality of errors, which is a necessary condition for the validity of statistical inferences. In financial studies, the stability of residuals becomes especially relevant when advanced analytical tools are incorporated, given that artificial intelligence contributes to optimizing the precision and consistency of predictive models ( Ren, 2021 ). Within this framework, the observed distribution suggests that the model adequately captures the structure of the data without relevant distortions.

The alignment observed in the P–P plot reinforces the consistency of the model, since the errors follow an expected pattern under normality conditions, supporting the reliability of the estimated coefficients. This result becomes even more relevant in research integrating financial literacy and the use of artificial intelligence, because statistical validity ensures that the relationships among variables are not biased. Evidence indicates that the interaction among financial literacy, digital fluency, and emerging technologies directly influences investment behavior and the quality of decisions in digital environments ( Pattnaik and Hota, 2025 ). In this context, the stability of residuals is associated with an adequate empirical representation of these interactions, avoiding overestimation or underestimation of the analyzed effects.

On the other hand, the absence of anomalous patterns in the residuals suggests that the factors included in the model consistently explain the variability in decision-making. This result is related to approaches that integrate financial and digital literacy as complementary dimensions for understanding economic behavior in technological environments ( Lyons and Kass-Hanna, 2021 ). Furthermore, it has been documented that financial literacy contributes to reducing behavioral biases and facilitates the adoption of financial technologies, thereby improving decision quality ( Aftab et al., 2025 ). At the same time, the combination of financial literacy and digital inclusion influences more responsible practices and a more efficient use of financial services ( Riwayati et al., 2025 ). The consistency observed in the residuals aligns with these approaches, reflecting that the model adequately integrates cognitive and technological dimensions in the analysis of decision-making.
