Theoretical implications

The present study makes several theoretical contributions. First, it integrates both the human-like and technical characteristics of AI chatbots into the S–O–R framework, thereby extending the application of this framework to research on AI chatbots and perceived addictiveness. Previous studies of AI chatbots have predominantly focused on user acceptance, continuance intention, or positive usage outcomes, or have explained user behavior from a single perspective, such as anthropomorphism, empathy, or system quality. The present study conceptualizes per­ ceived empathy and social presence as human-like stimuli and perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as technical stimuli. In doing so, it demonstrates that users’ psychological responses to AI chatbots result from the combined influence of human-like interaction cues and technical performance cues. Second, the present study incorporates trust into the formation mechanism of perceived AI chatbot addictive­ ness, thereby enriching existing explanations of the internal psychological processes underlying addictiveness. Previous research has primarily emphasized factors such as flow, cognitive absorption, loneliness, and attach­ ment19,164, while paying insufficient attention to the role of trust in the development of perceived addictiveness. The findings show that both categories of AI chatbot characteristics significantly influence trust, which in turn promotes emotional attachment and functional dependence. This suggests that trust is not only an important prerequisite for users’ acceptance and adoption of AI but also a key psychological bridge through which positive usage experiences may develop into potential overreliance on AI chatbots. Trust, therefore, does not necessarily produce only positive outcomes. When trust continues to strengthen and is transformed into attachment or depen­ dence, it may also be accompanied by an increase in perceived addictiveness. This finding extends the literature on human–AI trust beyond technology acceptance and usage intention to encompass potentially negative usage outcomes. Third, the present study finds that emotional attachment and functional dependence primarily operate as paral­ lel mediators, whereas the serial mediation pathway was not supported. This finding challenges the linear assump­ tion that functional dependence may gradually develop into emotional attachment. Users may form instrumental dependence because of AI chatbots’ high efficiency, or they may develop emotional attachment in response to the chatbots’ social presence and empathetic responses. Although these two forms of user–AI relationships are inter­ related, they do not necessarily emerge in a fixed temporal sequence. This finding suggests that future research should classify AI users more precisely according to their primary usage motivations and the types of relation­ ships they develop with AI, rather than relying on a single concept of attachment or dependence to explain all users.
Practical implications

The findings of the present study offer practical implications for AI chatbot designers, platform operators, user organizations, and relevant policymakers. First, the design objective of AI chatbots should not be limited to maxi­ mizing user trust and interaction duration; instead, greater emphasis should be placed on fostering an appropriate and well-calibrated level of trust. Because social presence, empathy, usefulness, and ease of use all strengthen trust, which in turn promotes attachment and dependence, platforms should avoid encouraging users to mis­ takenly believe that AI possesses genuine emotions, independent consciousness, or infallible judgment when enhancing human-like interaction. AI systems can help users develop a more accurate understanding of the nature of their responses through clear disclosure of their artificial identity, explicit explanations of their capability boundaries, and appropriate indications of uncertainty. Second, because social presence was the strongest predictor of trust among all the examined factors, design­ ers should exercise caution when using design elements that may excessively intensify users’ perceptions of a social relationship with AI chatbots. Chatbots may appropriately demonstrate politeness, patience, and contextual sensitivity; however, they should not encourage continued interaction through exclusive language, emotional manipulation, or suggestions that they possess human-like needs. For applications involving companionship,
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80455-8 Article in Press

psychological support, or the disclosure of personal emotions, users should be periodically reminded that AI can­ not replace real-world interpersonal relationships or professional services. When persistent negative emotions are detected, the system should also provide users with the option of seeking support from a human professional or other appropriate human service provider. Third, platforms should pay attention to the risk of dependence arising from functional convenience. Although perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are important conditions for increasing system adoption, exces­ sive convenience may also lead users to delegate an increasing number of cognitive tasks to AI. To reduce unintentional cognitive offloading, AI systems can provide tiered support according to the application context. For example, they may initially offer prompts, lines of reasoning, or suggestions for checking users’ work rather than consistently generating complete answers directly. In educational, design, and knowledge-work contexts, platforms may also introduce designated periods for independent thinking, prompts to verify information sources, and AI-free completion modes to preserve users’ autonomous judgment and problem-solving abilities. Fourth, because emotional attachment was the strongest direct predictor of perceived addictiveness, risk gov­ ernance should focus not only on the duration of use but also on the nature of users’ relationships with AI chat­ bots. Platforms may provide usage-time statistics, reminders during prolonged sessions, notifications concerning late-night use, and periodic suggestions to take breaks. They should also allow users to disable personalized memory, reduce proactive interaction prompts, and adjust the degree of emotional expression used by the chatbot. For users who exhibit a strong tendency toward emotional dependence, the system should avoid responses that encourage exclusive attachment and should remind them to maintain real-world social connections.
Limitations and future research directions

The present study has several limitations. First, it employed a cross-sectional survey and voluntary response sampling, and the data were collected primarily from AI chatbot users in China. Although the sample included respondents of different ages, educational backgrounds, and commonly used platforms, women aged 26–35 and respondents holding bachelor’s degrees were disproportionately represented. This sample composition may limit the generalizability of the findings to other cultural contexts, age groups, and usage settings. In addition, the recruitment strategy also introduces a potential sampling limitation. Encouraging respondents to forward the survey link to friends may have disproportionately reached individuals with similar demographic backgrounds, social connections, interests, and generative AI usage patterns. Such network homophily and self-selection could produce selection bias, reduce sample diversity, and limit the representativeness and generalizability of the find­ ings. Because referral pathways were not recorded, the extent of peer-referral participation and any resulting bias cannot be quantified or statistically corrected using the available data. Future studies should use more structured sampling strategies, recruit participants through diverse and independent channels, record recruitment sources where appropriate, and assess the robustness of results across recruitment groups. In addition, an additional limitation concerns the verification of respondents’ actual generative AI chatbot experience. Platform use was self-reported, and the study did not independently authenticate that respondents had used DeepSeek or the other named tools. Although attention checks and completion-time screening removed some low-quality responses, these procedures cannot rule out participation by individuals without relevant experience. The available data do not allow us to estimate how many, if any, such respondents remained in the final sample. Consequently, possible eligibility misclassification and associated response bias should be considered when interpreting the findings. Future research should implement an explicit prior-use eligibility question and, where feasible and ethically appropriate, corroborate experience using privacy-preserving evidence such as verifiable usage history or task- based demonstrations, together with prespecified quality-control rules. Second, cross-sectional data does not allow causal relationships among the variables to be fully established. Future research could employ longitudinal surveys or experimental designs to examine how trust, emotional attachment, functional dependence, and perceived addictiveness change dynamically over time as users continue interacting with AI chatbots.

Third, the present study focused on the mediating roles of trust, emotional attachment, and functional depen­ dence but did not incorporate individual differences among users. Factors such as loneliness, social anxiety, self-control, need for cognition, AI literacy, and established technology-use habits may alter the relationships proposed in the model. Future research could examine these factors as antecedents, moderators, or control vari­ ables to identify which user groups are more likely to shift from normal use to excessive dependence. Latent class analysis could also be used to distinguish between instrumentally oriented users, emotionally companionship- oriented users, and users with mixed forms of dependence, thereby providing a more nuanced explanation of how perceived addictiveness develops across different user groups. Fourth, the research model explained 37.4% of the variance in perceived addictiveness, indicating that other relevant factors remain unexamined. Future studies could investigate nonlinear and threshold effects. For exam­ ple, a moderate level of trust may facilitate effective use, whereas excessive trust may substantially increase the risk of dependence. In addition, the present study relied primarily on self-reported data collected at a single point in time. Although the common method bias tests did not indicate a serious problem, future research could further strengthen the robustness of the findings by using multi-source data, temporally separated measurements, and experimental manipulations. Fifth, although the present study distinguishes between emotional attachment and functional dependence, it conceptualizes trust as a unidimensional construct without explicitly differentiating cognition-based from affect- based trust. Previous research suggests that these two forms of trust have distinct psychological foundations165. Cognition-based trust is primarily associated with evaluations of competence, reliability, and dependability, whereas affect-based trust is rooted in perceived care, emotional concern, and relational connection. This distinc­ tion may be particularly important in the context of anthropomorphic AI chatbots, as their human-like conversa­ tional characteristics may elicit affective trust beyond users’ rational evaluations of technological performance. However, the trust items employed in this study predominantly capture cognitive evaluations of trustworthiness and do not provide sufficient measurement coverage to distinguish the two dimensions empirically. Consequently, the present findings cannot establish whether cognition-based and affect-based trust have different antecedents or consequences. Future research should employ validated multidimensional trust measures to investigate whether technical characteristics, such as perceived usefulness and ease of use, and human-like characteristics, such as perceived empathy and social presence, differentially influence these two forms of trust. Furthermore, future studies could examine whether cognition-based trust is more strongly associated with functional dependence, whereas affect-based trust is more closely related to emotional attachment, and whether these pathways have distinct implications for perceived AI chatbot addictiveness. Such investigations would provide a more nuanced understanding of trust formation and its consequences in human–AI interactions. Finally, although the literature review identifies anthropomorphism as a central concept in research on human- like AI, the present model does not estimate its independent effect. Perceived empathy and social presence capture specific relational perceptions but do not fully represent the broader attribution of human qualities or intentions to AI. Future studies should measure anthropomorphism alongside these constructs and compare alternative speci­ fications—for example, anthropomorphism as an antecedent of perceived empathy and social presence, or as a distinct predictor of trust—to establish their discriminant validity and incremental explanatory power.
Conclusions

Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) framework, the present study developed and empiri­ cally tested a theoretical model explaining how the human-like and technical characteristics of AI chatbots influ­ ence users’ perceived addictiveness. Based on an analysis of 345 valid survey responses, the findings indicate that perceived AI chatbot addictiveness does not arise directly from any single isolated characteristic. Instead, human- like and technical cues jointly shape users’ trust, which is subsequently transformed into emotional attachment or functional dependence. The present study extends the application of the S–O–R framework and human–AI trust
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-80455-8 Article in Press

research to the context of perceived AI chatbot addictiveness. It also provides a theoretical foundation for the responsible design of AI chatbots, the development of appropriately calibrated trust, and the governance of risks associated with user dependence166–171.

Architecture of a virtual simulation teaching platform designed for college students' innovation and entrepreneurship training and its empirical study
Tingyu Chen · Jie Liu · Guocai Yin · Xiaoyi Xuan
Received: 10 July 2026 / Accepted: 28 October 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Innovation and entrepreneurship education requires experiential and adaptive learning environments, but evi­ dence is often limited by weak theoretical integration, incomplete intervention reporting, and non-randomized designs. This study evaluated a theory-informed virtual simulation platform for entrepreneurial learning while explicitly accounting for allocation, instructional exposure, measurement quality, and clustering. A two-arm quasi-experimental study included 480 students from 12 intact classes. Baseline assessment preceded non- random classroom allocation to the virtual simulation platform (six classes; n = 240) or conventional train­ ing (six classes; n = 240); students did not self-select. Two instructors taught both conditions using common objectives, schedules, and assessment tasks over eight weeks. Multi-item measures underwent reliability and confirmatory factor analysis, performance tasks were scored by blinded independent raters, and primary analy­ ses used covariate-adjusted ANCOVA with classroom-, instructor-, exposure-, missing-data-, and alternative- composite sensitivity analyses. Baseline characteristics were comparable, although post-allocation attendance, active learning time, assignment completion, and participation were higher in the platform condition. Platform assignment was associated with a 6.96-point higher composite learning score (95% CI: 6.34–7.57, p < 0.001); the estimate remained 5.38 points (95% CI: 4.69–6.07) after exploratory adjustment for observed instruc­ tional exposure. Classroom-clustered and instructor-adjusted models were consistent. Engagement was the only significant specific indirect pathway, but it explained only 5.41% of the total association. Scale reliability, construct validity, and inter-rater reliability were acceptable to strong. The findings provide supportive, but not definitive causal, evidence that a structured virtual simulation environment is associated with better entre­ preneurial learning, engagement, and acceptability. The magnitude of benefit should be interpreted alongside exposure differences, possible novelty and Hawthorne effects, assessment alignment, classroom clustering, and the single-institution context.
Keywords Virtual simulation · Entrepreneurship education · Innovation training · Engagement · Cognitive load

Introduction

Innovation and entrepreneurship education must develop opportunity recognition, uncertainty management, business-model design, teamwork, and implementation capability rather than factual knowledge alone. Conven­ tional lectures and cases remain useful, but they provide limited opportunity for repeated decisions, immediate consequences, financial experimentation, and adaptive support. The present study therefore evaluates a virtual simulation platform as a pedagogical system rather than merely a digital delivery channel. Entrepreneurship pedagogy has shifted toward constructivist, practice-oriented, and experience-based designs in which learners build knowledge through action, feedback, and reflection1. This perspective predicts that plat­ form benefits should arise when students repeatedly formulate hypotheses, act within realistic constraints, observe consequences, and revise their decisions. Digital platforms can extend access, collaboration, analytics, and programme management, but many imple­ mentations remain limited to communication or content delivery2. The relevant research question is therefore not whether technology is present, but whether platform functions are coherently mapped to learning mechanisms and measurable competencies. Entrepreneurship programmes may influence intention through learning, inspiration, perceived control, norms, and resources3. Intention is nevertheless distal and should be complemented by direct measures of knowledge, planning, creativity, presentation, financial reasoning, and integrated performance. Simulation provides a safe cycle of decision, consequence, feedback, and revision. Serious games can repre­ sent dynamic entrepreneurial processes and permit experimentation without real financial risk, but their educa­ tional value depends on the validity of the scenarios, assessments, and feedback rather than on playfulness alone4. Gamification can improve motivation and participation, yet effects on deeper learning are inconsistent when game elements are not aligned with objectives and assessment5,4. Consequently, engagement should be treated as one possible process variable, not as proof of learning. The proposed platform integrates four complementary principles. Experiential learning is operationalized through iterative market and finance decisions; social constructivism through peer collaboration and instructor debriefing; cognitive-load management through staged complexity and adaptive feedback; and learning analytics through behavior logs and individualized recommendations. Virtual simulation effects are therefore expected to depend on the interaction between design, learner behavior, cognitive-affective experience, and assessment align­ ment rather than on any single technological module6. Game-based interventions may improve satisfaction and planned-behavior constructs, but short interventions often influence proximal engagement and competence more strongly than long-term entrepreneurial intention7. A multidomain evaluation is therefore required. Higher-order learning is most plausible when challenge, feedback, reflection, collaboration, and assessment form a coherent sequence8. In the present framework, adaptive feedback and analytics support self-correction, while mentor and peer interaction support explanation, critique, and knowledge construction. Digital entrepreneurship education also depends on creativity, digital literacy, and self-efficacy. Gamified online learning may influence digital entrepreneurial intention through policy cognition and digital self-efficacy9, while practice-oriented education may operate through creativity and digital readiness10. These constructs were therefore included as baseline variables, outcomes, or explanatory factors. Three unresolved issues motivate the study: insufficient mapping from platform modules to learning mecha­ nisms; limited reporting of psychometric and performance-assessment validity; and inadequate separation of plat­ form assignment from post-allocation exposure, classroom, instructor, and novelty effects. The study addresses these issues through an explicitly theory-linked architecture, transparent intervention reporting, broad perfor­ mance and experience outcomes, blinded scoring, classroom-aware sensitivity analyses, and cautious interpreta­ tion. Materials and methods

This two-arm quasi-experimental study evaluated the architecture, implementation, and outcome associations of a virtual simulation teaching platform used in innovation and entrepreneurship training between March and June 2025. The analytic sample comprised 480 students in 12 intact classes, with six classes assigned to the platform condition and six to conventional training. Because assignment was non-random, the analysis was designed to estimate adjusted associations rather than definitive causal effects. Figure 1 summarizes recruitment, baseline assessment, classroom allocation, instructional delivery, outcome assessment, and analysis.
Study design

Allocation occurred at the intact-classroom level after baseline assessment to reduce cross-condition contamina­ tion. Twelve existing classes of 40 students were matched descriptively by academic year and dominant major; six were assigned to the platform condition and six to conventional training according to timetable and computer- laboratory feasibility. Assignment was performed by a programme administrator who was not involved in out­ come scoring. Students enrolled before allocation, were not offered a condition choice, and did not self-select. Two instructors delivered both conditions: each instructor taught three platform classes and three conventional classes using a common manual, shared objectives, identical scheduled contact time, and the same assessment deadlines. The platform condition used scenario-based market and finance simulation, collaboration, adaptive feedback, analytics, personalization, and reflection. The comparator used lectures, cases, classroom exercises, and assignments without platform access. These design features reduce, but do not eliminate, selection, instruc­ tor, and classroom confounding.
Study setting, participants, and sampling

The study was conducted at the North China Institute of Aerospace Engineering among undergraduate students enrolled in curricular or co-curricular innovation and entrepreneurship modules. Eligibility required enrolment before condition assignment, baseline completion, participation in at least one instructional session, and an avail­ able primary post-training assessment. Baseline variables were gender, age, major, academic year, prior entre­ preneurship education, prior startup experience, family business background, prior digital-learning experience, digital literacy, innovation interest, entrepreneurial intention, entrepreneurial self-efficacy, entrepreneurship

Platform architecture and instructional mapping

The platform was designed as a layered pedagogical environment. Scenario modules created cycles of action, consequence, feedback, and reflection; collaboration and instructor debriefing supported social knowledge con­ struction; staged difficulty, interface cues, and adaptive feedback were intended to limit extraneous cognitive load; and event-level analytics supported personalization and process monitoring. Essential components were the simulation engine, aligned learning objectives, immediate consequence feedback, structured reflection, and common assessment criteria. Supportive components included dashboards, recommendations, resource retrieval, and optional immersive presentation features. The hypothesized pathway from design components to learner interaction, cognitive-affective processes, com­ petency development, and educational outcomes is summarized in Fig. 2. Table 1 then links the architecture to the variables used in the empirical evaluation.
Intervention delivery, fidelity, and technical implementation

Both conditions followed the same eight-week curriculum, comprising 16 scheduled 90-minute sessions and seven prespecified learning objectives. The conditions differed in instructional mode, not in objectives, deadlines, or summative assessment tasks. Procedure and data collection

Data collection proceeded in four ordered phases. First, students completed demographic, prior-experience, digital-literacy, innovation-interest, entrepreneurial-intention, self-efficacy, knowledge, and creativity measures before classroom assignment. Second, the eight-week instruction was delivered concurrently across conditions. Third, identical post-training tests and performance tasks were administered during the same two-week window. Fourth, self-report measures, platform logs, attendance records, assignment records, and assessor scores were linked using anonymized identifiers. Outcome assessors and the statistician received condition-masked files until scoring and the primary data-cleaning rules were finalized.

For platform classes, event logs captured logins, active platform minutes, completed scenarios, simulation completion, market and finance decisions, adaptive-feedback views, dashboard use, collaboration posts, and reflection submissions. For conventional classes, attendance, active task minutes, assignment completion, and participation were recorded using the same weekly schedule. Platform-specific fields were structurally not appli­ cable to the comparator and were never imputed. Fidelity was assessed from lesson-plan completion, platform availability, scenario completion, and independent observation of a 10% random sample of sessions.
Measures, psychometric validation, and scoring

Multi-item constructs used five-point Likert-type response options. Higher values indicated more of the con­ struct, except cognitive load, for which higher values indicated greater perceived burden. Item wording was adapted from established system-success, technology-acceptance, flow/immersion, entrepreneurial self-efficacy, planned-behavior, satisfaction/continuance, and cognitive-load scale families and was reviewed by three entre­ preneurship educators and two educational-technology specialists. A pilot with 48 students not included in the analytic sample was used to revise ambiguous wording. Construct scores were calculated as item means when at least 80% of items were completed. Data management and statistical analysis

Data screening checked identifiers, group labels, age and score ranges, duplicate records, class membership, assessor files, and consistency between condition and platform variables. The primary composite and all pre­ specified baseline covariates were complete. Twenty-two students had partial data on one or more secondary self-report scales; outcome-specific missingness ranged from 0.4% to 1.9%. Scale means were calculated when at least 80% of items were observed; otherwise the scale was treated as missing. Primary analyses used all 480 students. Secondary models used available outcomes, and a 20-dataset multiple-imputation analysis using pre­ dictive mean matching was conducted as a sensitivity analysis. Structurally inapplicable platform fields in the conventional group were not imputed. Students received written information about the purpose of the study, voluntary participation, data use, and the absence of academic penalty for non-participation; written informed consent was obtained before baseline measurement. Results
Participant characteristics, data completeness, and baseline comparability

The analytic sample contained 480 students in 12 intact classes, with 240 students and six classes in each instruc­ tional condition. Both instructors taught three classes per condition. As shown in Table 6, measured demographic, educational, psychological, and prior-experience variables were broadly comparable at baseline; absolute stan­ dardized mean differences for continuous variables were small, although non-random assignment means that unmeasured differences cannot be excluded. The primary composite and all primary-model covariates were complete. Twenty-two students had partial secondary-scale data, with similar proportions by condition. Measurement quality was acceptable to strong: multi-item alpha values ranged from 0.84 to 0.92, composite reliability from 0.85 to 0.93, AVE from 0.54 to 0.79, and blinded performance-rating ICCs from 0.87 to 0.92 (Tables 3 and 4). These results support score interpreta­ tion but do not remove possible response or assessment-alignment bias.
Training exposure and platform-use patterns

Table 7 shows equal scheduled contact time but unequal realized exposure. Platform students attended slightly more sessions, accumulated more active task time, completed more assignments, and had higher participation scores. These post-allocation differences may represent both mechanisms of an engaging instructional format and sources of confounding when comparing the platform with conventional delivery. Consequently, the unadjusted and baseline-adjusted estimates should not be attributed solely to the software architecture. Figure 3 summarizes platform-use distributions. Completion of the required simulations and scenarios was concentrated near the upper bounds, supporting implementation fidelity, whereas login frequency, active time, feedback views, collaboration, reflection, and the standardized use-intensity index retained sufficient variation for within-platform analyses. These distributions describe engagement among platform users and should not be interpreted as randomized dose–response evidence.
Primary outcome: composite learning performance

As shown in Table 8, platform assignment was associated with a 6.96-point higher adjusted composite learn­ ing score (95% CI: 6.34–7.57, p < 0.001), corresponding to Cohen’s d = 1.82, partial eta squared = 0.511, and approximately 10.2% of the conventional-group mean. The estimate was similar with classroom-clustered errors and instructor fixed effects. In the exploratory exposure-adjusted model, the estimate decreased to 5.38 points (95% CI: 4.69–6.07), a 22.7% attenuation, but remained statistically and educationally large. Because exposure measures were post-allocation, the primary and exposure-adjusted estimates answer different questions and nei­ ther establishes a randomized causal effect. Figure 4 shows the distributional separation and adjusted estimates. The upward shift was observed across the score distribution rather than being driven by isolated high performers. Secondary outcomes: educational performance, psychological and motivational outcomes, cognitive load, satisfaction, and continued-use intention

Table 9 and Fig. 5 show that all prespecified secondary outcomes favored the platform condition after FDR correction, with the direction for cognitive load indicating lower burden. The largest standardized associations occurred for knowledge gain, business-plan performance, financial literacy, recommendation intention, engage­ ment, and satisfaction; creativity, pitch performance, self-efficacy, entrepreneurial intention, and cognitive load showed smaller effects. The pattern was educationally coherent. Outcomes most directly practiced in the scenarios, planning, financial reasoning, and applied knowledge, showed the largest differences, whereas more distal or socially dependent competencies, such as entrepreneurial intention, creativity, and oral presentation, showed modest-to-moderate differences. This gradient also raises the possibility of assessment alignment because the platform repeatedly rehearsed decisions similar in structure, though not identical in content, to the common post-training tasks. Engagement and innovation awareness showed the strongest psychological differences, while entrepreneurial intention was the smallest statistically supported psychological effect. Satisfaction, recommendation, reuse inten­ tion, perceived value, and overall rating were higher in the platform condition. The modest reduction in cognitive load suggests that the added interaction did not increase perceived burden on average, but the self-reported nature of these outcomes remains susceptible to expectancy and novelty effects. The consistency across performance, experience, and continued-use outcomes supports practical relevance, but the effect sizes should not be interpreted as the isolated contribution of the platform software. The interven­ tion combined active practice, feedback, reflection, additional realized exposure, and a novel digital format, while the comparator represented conventional instruction. Table 9 retains complete numerical estimates; the text emphasizes patterns rather than repeating every value.
Predictors of outcomes within the virtual simulation platform group

Figure 6 presents standardized coefficients from simultaneous regressions within the platform condition. Use intensity and engagement were positively associated with composite learning performance, but the model explained only 5.0% of variance and its omnibus p value was 0.063. No measured platform variable reliably predicted post-training self-efficacy. These exploratory associations may reflect reverse causation or unmeasured motivation and should not be interpreted as causal dose effects.

Robustness and sensitivity analyses

Table 11 shows that the adjusted association remained positive under alternative covariate structures, HC3 errors, data-quality restrictions, attendance and prior-education restrictions, and major-field restriction. The additional classroom random-intercept, CR2 classroom-clustered, and instructor fixed-effect models yielded estimates close to the primary result, suggesting that the association was not explained solely by modelled classroom or instruc­ tor effects. The observed-exposure-adjusted model produced a smaller estimate of 5.38 points, representing 22.7% attenu­ ation relative to the primary estimate. This result confirms that realized attendance, active task time, assignment completion, and participation account for part of the group difference. Because these variables were measured after assignment and may be consequences of the platform condition, the model is a sensitivity analysis rather than a definitive estimate of the platform’s direct effect. Nevertheless, robustness to measured specifications cannot address unmea­ sured motivation, novelty, Hawthorne effects, differential peer dynamics, or residual assessment alignment. Across the original and added analyses, the direction and statistical support were stable, but the range of esti­ mands must be distinguished. Baseline-adjusted models estimate the association of condition assignment with outcome; classroom and instructor models address dependence and measured delivery factors; exposure adjust­ ment quantifies attenuation after observed participation; and alternative composites assess outcome construction. Collectively, these analyses support a substantial association while preserving the limits of causal inference.
Discussion

This study found that assignment to a theory-informed virtual simulation condition was associated with higher integrated entrepreneurial learning and more favorable experience outcomes than conventional instruction. The evidence is strengthened by baseline comparability, blinded performance scoring, measurement validation, and classroom-, instructor-, missing-data-, and outcome-construction sensitivity analyses. It remains observational at the condition level, however, because classroom assignment was not randomized and realized instructional exposure differed. The findings therefore support the pedagogical promise of experiential, technology-supported, action-oriented education without establishing that the software alone caused the observed gains11–14.

The theoretical contribution lies in the integration of experiential practice, social construction, cognitive-load management, and learning analytics. Scenario decisions created repeated action–feedback–reflection cycles; collaboration and debriefing supported explanation and critique; staged complexity and adaptive hints limited unnecessary processing demands; and analytics enabled individualized support. This positions the platform as a pedagogical architecture rather than a collection of digital features. Technologies are most likely to add value when these mechanisms are aligned with explicit objectives and common assessments11,12,14.

The very large effects on the composite, business-plan performance, and financial literacy require guarded interpretation. They may reflect genuine competency development through repeated decisions and immediate feedback, but also greater active task time, novelty, Hawthorne effects, closer task–assessment alignment, peer dynamics, or residual classroom differences. Blinded external rating and identical post-training tasks reduce grading bias, and classroom/instructor models were stable; nevertheless, exposure adjustment attenuated the primary estimate by 22.7%. The appropriate interpretation is a large association for the complete instructional package, not an isolated software effect15–17. The outcome gradient provides additional information. Planning, applied knowledge, and financial reason­ ing—competencies practiced repeatedly in the scenarios—showed the largest differences, whereas creativity and pitch performance improved less. These latter competencies may require more live critique, oral rehearsal, diverse role models, and mentor-led iteration than the present platform provided. The pattern supports construc­ tive alignment while simultaneously highlighting the risk that an intervention may appear especially effective on outcomes structurally similar to its practice activities12,16,17. Engagement, innovation awareness, self-efficacy, and intention all favored the platform, but the effect on inten­ tion was smallest. This distinction is theoretically plausible: engagement is proximal to the learning environment, whereas entrepreneurial intention also depends on identity, perceived feasibility, risk, social norms, labor-market conditions, and career expectations. Short-term simulation may therefore alter competence and engagement more readily than durable entrepreneurial orientation18,16. Higher satisfaction, recommendation, reuse intention, perceived value, and course rating indicate acceptabil­ ity, not necessarily superior learning mechanisms. Within the platform group, satisfaction was associated with personalization and lower cognitive load, while learning was associated with use intensity and engagement. Institutions should therefore evaluate learning and user experience separately rather than treating satisfaction as a proxy for competence. This distinction is consistent with systems-success research in management education19. The modest reduction in cognitive load suggests that interaction and immersion did not impose greater aver­ age burden, plausibly because tasks were staged and feedback was available. Nonetheless, cognitive load was self-reported and may vary by prior digital experience, accessibility needs, and device quality. Immersion should remain subordinate to instructional clarity because presence and technological richness do not guarantee learning and can become distracting when complexity exceeds processing capacity20,21. The mediation analysis should not be read as showing that engagement is the primary mechanism. The engage­ ment-specific indirect association represented only 5.41% of the total, the combined indirect effect was inconclu­ sive, and mediator and outcome timing did not establish temporal order. Repeated decision practice, immediate consequence feedback, feedback uptake, reflection quality, collaboration, and active exposure are plausible addi­ tional pathways. Future work should collect time-ordered process data, including decision trajectories, hint use, revisions, interaction sequences, and competency growth curves22,18,15. The non-significant indirect paths through immersion and perceived usefulness reinforce the distinction between positive experience and productive learning. A platform may feel immersive or useful without chang­ ing the cognitive operations required for transfer. Design evaluation should therefore test whether each module elicits explanation, retrieval, decision comparison, error correction, and reflection rather than relying on presence, novelty, or self-reported value alone20,21. The within-platform models were exploratory and explained limited variance. Their outcome-specific pattern is still useful: active use and engagement were more relevant to learning, while personalization and cognitive manageability were more relevant to satisfaction. Because motivated or higher-performing students may use the platform more intensively, these associations cannot establish a dose effect. Randomized feature-level experi­ ments or sequential micro-randomized designs are needed to isolate the contribution of feedback, collaboration, personalization, reflection, and analytics22,19,18. Practical implementation requires more than software access. Institutions should map scenarios to curricu­ lum outcomes, provide shared rubrics, train instructors in facilitation and debriefing, calibrate assessors, main­ tain reliable browser and network access, protect behavioral-log data, and provide instructional-design and IT

support. A phased rollout with fidelity monitoring is preferable to immediate institution-wide deployment. The pilot resource profile in Table 2 offers a planning benchmark, but no formal cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted; development, localization, maintenance, cybersecurity, accessibility, and content-update costs may materially affect sustainability. Generalizability is limited by the single Chinese institution, one semester, undergraduate sample, local entre­ preneurship curriculum, and available infrastructure. Educational cultures differ in classroom participation, tol­ erance of uncertainty, teamwork, instructor authority, and assessment practice. Adaptation to other countries, disciplines, or institutions would require localized cases, language, legal and market assumptions, accessibility review, and validation of measurement invariance. Multi-institutional and international studies should exam­ ine effectiveness, equity, scalability, and infrastructure-dependent heterogeneity. Immersive features should be adopted selectively and tied to pedagogically meaningful tasks20,21. Additional limitations include non-random classroom assignment, only 12 clusters, potential unmeasured motivation and digital affinity, novelty and Hawthorne effects, unequal realized exposure, short follow-up, self- reported experience outcomes, possible task–assessment alignment, and absence of a formal economic evaluation. Blinding and inter-rater reliability reduce but cannot eliminate measurement bias. The mediation analysis was temporally limited, and robustness analyses address only measured alternatives. Future randomized or stepped implementation studies should use longer follow-up, independent transfer tasks, process-level logs, cost and sus­ tainability outcomes, accessibility analyses, and preregistered multilevel models. The reproducibility materials described below are intended to facilitate such work.
Conclusion

In this classroom-level quasi-experimental study, a structured virtual simulation instructional package was asso­ ciated with substantially higher entrepreneurial learning performance, engagement, satisfaction, and continued- use perceptions than conventional training, with a modest reduction in perceived cognitive load. The association remained under classroom, instructor, missing-data, and alternative-composite analyses but attenuated after adjustment for unequal realized exposure. Engagement accounted for only a small fraction of the total associa­ tion and should not be treated as the dominant mechanism. The findings justify further rigorous evaluation and carefully resourced implementation, not a definitive claim that the platform alone caused the observed outcomes or that effects will generalize unchanged across institutions and cultures.

articles.title: The dual cognitive pathways linking speed-watching short-form videos to self-efficacy and academic burnout among Chinese University Students

ARTICLE | Article in Press
The dual cognitive pathways linking speed-watching short-form videos to self-efficacy and academic burnout among Chinese University Students
Xiaoliang Liu · Anran Liu · Tianyuan Liu · Fengjie Li · Jinglu Yan · Qi Lu · Changanqi Xu · Yang Yang
Received: 14 March 2026 / Accepted: 29 October 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract As short-form videos become widely used in higher education, speed-watching has become a common self- directed learning strategy, yet the cognitive mechanisms linking it to learning outcomes and psychological states have not been systematically examined. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory, this study proposes and tests a dual-pathway moderated mediation model using a sample of 3,000 Chinese university students. The results reveal that speed-watching exhibits countervailing associations. It is positively associated with per­ ceived knowledge acquisition, with lower extraneous cognitive load serving as a parallel mediator of this asso­ ciation, yet is also associated with information overload when input exceeds working memory capacity. These two cognitive states serve as parallel mediators linking speed-watching to academic psychological outcomes. Perceived knowledge acquisition shows correlations with higher self-efficacy and lower academic burnout, whereas information overload is associated with lower self-efficacy and higher burnout. Cognitive failure functions as a boundary condition. Students with high cognitive failure are more susceptible to information overload and less able to convert speed-watching into knowledge gains, thereby experiencing stronger adverse psychological outcomes. These findings clarify the dual mechanisms of accelerated video-based learning and provide theoretical and practical guidance for designing digital learning strategies that account for individual cognitive differences.
Keywords Speed-watching · Cognitive failure · Perceived knowledge acquisition · Information Overload · Academic burnout · Self-efficacy
Introduction

Video-based content has become central to college students’ informal learning. With the rise of short-form plat­ forms such as TikTok and Instagram Reels, instructional content is shifting from lengthy lectures to brief, high- density videos1. This abundance of information, however, intensifies perceived time pressure among learners. According to Rosa’s Social Acceleration Theory, technological acceleration compels individuals to compress

Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1 Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1

daily activities in response to growing social demands2,3. In this context, speed-watching (viewing at > 1.0× speed) has become more than an entertainment habit. It has increasingly been adopted in academic learning contexts alongside growing volumes of digital video content, while also allowing students to regain control over their learning time4. Speed-watching short-form videos (SVs) poses a tension in educational psychology. While learners increas­ ingly adopt this practice to accelerate perceived knowledge acquisition (PKA), it may conflict with the constraints of working memory. According to Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), working memory capacity is strictly bounded when processing novel stimuli. Given the rapid pacing and high information density typical of SVs, accelerated playback amplifies audiovisual input and heightens susceptibility to information overload (IO). Whether speed- watching serves as an effective learning strategy or undermines deep processing thus remains empirically unre­ solved. Clarifying the cognitive mechanisms involved is necessary for informing interventions that help learners, educators, and platform developers maintain educational quality5. Despite growing interest in how video playback speed affects learning, the existing literature presents three gaps. First, prior studies predominantly examine long-form lectures in formal settings6,7, neglecting short-form videos whose faster pacing and fragmented structure likely impose distinct cognitive load demands during speed- watching. Second, the underlying mechanisms remain unresolved. Contradictory findings suggest that speed- watching is associated with either enhanced attention or impaired comprehension, implying the coexistence of competing cognitive pathways, with one associated with perceived knowledge acquisition and another associated with information overload. Yet few models have integrated these dual pathways to examine how they jointly relate to self-efficacy and academic burnout. Finally, the literature largely overlooks individual cognitive dif­ ferences. It remains unclear how cognitive failure, a trait reflecting susceptibility to everyday attentional and memory errors, moderates the association between speed-watching and learning processes. To address these gaps, this study proposes a moderated mediation model examining how speed-watching short-form videos is related to the academic psychological states of university students. The model incorporates perceived knowledge acquisition and information overload as parallel mediators linking speed-watching to self- efficacy and academic burnout. Cognitive failure serves as a moderator that shapes an individual’s capacity to manage the cognitive load imposed by accelerated playback. We hypothesize that among students with high cog­ nitive failure, speed-watching is more likely to be related to information overload than to perceived knowledge acquisition. This study contributes to the existing literature in three ways. First, it extends Cognitive Load Theory from formal educational settings to the informal consumption of short-form videos at accelerated speeds. Second, by incorporating perceived knowledge acquisition and information overload as parallel mediators, it clarifies the competing cognitive pathways connecting speed-watching to academic psychological states. Third, the intro­ duction of cognitive failure as a moderator provides a framework for analyzing individual differences in how students respond to accelerated playback, offering implications for both educators and platform designers.
Theoretical background and hypotheses
Speed-watching of short-form videos: drawing on a cognitive overload perspective

SVs have emerged as a major medium for perceived knowledge acquisition among the youth while simultane­ ously influencing their cognitive patterns and learning habits8.Within this context, accelerated viewing behaviors such as speed-watching have drawn scholarly attention. Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) offers a critical framework. CLT posits that learning depends on working mem­ ory9, which is limited in capacity10. When informational demands exceed this capacity, learning is impaired. CLT distinguishes three types of cognitive load: (1) Intrinsic Cognitive Load (ICL), determined by the inherent complexity and element interactivity of the learning material, reflecting task difficulty; (2) Extraneous Cognitive
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1 Article in Press

Load (ECL), imposed by the way information is presented and organized, which should be minimized11; and (3) Germane Cognitive Load (GCL), a constructive load12 supporting schema construction and deep learning, con­ tributing to meaningful learning. Although CLT was originally developed for structured instruction, its core tenet is equally relevant to infor­ mal learning contexts where learners exercise control over pacing, such as speed-watching short-form videos. Extending CLT to this setting represents both a theoretical boundary expansion and a test of its explanatory power in self-directed learning. In this study, we adopt a theoretically grounded proxy approach to indirectly examine CLT mechanisms: perceived knowledge acquisition is operationalized as an indicator of successful germane load processing (i.e., schema construction), whereas information overload is conceptualized as a state in which extraneous load exceeds available working memory capacity13. Specifically, we propose a dual-pathway model: on the facilitative pathway, moderate acceleration promotes perceived knowledge acquisition by reducing redundant information and sustaining attentional engagement, which in turn enhances self-efficacy and alleviates academic burnout; on the detrimental pathway, excessive speed increases information density per time unit, over­ loading extraneous processing demands and leading to information overload, which subsequently undermines self-efficacy and exacerbates burnout. Both opposing pathways are hypothesized to be moderated by individual differences in cognitive failure propensity. This integrated model not only tests the boundary conditions of CLT in informal learning contexts, but also illuminates the psychological trade-offs inherent in accelerated digital learning.
The upside of speed: perceived knowledge acquisition in speed-watching of short-form videos

According to CLT, moderately accelerated viewing (e.g., at 1.5× to 2.0× speed) may facilitate greater perceived knowledge acquisition through two primary mechanisms. First, it is associated with lower ECL, as it enables learners to filter redundant information and concentrate on core content14. Second, it is associated with higher GCL, as it demands sustained attention and promotes more efficient allocation of cognitive resources, thereby supporting schema construction and automation15. Furthermore, studies confirm that university students can watch videos at increased speeds (up to double speed) without significant detriment to perceived knowledge acquisition. In fact, the time-saving efficiency of speed-watching allows students to cover more material and effectively learn new content, often achieving comparable or even better learning outcomes. Thus, we propose the following hypothesis.

Hypothesis 1 Speed-watching of short-form videos is positively related to perceived knowledge acquisition. Self-efficacy refers to individuals’ belief in their ability to achieve specific goals, mainly derived from mas­ tery experiences. From the CLT perspective, moderate acceleration displays negative correlations with ECL and corresponds with improved learning efficiency, providing more successful mastery experiences. This perceived effectiveness is linked with greater learner confidence. In the context of SVs learning, self-efficacy manifests mainly in learners’ perceived learning efficiency and their sense of autonomy over the learning process. On one hand, successfully mastering more content per unit time through faster playback is associated with greater con­ fidence in learners’ capabilities. On the other hand, the ability to autonomously control playback speed fulfills learners’ need for autonomy, thereby showing positive correlational ties with their learning motivation16. Thus, we propose the following hypothesis.
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1

Hypothesis 2 Speed-watching of short-form videos is indirectly positively related to self-efficacy through per­ ceived knowledge acquisition. Academic burnout is a state of reduced learning enthusiasm and negative attitudes caused by sustained academic pressure, characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment. Drawing on CLT, effective learning is associated with optimized GCL. Meanwhile, this effective learning is nega­ tively correlated with accumulated ECL stemming from learning difficulties or slow progress, and also shows a negative association with cognitive overload and its accompanying psychological exhaustion. When university students successfully acquire knowledge through speed-watching, this learning efficacy may be associated with lower burnout in two ways. First, successful knowledge acquisition creates a positive feedback loop, showing negative links with the frustration and emotional drain associated with ineffective study. Second, the efficiency gained from using an acceleration strategy mitigates time pressure, thereby presenting negative associational ties with cognitive burden and psychological strain during learning. Thus, we propose the following hypothesis.
Hypothesis 3 Speed-watching of short-form videos is indirectly negatively related to academic burnout through perceived knowledge acquisition.
The downside of speed: information overload in speed-watching of short-form videos

Information overload refers to the subjective state where information input exceeds individual processing capac­ ity, resulting from an imbalance between external stimuli and cognitive processing capabilities. In essence, it reflects a condition of ECL. According to CLT, this occurs because individuals possess limited cognitive capac­ ity for absorbing and processing information. Evidently, when short-form videos are played at excessively high speeds, information input per unit time increases rapidly, exhausting cognitive resources17, exceeding working memory limits, and increasing ECL18.Once playback speed surpasses a threshold, learners suffer from incom­ plete encoding, missed information19, and poor comprehension, which is associated with information overload. Thus, we propose the following hypothesis.

Hypothesis 4 Speed-watching of short-form videos is positively related to information overload. According to CLT, information overload serves as a mediating factor between speed-watching and self-efficacy. From an information technology perspective, self-efficacy is reflected in a user’s ability to effectively navigate digital environments and achieve perceived knowledge acquisition. Inefficient information processing is asso­ ciated with sustained cognitive expenditure17, mental fatigue20 and dissatisfaction. Excessive ECL is linked to depleted working memory resources and barriers to knowledge construction, thereby weakening perceived com­ petence21 and reducing self efficacy. Thus, we propose the following hypothesis.

Hypothesis 5 Speed-watching of short-form videos is indirectly negatively related to self-efficacy through infor­ mation overload. Within the CLT framework, information overload also acts as a key mechanism linking speed-watching to aca­ demic burnout. High-speed viewing is associated with greater information density and higher ECL, straining working memory22. Frequent information overload requires extra cognitive effort, linked to cognitive fatigue and emotional exhaustion. Consistent with evidence that information overload predicts academic burnout, prolonged exposure corresponds with higher academic pressure, anxiety and burnout symptoms, and shows correlational ties to poorer student mental health, learning engagement and daily functioning, .Thus, we propose the following hypothesis.
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1 Article in Press
Hypothesis 6 Speed-watching of short-form videos is indirectly positively related to academic burnout through information overload.
The Moderating Effect of Cognitive Failure on Perceived Knowledge Acquisition and Information Overload

Cognitive failure refers to individuals’ difficulties in performing routine tasks, characterized by attentional lapses and mind wandering. Unlike working memory capacity—which reflects optimal-state resources and maps directly onto CLT—cognitive failure captures trait-level attentional stability in ecologically valid contexts, moderating the translation of accelerated demands into subjective load experiences. It is related to cognitive function23, learning performance23, emotional well-being24, and academic adaptation. From the CLT perspective, cognitive failure reflects unstable cognitive capacity and working memory overload, which disrupts attentional control and impairs complex information processing. Cognitive failures are posited to strengthen the positive relationship between speed-watching and information overload. Individuals with higher cognitive failures often exhibit poorer attentional control and information-fil­ tering capabilities, making them more vulnerable to high-density information stream under accelerated playback. According to CLT, higher playback speed increases ECL25. Individuals with higher cognitive failures can hardly filter or organize information efficiently under fast playback, which is associated with faster depletion of working memory resources and more severe information overload.

Hypothesis a Cognitive failures positively moderate the relationship between speed-watching of short videos and information overload, such that the positive relationship is stronger (vs. weaker) when the level of cognitive failures is higher (vs. lower). Based on the moderating effect of cognitive failures in the relationship between speed-watching of short-form video and information overload, we further propose that cognitive failures may positively moderate the indi­ rect association between speed-watching and academic burnout via information overload. Individuals with more cognitive failures tend to experience more severe information overload. This overload may be associated with accelerated depletion of cognitive resources, which in turn is linked to emotional exhaustion, reduced academic accomplishment, and learning disengagement, thereby showing a positive association with academic burnout. Conversely, lower levels of cognitive failure are negatively associated with this indirect relationship. Similarly, cognitive failures amplify the negative indirect association between speed-watching and self-effi­ cacy via information overload, as high-failure individuals experience stronger competence-threatening feedback from overload, whereas low-failure learners manage cognitive demands better, attenuating this detrimental path­ way. Thus, we propose the following hypotheses.

Hypothesis b Cognitive failures positively moderate the indirect relationship between speed-watching of short videos and academic burnout via information overload, such that the positive indirect association is stronger (vs. weaker) when the level of cognitive failures among university students is higher (vs. lower).

Hypothesis c Cognitive failures negatively moderate the indirect relationship between speed-watching of short videos and self-efficacy via information overload, such that the negative indirect association is stronger (vs. weaker) when the level of cognitive failures among university students is higher (vs. lower). Cognitive failures may weaken the positive association between speed-watching and perceived knowledge acqui­ sition. Working memory is responsible for selecting, organizing, and integrating information during knowledge acquisition26, which is crucial for processing high-density information from accelerated playback. Cognitive
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1

failures impair working memory function and cognitive control27, reducing sustained attention on core con­ tent and hindering effective information encoding and storage28. This is associated with mind-wandering, atten­ tional lapses and memory errors, restricting GCL allocation and impeding schema construction and knowledge integration. Although speed-watching theoretically benefits perceived knowledge acquisition, individuals with high cog­ nitive failures show poor metacognitive monitoring and fail to adjust cognitive strategies flexibly. They cannot leverage the attentional advantages of faster playback or convert saved time into deep learning, which may limit perceived knowledge acquisition efficiency. Thus, we propose the following hypothesis.

Hypothesis a Cognitive failures negatively moderate the positive relationship between speed-watching of short videos and perceived knowledge acquisition, such that the positive relationship is weaker (vs. stronger) when the level of cognitive failures is higher (vs. lower). Furthermore, cognitive failures moderate the indirect association between speed-watching and academic burnout and self-efficacy via perceived knowledge acquisition. Speed-watching displays correlational links to reduced learning frustration and emotional exhaustion alongside improved perceived knowledge acquisition efficiency and academic accomplishment. However, individuals with high cognitive failures have impaired selective atten­ tion regulation and hypermedia content comprehension, failing to achieve substantial knowledge gains and blocking the burnout-alleviating pathway23. Thus, the negative indirect association via perceived knowledge acquisition is weaker under high cognitive failures. Similarly, cognitive failures negatively moderate the positive indirect association between speed-watching and self-efficacy through perceived knowledge acquisition. Self-efficacy development depends heavily on successful mastery experiences; while speed-watching is linked to such experiences alongside knowledge gain and stronger perceived competence, individuals prone to cognitive failures gain limited and unstable mastery experiences, failing to form stable self-efficacy judgments. This positive indirect association is thus weakened for these indi­ viduals. Thus, we propose the following hypotheses (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1 Hypothesized Model.

Hypothesis b Cognitive failures negatively moderate the indirect relationship between speed-watching of short videos and academic burnout via perceived knowledge acquisition, such that the negative indirect association is weaker (vs. stronger) when the level of cognitive failures among university students is higher (vs. lower).

Hypothesis c Cognitive failures negatively moderate the indirect relationship between speed-watching of short videos and self-efficacy via perceived knowledge acquisition, such that the positive indirect association is weaker (vs. stronger) when the level of cognitive failures among university students is higher (vs. lower).
Measures
Participants

Participants were recruited from multiple higher education institutions across East, Central, and West China using a convenience sampling approach. The sampled institutions strategically spanned three distinct tiers to ensure structural diversity: three-year vocational colleges, four-year regular undergraduate universities, and national key universities. A total of 3,000 students voluntarily accessed and completed the self-reported questionnaires online. To safeguard data integrity and eliminate potential selection bias, three rigorous, predefined exclusion criteria were executed sequentially to clean the raw dataset: (1) careless responding, flagged by failing embedded lie- detection or attention-check items (e.g., Please select “Agree” for this item); (2) rapid responding, operational­ ized as an overall completion time substantially below the pilot-tested threshold (e.g., less than 90 s), indicating rushing behavior; and (3) logical contradictions, identified through highly inconsistent responses on logically paired or reverse-coded items. Following this rigorous data-cleaning procedure, 2,372 participants’ data remained valid for subsequent analy­ ses, yielding a final valid response rate of 79.07%. The respondent-to-item ratio was 39.53, which is substantially higher than the widely accepted psychometric criterion of 10:1. This study was approved by the Ethics Commit­ tee of Wuhan University (approval number: WHU-HSS-IRB2025041). Informed consent was obtained from all participants at the beginning. All methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. Within the final analytical sample (n = 2,372), 47.47% were male (n = 1,126), and the average age was 21.13 years (SD = 2.05). In terms of academic degrees, 16.10% were associate-degree students (n = 382), 67.33% were undergraduate students (n = 1,597), and 16.57% were graduate students (n = 393). Regarding institutional clas­ sifications, 16.10% of the participants were enrolled in three-year junior/vocational colleges (n = 382), 40.89% in four-year ordinary universities (n = 970), and 42.45% in national key universities (n = 1,007).
Measurement
Speed-watching of short-form video scale

To evaluate students’ speed-watching of short-form video, we developed a 5-item scale assessing the frequency of specific accelerated viewing behaviors. Rather than capturing a specific continuous playback multiplier, the scale measures how often students engage in behaviors including using built-in playback multipliers, holding the screen for temporary acceleration, scrubbing the progress bar, and rapidly swiping to subsequent videos. All items were answered using a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Higher scores indicate more speed-watching behaviors. A sample item is, I use the built-in playback multipliers to watch videos. The Cronbach’s α of this research is 0.848, and McDonald’s ω is 0.843. This scale also shows good validity, with CFI of 0.995, TLI of 0.983, RMSEA of 0.062 and SRMR of 0.011.
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1
Information overload scale

To measure the extent of information overload, we adapted Williamson & Eaker’s scale. Each item was measured using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Sample item includes “I feel overwhelmed when processing large amounts of information”. The Cronbach’s α of this research is 0.879 and McDonald’s ω is 0.880. This scale also shows good validity, with CFI of 0.994, TLI of 0.979, RMSEA of 0.075 and SRMR of 0.014.
Perceived knowledge acquisition scale

Perceived knowledge acquisition condition was measured by our self-developed scale, with 5 items ranging from 1(strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). A sample item of this scale is “Speeding up short videos helps me learn more knowledge and information”. The Cronbach’s α of this research is 0.899 and McDonald’s ω is 0.898. This scale also shows good validity, with CFI of 0.995, TLI of 0.988, RMSEA of 0.057 and SRMR of 0.01.
Academic burnout scale

To evaluate the extent of academic burnout, this research utilized a 10-item burnout scale, ranging from 1(strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Sample item includes “I am suffering from academic burnout”. The Cronbach’s α of this research is 0.942, and McDonald’s ω is 0.941. This scale also shows good validity, with CFI of 0.98, TLI of 0.969, RMSEA of 0.072 and SRMR of 0.022.
Self-efficacy scale

To reflect the degree of students’ learning self-efficacy, the current research adopted the 10-item general per­ ceived self-efficacy scale. Each item was measured using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Sample item includes “If I try my best, I can always find a solution”. The Cronbach’s α and McDonald’s ω of this research are both 0.940. This scale also shows good validity, with CFI of 0.977, TLI of 0.964, RMSEA of 0.076 and SRMR of 0.023.
Cognitive failure scale

Cognitive failure condition was measured by a 25-item scale, ranging from 1(strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). A sample item of this scale is “I feel difficult to make decisions”. The Cronbach’s α and McDonald’s ω of this research are both 0.954. This scale also shows good validity, with CFI of 0.918, TLI of 0.903, RMSEA of 0.072 and SRMR of 0.056.
Control variables

Previous research indicated that individuals’ demographic characteristics could have influence on their internet usage. Consequently, students’ age, gender, educational level, school type, and socio-economic status (SES) were controlled for alternative explanations.
Statistical analysis

To gain a comprehensive understanding of the data and test the proposed hypotheses, a systematic approach was employed through the use of SPSS 29 and Mplus 7.4. Firstly, Pearson correlation analysis was conducted to investigate the associations among the research variables, which could provide a preliminary understanding of the interrelationships among the used constructs, and lay foundation for further hypotheses modeling. Next,
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1 Article in Press

structural equation modeling (SEM) with maximum likelihood (ML) estimator was performed. The direct, indi­ rect, and conditional associations among speed-watching of short-form video, information overload, perceived knowledge acquisition, academic burnout, self-efficacy and cognitive failure were calculated.
Results
Common method bias analysis

As the data of this research were all self-reported, it may cause common method bias. Consequently, two methods were conducted to test the impact of common method bias. Firstly, we adopted Harman’s single-factor analysis using exploratory factor analysis. Here, we combined all the variables into one factor and the result showed that the single factor explained only 26.15% of the variance, less than 40%29. To be more rigorous, we also performed the unmeasured latent method factor approach within our SEM framework. The results showed that adding the common method factor did not significantly improve the model fit (ΔCFI = 0.01, ΔTLI = 0.009, ΔRMSEA = 0.002), all of which fell well below the recommended threshold of 0.0230. Furthermore, the average variance explained by the method factor was 4.63%, which is below the 25% benchmark. Therefore, CMB does not substantively distort the findings or relationships examined in this study.
Descriptive analysis

The study revealed significant associations among various research variables, including speed-watching of short- form video, information overload, perceived knowledge acquisition, academic burnout, self-efficacy, and cogni­ tive failure. Specifically, speed-watching of short-form video was positively associated with information overload (r = 0.451, p < 0.001) and perceived knowledge acquisition (r = 0.381, p < 0.001). Furthermore, information overload dem­ onstrated a positive correlation with academic burnout (r = 0.335, p < 0.001) and cognitive failure (r = 0.325, p < 0.001). In addition, perceived knowledge acquisition was found to be positively associated with self-efficacy (r = 0.406, p < 0.001). Moreover, academic burnout was strongly and positively correlated with cognitive failure (r = 0.536, p < 0.001), while exhibiting a negative relationship with self-efficacy (r = -0.090, p < 0.001). Addition­ ally, cognitive failure was negatively associated with self-efficacy (r = -0.107, p < 0.001). Further details regard­ ing these correlations are presented in Table 1.
Measurement model

To establish the discriminant validity of the tested variables, a set of confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) were con­ ducted on all items, evaluating the goodness-of-fit of the measurement model. A series of tests were performed to compare the hypothesized 6-factor model, which included speed-watching of short-form video, information

In this study, the VIF values for all predictor variables ranged from 1.132 to 1.393, and the tolerance values ranged from 0.718 to 0.884. These values are well within the acceptable range, indicating that multicollinearity is not a concern in the current analysis.
Hypotheses testing
Mediating effects

To gain a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between speed-watching behavior and learning out­ comes, both the direct and indirect associations within the proposed model were investigated. The specific results of the structural paths are presented in Table 2. Regarding the control variables, students’ gender (estimate = 0.127, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.094, 0.160]), educa­ tional level (estimate = 0.079, p = 0.002, 95% CI [0.036, 0.122]), and socio-economic status (SES) (estimate = 0.041, p = 0.036, 95% CI [0.008, 0.073]) were found to have significant relationships with their speed-watching of short- form video. As for the direct effects, a significant positive relationship between speed-watching of short-form video and information overload was discovered (estimate = 0.417, p < 0.0001, 95% CI [0.379, 0.453]). This indicates that as speed-watching behavior increases, students are more likely to experience information overload. Similarly, speed-watching of short video was positively related to perceived knowledge acquisition (estimate = 0.393, p < 0.0001, 95% CI [0.355, 0.429]). Thus, hypothesis 1 and hypothesis 4 were demonstrated.
