To assess the validity of the statistical mediation hypotheses, bootstrapping analyses were conducted. The sig­ nificance of the indirect mediation associations was determined by examining the 95% bias-corrected confidence interval (CI). Perceived knowledge acquisition was found to influence the relationship between speed-watching of short- form video and the outcome variables. Specifically, a significantly positive indirect association was observed between speed-watching of short-form video and self-efficacy through perceived knowledge acquisition (esti­ mate = 0.169, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.145, 0.195]). Finally, speed-watching of short-form video was indirectly nega­ tively related to academic burnout through perceived knowledge acquisition (estimate = -0.031, p = 0.003, 95% CI [-0.048, -0.014]). Consequently, hypothesis 2 and hypothesis 3 were confirmed. Furthermore, the analysis revealed that the indirect association between speed-watching of short-form video and self-efficacy through information overload was significantly negative (estimate = -0.039, p = 0.01]), as the bias-corrected CI did not contain zero (95% CI [-0.056, -0.023]). Additionally, speed-watching of short-form vid­ eos was indirectly positively associated with academic burnout through information overload (estimate = 0.146, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.126, 0.167]). Thus, hypothesis 5 and hypothesis 6 were supported. These findings suggest that speed-watching of short-form video shows countervailing associations with aca­ demic psychological outcomes. Specifically, it is indirectly related to higher academic burnout and lower self- efficacy through information overload, while it is also indirectly associated with lower academic burnout and higher self-efficacy through perceived knowledge acquisition.
Moderating effects

This study also investigated the potential moderating role of cognitive failure on the relationships between speed- watching of short-form video and perceived knowledge acquisition, and information overload. To test these moderation effects, interaction terms were created using a mean-centering approach to reduce potential multicol­ linearity and improve the interpretability of the results (see Table 3). First, cognitive failure positively moderates the direct relationship between speed-watching of short-form video and information overload (estimate = 0.088, p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.047, 0.131]). This result indicates that cognitive failure exacerbates the relationship between speed-watching behavior and information overload. That is, individuals with high cognitive failure showed significantly higher levels of information overload associated with speed-watching compared to those with low cognitive failure (see Fig. 2). Simple slope analyses revealed that the relationship between speed-watching of short-form video and information overload were both signifi­ cant at high level (estimate = 0.50, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.440, 0.560]) and low level of cognitive failure (esti­ mate = 0.28, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.210, 0.345]). Moderated mediating effects

To further examine the conditional indirect associations between speed-watching behavior and learning out­ comes, we tested whether these indirect associations varied across different levels of cognitive failure. The index of moderated mediation was calculated to assess the significance of these conditional associations (see Table 4). Table 4 indicates that cognitive failure significantly positively moderates the indirect relationship between speed-watching behaviors and academic burnout through information overload (estimate = 0.035, p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.019, 0.053]). Specifically, simple slope analyses suggested that the indirect positive association between speed-watching and academic burnout through information overload was stronger for individuals with high cog­ nitive failure (estimate = 0.160, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.137, 0.185]) compared to those with low cognitive failure (estimate = 0.09, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.065, 0.115]). This suggests that cognitive failure positively moderates the indirect relationship between speed-watching of short videos and academic burnout via information overload. Thus, hypothesis 7b was demonstrated. Similarly, for the path from speed-watching to self-efficacy via information overload, the index of moderated mediation was significantly negative (estimate = -0.008, p = 0.019, 95% CI [-0.016, -0.004]). The results indicate that the negative indirect association between speed-watching and self-efficacy through information overload is stronger as cognitive failure increases To be more specific, the indirect positive effect of speed-watching on self- efficacy through information overload was stronger for individuals with low cognitive failure (estimate = 0.038, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.023, 0.054]) compared to those with high cognitive failure (estimate = -0.115, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-0.163, -0.068]). Therefore, hypothesis 7c was supported. When perceived knowledge acquisition serves as the mediator, the results suggest significant moderated media­ tion effects as well. To be more specific, cognitive failure significantly moderates the indirect association between

speed-watching behaviors and academic burnout through perceived knowledge acquisition (estimate = 0.007, p = 0.033, 95% CI [0.003, 0.014]). Simple slope analyses indicated that the negative indirect association was stronger for individuals with low cognitive failure (estimate = -0.034, p = 0.002, 95% CI [-0.052, -0.016]) and weaker for those with high cognitive failure (estimate = -0.019, p = 0.012, 95% CI [-0.034, -0.008]). Thus, hypoth­ esis 8b was confirmed. Finally, for the association between speed-watching behavior and self-efficacy through perceived knowledge acquisition, the index of the moderated mediation was significantly negative (estimate = -0.034, p = 0.012, 95% CI [-0.058, -0.013]). This finding of simple slope analyses implies that the positive indirect association is weaker for individuals with high cognitive failure (estimate = 0.094, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.07, 0.119]) compared to those with low cognitive failure (estimate = 0.163, p < 0.001, 95%CI [0.13, 0.199]). Consequently, hypothesis 8c was demonstrated. To better report the moderated mediation effects, in addition to the standardized simple slope analyses, we have also implemented the Johnson-Neyman (J-N) region of significance approach to precisely identify the thresh­ olds of the moderator. Among all four tested moderated mediation models, the results showed that there were no statistical significance transition points within the observed range of cognitive failure. Specifically, the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the conditional interaction effect did not include zero across the entire spec­ trum of observed cognitive failure scores. Combined with the simple slope results, this finding indicates that the mediated relationship remains robustly significant for all individuals in our sample, regardless of their level of cognitive failure. Considering the statistical interactions are small and may not represent meaningful individual differences, we calculated Cohen’s inline-eq-IEq1 specifically for the interaction term (Speed watching × Cognitive failure) predicting each of the two mediators (Perceived knowledge acquisition and Information overload). For the first-stage model pre­ dicting Perceived knowledge acquisition, the incremental inline-eq-IEq2 yielded a Cohen’s inline-eq-IEq3 of 0.014, and for the first-stage model predicting Information overload, the Cohen’s i nline-eq-IEq4 was 0.012, which are both statistically significant, but modest. Though Cohen’s inline-eq-IEq5 in present research are lower than 0.02, methodological literature31,32 notes that due to the compounding of measurement errors, the average interaction effect size (Cohen’s inline-eq-IEq6) in non-experimental social science field research is approximately 0.009. Therefore, while our observed Cohen’s inline-eq-IEq7 of 0.014 and 0.012 were small according to Cohen’s33 absolute benchmarks, it is highly typical for real-world survey data. To formally evaluate whether the current sample size (N = 2372) was sufficient to yield reliable conclusions for the complex model, a simulation-based power analysis was conducted using the Monte Carlo method with 5,000 replications34. Based on the estimated standardized path coefficients and residual variances from our empirical model, the simulation results revealed that the statistical power (% SIG) to detect the four specific indirect inter­ actions was 0.999 (SV—IO—LB), 0.929 (SV—PKA—LB), 0.995 (SV—IO—EF), and 0.984 (SV—PKA—EF) respectively. Given that all statistical power values substantially exceed the standard recommended threshold of 0.8035, the current sample size is deemed robustly sufficient to ensure the validity and statistical stability of the mediation effects. In summary, high levels of cognitive failure are related to not only stronger negative indirect associations (via information overload) but also weaker positive indirect associations (via perceived knowledge acquisition), con­ firming the critical moderating role of cognitive resources.
Discussion

Grounded in CLT, this study develops a moderated mediation framework in which perceived knowledge acquisi­ tion and information overload mediate the relationships between speed-watching and self-efficacy and academic burnout, with cognitive failure serving as a boundary condition. First, this study identifies countervailing associations of speed-watching short-form videos with the learn­ ing processes of university students. These results align with Cognitive Load Theory. Specifically, moderate
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1 Article in Press

speed-watching is linked to denser information flow within a compressed timeframe36 and more effective filtering of redundant elements such as repetitive scenes or prolonged pauses. This pattern is associated with lower extra­ neous cognitive load and more efficient allocation of limited cognitive resources to essential content, which in turn shows a positive correlational association with the overall efficiency of perceived knowledge acquisition37. Conversely, playback speeds exceeding cognitive thresholds are associated with an information density38 that exceeds working memory capacity39. This may be associated with delayed processing, fragmented logical con­ nections40, and information overload. Such overload reflects a state in which excessive extraneous cognitive load is associated with working memory saturation, corresponding to insufficient capacity for the germane processing essential to schema construction41. Second, this study identifies PKA as a mediator in the relationship between speed-watching short-form videos and academic psychological states among university students. Speed-watching SVs shows a positive indirect association with SE and shows a negative indirect association with LB through PKA. This mediating pathway reflects a motivational–emotional sequence associated with the efficient utilization of cognitive resources. When applied moderately, speed-watching is associated with lower extraneous cognitive load, which corresponds to learners’ ability to construct knowledge schemas more effectively within constrained timeframes42. Such success­ ful knowledge construction serves as a primary source of efficacy information43, which is associated with higher self-efficacy. Simultaneously, efficient PKA is associated with reduced frustration and psychological fatigue asso­ ciated with cognitive impediments during information processing, which are key correlates of academic burnout. These findings position PKA as a mechanism that corresponds to the statistical translation of cognitive gains into motivational and emotional benefits following cognitive load optimization.Given that our measure captures perceived rather than objective knowledge gains, this interpretation pertains to subjective learning experiences. Third, this study identifies information overload as a negative mediator in the relationship between speed- watching and academic psychological states. Within the CLT framework, information overload is conceptualized as a state of extraneous load saturation, characterized by taxed working memory capacity, which in turn is asso­ ciated with impaired learning. Speed-watching is associated with information overload44, which shows a nega­ tive indirect association with self-efficacy and a positive indirect association with academic burnout, consistent with cognitive load theory’s prediction that information overload is associated with impaired task performance and emotional well-being. Specifically, information overload is indicative of substantial cognitive resources45, which in turn is related to impeded effective extraction and processing of core knowledge. This processing dif­ ficulty is accompanied by self-doubt regarding one’s capacity to complete information-processing tasks, which in turn shows a negative correlation with self-efficacy46. Concurrently, information overload is accompanied by cognitive fatigue characterized by task resistance and energy depletion, which in turn corresponds to academic burnout. This mediating pathway reflects a statistical pattern consistent with the transition from cognitive strain to emotional impairment when information density exceeds processing thresholds. That said, this observed media­ tion may partly reflect a reciprocal pattern wherein speed-watching and perceived overload mutually influence each other. Disentangling this dynamic requires longitudinal cross-lagged designs. In addition, caution is war­ ranted when generalising these findings beyond the Chinese higher education context. Fourth, cognitive failure positively moderates the relationship between speed-watching and information over­ load. Students with high cognitive failure possess limited cognitive resource reserves, as inattentiveness and memory errors are associated with higher processing costs and lower overload thresholds, showing a stronger positive correlational link. The heightened information density from speed-watching thus more readily exceeds these thresholds, among students with higher cognitive failure47, though this moderating effect was modest in magnitude (suggesting cognitive failure operates as a partial rather than dominant boundary condition). Further analysis reveals that cognitive failure also moderates the indirect effect of speed-watching on academic psycho­ logical states through information overload. Among high-cognitive-failure students, speed-watching corresponds to intensified information overload and is associated with accelerated resource depletion, which is accompanied by emotional exhaustion and is associated with aggravated academic burnout48. The frustration accompanying such overload also is accompanied by a perceived lack of competence, which in turn shows a negative association
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1

with self-efficacy49. In contrast, students with low cognitive failure demonstrate stronger resource allocation and cognitive flexibility, such that the indirect effects on both burnout and self-efficacy are substantially weaker, though these differences should be interpreted with caution given the modest effect sizes, and their educational or practical significance warrants further investigation. Finally, cognitive failure negatively moderates the relationship between speed-watching and perceived knowl­ edge acquisition. Although speed-watching is statistically associated with learning perceptions by concentrating resources on core information50, students with high cognitive failure are related to working memory limitations that are associated with impeded processing51. Attention dispersion and interrupted thinking are associated with these students’ difficulty in translating reduced extraneous load into knowledge gains52, correspondingly weaken­ ing the positive link between speed-watching and acquisition at the perceptual level, with a similarly modest mod­ eration effect. Cognitive failure also moderates the indirect effect of speed-watching on academic psychological states through the perceived knowledge acquisition pathway. For students with high cognitive failure, impaired knowledge accumulation is associated with reduced cognitive gains necessary to alleviate fatigue and reduce aca­ demic burnout. These students also are less likely to derive mastery experiences from speed-watching53, which in turn shows a negative association with self-efficacy. In contrast, students with low cognitive failure show stronger indirect effects on both burnout reduction and self-efficacy enhancement.
Theoretical implications

Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory, this study develops and tests a moderated mediation framework to statisti­ cally model how speed-watching short-form videos is related to the academic psychological states of university students. Beyond confirming the countervailing associations of speed-watching, the findings offer several theo­ retical contributions. First, previous research on speed-watching has focused primarily on time efficiency or entertainment experi­ ences54, with limited attention to how speed-watching is associated with cognitive processes in academic con­ texts, even as short-form videos have become essential learning resources for university students40. This study addresses this gap by demonstrating that speed-watching is positively linked to perceived knowledge acquisition through filtering of redundant information and lower extraneous cognitive load, while also being associated with information overload. These findings reposition speed-watching as an active cognitive resource allocation strategy rather than a simple time-saving tool55, shifting the analytical focus from general user efficiency to the specific demands of academic learning. Second, although communication research has examined information overload in digital media, this work largely remains at a macro level56, with few studies analyzing the link between accelerated playback and informa­ tion overload in educational settings. Drawing on cognitive load theory, this study identifies information overload as the primary cognitive challenge of speed-watching. Accelerated viewing correlates with greater information input beyond working memory capacity, which corresponds to excessive extraneous load and is associated with disrupted processing. These findings ground macro-level insights from communication research in the specific context of short-form video learning, and suggest a redirection of attention from the enabling effects of technol­ ogy to the cognitive constraints it imposes. Third, existing research on the associations of speed-watching yields divergent conclusions: some studies suggest it enhances acquisition by filtering redundant information57, while others indicate that resulting overload impairs cognitive function58. However, most work examines these associations in isolation without accounting for their coexistence59. This study addresses this gap by incorporating perceived knowledge acquisition and information overload as parallel mediators within a single framework grounded in Cognitive Load Theory. The results show that speed-watching aligns statistically with acquisition under lower extraneous load, while it is also associated with information overload when information input exceeds processing thresholds. These findings indicate that these concurrent links are consistent with the dynamic interplay between cognitive resource optimi­ zation and depletion.
Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1 Article in Press

Fourth, research grounded in Cognitive Load Theory often assumes a relatively uniform cognitive load thresh­ old. Although some studies acknowledge individual differences in cognitive abilities, the omission of cognitive failure from theoretical models limits their capacity to explain why identical speed-watching behaviors produce divergent outcomes60. This study introduces cognitive failure as a moderator, a variable particularly relevant to university students whose cognitive vulnerabilities directly affect information processing. The results show that cognitive failure moderates both the direct associations of speed-watching with information overload and per­ ceived knowledge acquisition and the indirect associations with self-efficacy and academic burnout through these mediators. This moderated mediation pattern indicates that the cognitive load threshold is not a fixed parameter but a dynamic value correlated with individual cognitive traits, suggesting that the associations related to acceler­ ated playback cannot be assessed independently of individual differences.
Practical implications

The findings of this study offer empirically supported insights for learners, educators, and platform designers. First, our data reveal a dual pathway associated with short-form video consumption habits. Students who report a higher frequency of speed-watching simultaneously report higher perceived knowledge acquisition and greater information overload. While perceived knowledge acquisition is positively associated with increased self-efficacy and reduced academic burnout, information overload is linked to diminished self-efficacy and exacerbated burn­ out. Therefore, educators and learners must recognize that speed-watching functions as a double-edged sword rather than a uniformly beneficial learning strategy. Second, considering the significant association between speed-watching and information overload, our find­ ings highlight the critical need for active information management. Because specific velocity thresholds were not evaluated in this study, interventions should focus on structured viewing strategies rather than prescribing arbitrary speed limits. Learners should be encouraged to monitor their subjective feelings of cognitive burden and pause periodically to synthesize content before proceeding. Third, and most importantly, our moderation analysis demonstrates that the association between speed- watching and information overload is significantly stronger for individuals with high cognitive failure, while the positive pathway via perceived knowledge acquisition is weakened. This indicates that speed-watching has heterogeneous effects depending on student cognitive characteristics. Consequently, educators should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach. For vulnerable students prone to cognitive failure, particularly those experiencing attention deficits or working memory lapses, educators can embed reflection pauses such as comprehension checks or brief summaries within digital assignments to reduce extraneous cognitive load. For platform design­ ers, we recommend implementing ethical algorithmic interventions. Instead of fixed speed caps, platforms could utilize behavioral fatigue detection by monitoring erratic viewing patterns like continuous acceleration coupled with frequent skipping. This mechanism could subsequently trigger gentle break suggestions or offer customiz­ able focus modes that temporarily simplify the interface, thereby supporting users in managing overload based on their specific cognitive capacities.
Limitations and future research directions

While this study identifies dual mechanisms of speed-watching in short-form videos, several limitations should be noted. First, the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences and temporal tracking. The observed mediation might reflect a reciprocal feedback loop between speed-watching and information overload rather than a unidi­ rectional pathway. Given the cross-sectional design, the reported associations are correlational and do not support causal claims about the direction of influence between the two constructs61. Future research should adopt longi­ tudinal or cross-lagged panel designs to clarify these relationships.
Scientific Reports Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78932-1

Second, the speed-watching measure lacks behavioral and contextual granularity. Behaviorally, the scale com­ bines accelerated playback and skipping. This requires caution because acceleration retains complete information and might drive the positive pathway, whereas skipping causes information loss and could trigger the negative pathway. Because these behaviors formed a single factor in our data, their independent effects remain entangled. Consequently, the composite score limits our ability to definitively attribute the positive pathway to accelera­ tion or the negative pathway to skipping, qualifying theoretical interpretations that assigns distinct cognitive mechanisms to different viewing actions. Contextually, the measure assesses general viewing habits without separating academic from entertainment content. Although entertainment-driven habits may spill over into learn­ ing contexts, processing different content types likely involves distinct cognitive mechanisms. Moreover, relying solely on subjective perceptions without objective behavioral logs or learning performance tests leaves open the question whether the mediation effects reflect genuine cognitive processing or perceived experiences, tempering theoretical claims about actual learning benefits. Future research should develop multidimensional scales and use objective tracking to isolate the effects of specific viewing actions and content domains. Third, relying on a single self-report survey risks common method variance inflating the observed relation­ ships. The dual pathway findings might partially reflect optimistic versus pessimistic response styles rather than distinct cognitive mechanisms. Furthermore, without behavioral validation, self-reported perceived knowledge acquisition does not equal demonstrated learning. Thus, the positive pathway results cannot represent objec­ tive learning benefits. Future studies should employ multi-informant designs, behavioral tracking, and objective knowledge tests. Fourth, omitting confounding variables may bias estimates and overstate conclusions. Specifically, academic ability could confound the perceived knowledge acquisition pathway, as higher ability students might process accelerated information more efficiently. Similarly, course workload could confound the information overload pathway, since students facing high academic pressure may report greater overload regardless of their media habits. In addition, unmeasured confounders like prior media literacy or task demands may further bias these estimates. The sample was also restricted to Chinese college students. While this provides a valuable reference for understanding speed-watching in East Asian educational contexts where academic pressure and short-form media use are especially salient, findings may not directly generalise to other cultural or educational settings. Future cross-cultural studies are needed to compare and extend these findings across diverse educational systems.
Conclusion

Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory, this study examines associations between speed-watching short-form vid­ eos and academic psychological states of university students. The findings exhibit countervailing associations: speed-watching is positively related to perceived knowledge acquisition, which is further associated with higher self-efficacy and lower academic burnout, while it is simultaneously positively linked to information overload, which is associated with lower self-efficacy and higher burnout. Cognitive failure moderates the associations, such that speed-watching functions as an efficiency-enhancing strategy for students with low cognitive fail­ ure but becomes a source of cognitive strain for those with high cognitive failure. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual cognitive differences when evaluating the role of accelerated playback in educational contexts.

paragraphs: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
REVIEW | Article in Press
A systematic literature review of the impact of blended learning on cross-cultural communication, student satisfaction, and inclusive education
Rong Zhou ●Minli Tang
Received: 28 February 2025 / Accepted: 21 October 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract The intentional integration of online and face-to-face teaching and learning (blended learning, BL) has increasingly gained traction, but the evidence about the effectiveness of BL on cross-cultural communication, student satisfaction, and inclusive education has not been synthesized equally. We conducted an open search using PRISMA 2020 in seven databases (Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, PsycINFO, Education Source, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar) for peer-reviewed publications in English or Chinese from 2013 to 2024. We identiﬁed 22 studies from 1398 that ﬁt our criteria. Due to heterogeneity in study design, measurement, and settings, the results were synthesized thematically. Across the research, the most robust ﬁndings related to intercultural, including studies showing BL was often associated with improved intercultural awareness (deﬁned in this study as learners’ capacity to perceive, interpret, and reﬂect on cultural difference), and cross-cultural communication, particularly where there was a structured approach to online interaction and connection with face-to-face reﬂection. Most studies also found positive satisfaction with regard to learner-centred design, engagement, and instructor presence. Evidence on inclusive education—here referring to equitable participation and access for students with diverse linguistic, cultural, and ability backgrounds—was more limited and more conditional. Overall, BL appears to be a promising approach for strengthening intercultural learning and, under supportive design conditions, student satisfaction. Its contribution to inclusion is plausible but remains less conclusive because the evidence base is comparatively small and uneven, and is dominated by short-term studies that rely on self-report and seldom use controlled designs. These ﬁndings suggest that educators should design BL with explicit intercultural and access goals, while future research should adopt stronger and more comparable designs to clarify when, for whom, and in what forms BL is most effective.
Introduction

The intentional combination of online and face-to-face learning- the so-called blended learning (BL) has ceased to be the result of contingency, and it has become a regular part of modern instruction and education. With its ability to expand accessibility, diversify participation, and offer more multifaceted forms of interaction, BL is commonly offered as a substitute to either mode as the institutions work to ensure their institutions are both pedagogically sound and socially responsible. However, its effects are not often analyzed in their entirety. Much of the literature that still exists separates speciﬁc results, such as course performance, satisfaction, or speciﬁc skills, without addressing the role

of BL in inﬂuencing intercultural communication, student experience of learning, and practicing social inclusion, all in the same learning ecologies. The reason we tie these threads together is not only to ensure consistency between ideas but strategy: courses are not just singular educational outcomes, nor are social policy arguments related to computing infrastructure and staff training a simple single object. An integrative synthesis is therefore necessary because these outcomes are not experienced separately in practice. The same blended design decision—for example, whether interaction is synchronous or asynchronous, whether participation is multimodal, or whether instructor support is visible online—can simultaneously shape intercultural exchange, student satisfaction, and inclusion. Reading these outcomes together allows the review to speak more directly to course design, institutional planning, and policy than a single-outcome review can do. We use a theoretically informed, three-lens approach in our review. To begin with, the importance of cross-cultural communication lies in the fact that classrooms are becoming more and more diverse and often cross-border. Inter- cultural competence models (e.g., Byram; Deardorff) conceptualize competence as an attitude (openness, curiosity), knowledge (of self and others), and abilities (interpretation, interaction) that can be developed through directed contact and reﬂection. Combining asynchronous forums, mediated collaboration, and face-to-face discussion, BL environments viably increase the possibilities of contact, as well as support reﬂection. Social Presence Theory also provides the idea of the potential to increase the awareness of being with others in technologically rich interactive environments through which more genuine communication can occur between cultures when learning activities are strategically created to constitute a community-building. In this review, intercultural competence and social presence function not merely as background theories, but as analytic lenses for explaining why some blended designs generate stronger cross-cultural dialogue than others. Second, student satisfaction should be discussed as a factor that is related to persistence, engagement, and perceived learning. The Self-Determination Theory (SDT) can be helpful: when learning situations satisfy needs in autonomy, competence, and relatedness, then satisfaction will grow. BL has the potential to reinforce autonomy by offering ﬂexibility of pace and option of pathways, competence as a result of immediate feedback and use of multimodal resources, and the relatedness as a result of the program of structured peer interaction, both online and in person. Simultaneously, it is also these needs that can be frustrated by the same design when technology malfunc- tions, there is a lack of instructor presence, or the workload is not properly calibrated, which makes us understand that these advantages of BL are not instantly technology dependent but are contingent upon pedagogical and organiza- tional decisions. SDT is used here to interpret satisfaction ﬁndings in terms of whether BL designs actually support autonomy, competence, and relatedness, rather than assuming that ﬂexibility alone is beneﬁcial. Third, inclusive education is not said to inﬂuence access to a wider breadth of inclusion but also to meaningful participation of learners with diverse abilities, language, and life circumstances. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) suggests various ways of engagement, representation, and action/expression. BL is well placed to implement such principles by providing recorded and live sessions, text, audio, and video-based resources, and different assessment forms. Nonetheless, inclusion goes past choice: it involves not only managing the digital divide (applicable to devices, connectivity, and digital literacies) but also integrating access as well as culturally sustaining pedagogy into course design. The absence of these promises can even facilitate or increase the current inequalities at BL. UDL likewise provides a criterion for distinguishing between BL that is merely multimodal and BL that is genuinely inclusive in participation and access. Several reviews and primary studies have already examined components of this terrain—for example, links between BL and student satisfaction, or the role of technology-mediated interaction in intercultural learning. Rather than claiming to be the ﬁrst, we position this review as an integrative synthesis that reads these strands together within a consolidated framework. We map how BL has been reported to affect (a) intercultural communication and com- petence, (b) student satisfaction, and (c) inclusive practices and outcomes, and we consider the conditions under which these effects are realized or constrained. This is an integrative approach; design of tasks, facilitation, and technology use often affects several of these areas simultaneously. Accordingly, the contribution of the present review is not only to summarize three adjacent strands of evidence, but to examine where they overlap, where they diverge, and under what design conditions gains in one domain may coincide with constraints in another.

In accordance with PRISMA 2020, we made a systematic search and thematic synthesis of peer-reviewed papers over the past ten-year period. We theoretically base our analysis on intercultural competence and social presence (to the cross-cultural outcomes), SDT (to satisfaction), and UDL (to the inclusion). With this scaffolding, we can read patterns among heterogeneous contexts and strategies, and see where evidence is thickest, where it is mixed, and where it is thin. The review addresses three questions:

(1) Cross-cultural communication: In what ways, and under what design conditions, does BL inﬂuence learners’ intercultural communication and competence? (2) Student satisfaction: How does BL shape student satisfaction and related perceptions of learning, and which elements of course design appear most consequential? (3) Inclusion and diversity: How is BL implemented to include and ensure diversity, and what outcomes (intended or unexpected) are reported?
Method
Search strategy

We used the PRISMA 2020 guidance to plan and report the review. We explored Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, ERIC, PsycINFO, Education Source, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar to ensure maximum coverage and transparency. We restricted our search to peer-reviewed articles (with some grey literature such as theses and research reports) in English or Chinese published between 2013 and 2024. Our initial search took place on 8th September 2023, with an extra “sweep” in early 2024 to include any papers published in 2024. All duplicates were removed before screening. Sample search query (used in one database; syntax modiﬁed for others): (blended OR hybrid OR “ﬂipped classroom”) AND (intercultural OR “cross-cultural” OR “cultural competence”) AND (satisfaction OR engagement OR perception) AND (inclusive OR diversity OR disability OR “special edu- cation” OR “diverse learners”) AND (year: 2013-2024) AND (language: English OR Chinese) Syntax speciﬁc to search databases (e.g., ﬁeld tags, wildcard symbols) was used where appropriate.
Eligibility criteria

The inclusion criteria included empirical studies (quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods) of blended learning that relate to at least one of the selected domains (intercultural/cross‑cultural communication, student satisfaction/ engagement, or inclusive education), published in 2013–2024 in English or Chinese, and are in scholarly sources. We made a small exception to the 2013 cut-off date where snowball sampling revealed a handful of studies with pre-2013 publication dates that were repeatedly cited as seminal in later research on BL (for example, early research on intercultural collaboration in BL). These were included to provide background for later empirical work, but not given equal weight in the drawing of conclusions. Exclusion criteria excluded non‑scholarly records; studies about BL that did not engage with the three domains; papers focused on studies focused exclusively on early e-learning platforms or models no longer considered part of up-to-date BL; and studies with insufﬁcient methodological information (e.g., no study results described). For grey literature, only those that included sufﬁcient methodological detail (i.e., doctoral theses and institutional reports) were categorised; conference abstracts and opinion articles were excluded.

Quality appraisal and risk of bias

We critically appraised all studies, using the appropriate CASP (Critical Appraisal Skills Programme) instrument for each study design. Two reviewers independently rated: (i) clarity of aims and appropriate method; (ii) sample and data collection; (iii) analytic rigour and clarity; and (iv) consideration of bias or limitation. Each study received an overall quality rating (high, moderate, or low). No study was excluded on quality grounds; instead, the quality ratings informed how we interpreted the evidence. For quantitative and quasi-experimental designs, we noted likely sources of bias such as selection bias, measurement bias, instructor/implementation effects, and limits to transferability. For qualitative designs, we considered credibility and trustworthiness, including researcher reﬂexivity, depth/saturation of data, and triangulation. Because the designs, measures, and outcomes were highly heterogeneous, neither a formal publication-bias test nor a meta-analysis was feasible. Instead, we relied on narrative thematic synthesis and explicitly weighted higher-quality evidence more heavily in the interpretation of results. Full appraisal criteria are provided in Table 2 (Tables 2–1 ~ 2–5) in Appendix, which reproduce the CASP-style questions used for qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies in this review (Sidhu and Gage, 2021).
Data extraction and thematic synthesis

Using the three research questions mentioned earlier as a conceptual framework, the study collected and documented data with the author’s identity, publication year, study objectives, research questions, research methodologies, and participants (refer to Table 3 in Appendix). We extracted author/year, context, participants, BL design/features, methods, outcomes for each focal domain, and noted mediating factors and limitations (see Table 4 in Appendix for an overview of included studies). We then conducted an inductive thematic analysis, following an inductive thematic analysis approach inspired by Braun and Clarke (2006), coding study ﬁndings line‑by‑line within each domain (intercultural, satisfaction, inclusion) (see Table 5 in Appendix). Two coders independently developed and recon- ciled a shared codebook. Disagreements in coding or theme labels were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. Codes were iteratively clustered into themes and subthemes, which were reviewed against the full dataset. Analysis proceeded until thematic saturation (no substantively new themes) was reached. We report simple counts of studies per theme as a qualitative indicator of prevalence, complementing the narrative synthesis; no meta‑analysis was attempted due to design and measure heterogeneity.
Results

There were a total of 22 studies reviewed, with an array of educational settings being represented (university courses, professional training programs, and K-12 settings) and studying in different countries and cultural contexts. Out of these data, 15 studies were mainly involved with either cross-cultural communication or intercultural competence in BL, 7 studies involved student satisfaction and performance outcomes, and 5 studies speciﬁcally dealt with factors of inclusive education and diversity (some studies had several themes). To be more transparent, we summarize the ﬁndings in accordance with these three important topics (RQ1, RQ2, and RQ3). In each subsection, we provide a thematic synthesis of our ﬁndings and the number of studies that support each key ﬁnding or observation (as appraised via CASP). At the same time, the evidence base was not uniformly strong or uniformly positive. The included studies differed substantially in design quality, sample size, duration, and outcome measurement, and

several reported conditional, mixed, or context-dependent ﬁndings rather than unqualiﬁed beneﬁts. The thematic synthesis below therefore attends not only to positive outcomes but also to the limitations, tensions, and imple- mentation conditions visible across the corpus. It also reads the corpus against its methodological grain: because most of the included studies were short-term, relied on self-report, and lacked controlled comparisons, even consistent positive ﬁndings are treated here as indicative rather than conﬁrmatory (we return to these constraints in the critical appraisal of the evidence base, Section “A critical appraisal of the included studies”).
Theme 1: blended learning and cross-cultural communication

The 15 out of 22 studies (RQ1) reviewed were those that studied cross-cultural communication or intercultural competence in blended learning environments. The quality appraisal results using CASP revealed that the evidence in this area was mostly moderate, and selected high-quality studies provided support to the results in a very strong way. The general conclusion in all these studies is that blended learning has the potential to improve cross-cultural communication and intercultural competence of the students (Dai, 2021). Almost all these studies presented positive effects of BL on cross-cultural communication skills or cultural awareness amongst learners. These studies indicate that the combination of online and face-to-face interaction (is the property of a BL environment) provides more opportunities to students who belong to diverse cultural backgrounds to interact with each other in a richer way than in the case of a traditional classroom only. Online interactive elements of BL (e.g., discussion forums, collaborative projects, and other online interactions) were expected to facilitate intercultural exchange very often. Indicatively, both Chen (2021) and Shi (2022) con- cluded that, through integrating online discussions and co-curricular activities in language and communication courses, students became much better equipped in terms of their intercultural knowledge and communication skills. As a result of such studies, BL allowed students to carry on conversations outside of the classroom as well as ponder over cultural differences, which resulted in a better understanding and appreciation of differences in opinion. In a study performed with Chinese college students in an intercultural communication course, Chen stated that com- parison between the BL (self-paced learning online modules and live chat sessions) allowed the students to develop a conceptualization of intercultural communicative competence. Likewise, Shi (2022) found that the ﬂipped classroom BL model that involved teaching of cultural materials before the session enabled more time in class, which was dedicated to intercultural dialogue, so the students felt more self-conﬁdent when engaging with peers of other cultures. A number of researchers reported that cross-cultural interaction in BL best happens when it is deliberately made (KS and Batta, 2023). It was revealed that a blended format of learning the foreign language (combining online forums and multimedia materials) enhanced intercultural literacy and communication skills among students (Muresan and Radu, 2010), whose intercultural learning required both online (discussion) and face-to-face interaction with their cultural materials and classmates. The same is Lopez-Varela Azcarate (2007) (pre-2013 study), who focused on the advantages of implementing traditional classroom work, with online cultural classes, but in her article, BL was applied to teach interculturalism, using literature, and students enjoyed the combination of the online and in-person learning formats. Such studies indicate that one of the potential effective strategies of intercultural competence enhancement is the incorporation of culturally rich materials in the online component of a BL course (case analysis in a different country, virtual exchange projects, classes in other countries). In general, most of the studies included in it, i.e., about 12 of 15 studies, were centered around this theme and found that students in a BL setting were more apt to improve intercultural communication skills or cultural awareness than the students in a traditional setting. The students usually gained a clearer insight into the differences in cultures, had a more positive attitude towards other cultures, and had a higher level of conﬁdence in cross-cultural commu- nication. Indicatively, in a qualitative study investigating adult educators participating in a blended global education program, Gironda (2019) discovered that, through the BL format (online learning with periodic current in-person classes), learners were free to express their cultural experiences and practices, which additionally contributed posi- tively to cross-cultural education. Among the studies, one of the most common reasons to explain why these positive

effects were achieved is that BL is ﬂexible in its avenues of communication: perceived shy and/or reticent students may feel more at ease expressing themselves in online forums, hence leading to intercultural discussion that would not be reﬂected in a traditional face-to-face classroom setting. It can be pointed out that not everything was so positive. Some of the studies indicated obstacles and limitations to the application of BL in cross-cultural communication. Nicolson and Uematsu (2013) noted that face-to-face sessions were important in creating rapport between students of dissimilar cultures in the blended environment, and only meeting in person at the beginning could allow engaging in the online-only interaction without some mis- understanding occurring. They underscored such matters as the variant of the communication styles and the necessity of establishing trust, saying that BL educators must thoroughly scaffold the online and ofﬂine communication in order to be able to enjoy the maximum beneﬁts of the diversity. That is, thorough pedagogical planning and support frameworks, in addition to a simple adoption of blended format, are what are required to guarantee any meaningful intercultural exchange. Researchers Kack et al. (2014), researching a Nordic-Baltic blended course on autism intervention, discovered that institutional differences had to be addressed when one country (i.e., teacher) and another country (i.e., student) had to collaborate, to facilitate a beneﬁcial effect on communication. These more subtle implications suggest that, though BL offers a valuable platform of cross-cultural learning, it is up to the educator to take the initiative to remove the cultural barriers (e.g., by setting up explicit communication practices or including cultural diversity celebratory activities at the very beginning of a course). These studies complicate any simple claim that BL automatically enhances intercultural communication: where trust-building, facilitation, or institutional coordination were weak, the blended format functioned more as a logistical arrangement than as a pedagogical driver of intercultural learning. In addition, most studies (around eight of the cross-cultural studies) reported that BL provided a platform to engage in cross-cultural contact, which otherwise would not have been available on a fully in-person or fully online platform. Blended courses tended to bring together students studying in varying campuses or countries through a combination of similar components online, and essentially increase the size of the classroom to the world. As an example, Sugie (2014) introduced a hybrid system that links language learners in Japan and China via an online learning system. They discovered that students liked the unique opportunity of communicating with young native speakers of the second language and developed positive impressions about one another. Although the process experienced some challenges with communication (students did not have the initial skills on how to express themselves completely), it helped them feel more motivated to learn, and thus, they had conﬁdence in their ability to use the foreign language. This evidence highlights the fact that BL would provide a medium through which there would be a cross-cultural exchange between cultures, thus, the learners might gain some experience in how to communicate across different cultures. In these studies, students in BL settings tended to establish friendships or peer groups that cut across cultural boundaries, which were enabled by online communication tools. It can be concluded that, based on the reviewed evidence, blended learning is typically linked to the beneﬁcial effects on the cross-cultural communication skills of students. The learners in the blended setups would gain increased cultural sensitivity, and BL would offer them a realistic platform to train intercultural communication. Most of the research (about 12 out of 15 in this ﬁeld) has stated obvious positive gains, whereas a handful cited that strict measures should be followed in implementation in order to get past the initial intercultural barriers. Blended learning —consciously and premeditated with the intercultural goals in mind—seems a bright way of introducing learners to the active work in diverse and globalized situations. However, their limited nature posed a risk to the generalization of the ﬁndings found in these studies since most of them were small or speciﬁc to the environment.
Theme 2: blended learning and student satisfaction and performance

Eight of the 22 included studies (RQ2) examined how blended learning affects student satisfaction and related outcomes (such as student engagement and academic performance). The research evidence in these studies was assessed as moderate quality based on CASP; a combination of qualitative and quantitative designs and one sig- niﬁcant older study providing baseline data. In summary, these studies reported that student satisfaction is higher in
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-09679-3 Article in Press

blended learning programs with appropriate implementation. However, satisfaction is not automatically guaranteed by BL itself; it depends on how the approach is executed and whether certain conditions (e.g., effective pedagogy and support) are met. The majority of the studies that assessed student satisfaction indicated that BL was higher than traditional learning, given that the course was learner-based. Indicatively, McPhee and Pickren (2017) observed that ﬁrst-year interna- tional students in a blended geography course were happy about a balance of online and face-to-face learning, indicating that it made learning more entertaining and enjoyable. Students, especially these ones, found culturally relevant discussion and multimedia tasks of particular importance because they enhanced the learning experience. The blended model gave them an opportunity to study at their own speed using the internet and then to use the information in physical classes; anxiety decreased, and fun increased (a sign of satisfaction). The same situation occurred in the study by Lee et al. (2022), who discovered that in a social work course with BL, the students only reacted in a positive way once the curriculum prioritized the learners over the teachers, i.e., when exercises of active learning and interactive simulation (enhanced by the BL technology) were made primary as compared to a traditional lecture. The students in the study conducted by Lee et al. were also more competent and satisﬁed, as the BL environment gave them more agency in the learning process (i.e., they could choose when to watch the online modules or do role-play exercises in the classroom, which helped to reinforce the online material). Flexibility is a generally quoted strength of BL, as far as satisfaction is concerned. Students claim that the versatility of BL in terms of time and the ability to adapt to various types of schedules and learning speeds results in comfort and happiness (Magnier-Watanabe et al., 2011) (pre-2013 research) and others. The cross-cultural MBA course by Magnier-Watanabe would have allowed the students to appreciate the online access to lectures and preliminary preparation for the face-to-face workshops; this aspect of the course proved to be signiﬁcant, especially when it comes to people who are also in employment (this aspect can have a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on their satis- faction). Another beneﬁt that many students enjoy about the learning modes of the BL is the combination of different learning resources videos, readings, online forums, and classroom interaction - a mixture that allows catering to various inclinations, ensuring that learners will be more engaged and less bored. One of the previous studies reﬂected in the snowballing study, Lopez-Perez et al. (2011) (pre-2013 study), has been quantitatively related to BL in terms of better outcomes of the courses, as well as it has been observed that fewer students drop out and are more satisﬁed in sections where only the face-to-face method is employed. They attributed this to the constant feedback and rein- forcement that BL environments can offer and also the feeling of greater control over their learning that students have. A very distinct picture comes out of these studies that, in case BL is done right, i.e., as interactive, student- centered, and well-supported, students tend to report increased satisfaction than in the traditional class formats. Most of these studies (about six of seven that concentrated especially on student satisfaction) found the net positive impact of BL on the student satisfaction rating of their learning experience. Improved understanding, enhanced engagement, and convenience were also identiﬁed as the main causes of increased satisfaction among students. Notably, in most instances, satisfaction was also correlated positively with performance; increased satisfaction also indicated the same or improved performance relative to traditional formats, and this indicates that students were not only happier but could be learning more organically as well. In the studies, a number of factors were identiﬁed to be signiﬁcant in inﬂuencing the student satisfaction with BL:

(1) Active participation and interaction: students had greater satisfaction when BL courses involved them actively (through discussions, through group work, etc.) in contrast to when the online aspect was viewed as a one-directional content dump (Knoblauch, 2022). (2) Student-centered course design: Blended courses that were designed based on the needs and backgrounds of students were likely to produce greater levels of satisfaction. To illustrate, providing individualized learning, adding student feedback to change the course, or adding content that aligns with the various interests of students all led to an improved learning process. (3) Multimedia resources: The use of videos, readings, simulation games, and online discussions and forums, which were tailored to the needs of different learning styles, prevented boredom.

(4) Instructor presence and support: The students expressed high satisfaction when instructors were available and interested in both online and face-to-face classes - e.g., responding to questions in forums, marking assignments on time, and actively leading discussions. On the other hand, in cases where students felt abandoned in the course of the web-based events, the students became frustrated.

It is interesting to note that numerous these factors were derived using qualitative student feedback in the studies, although some of them were not necessarily assessed as outcome variables. In spite of the overall favorable readings, there were also some challenges and ambivalent outcomes of satisfaction in the review. As an example, technical failures may negatively impact the satisfaction of students. In case students have to deal with unreliable technology, platform crashes, or a lack of proper technical support, their experience in BL may become sour, irrespective of the pedagogy. One example was that in an inclusive education program, in the case of using BL, schools could not permit unequal access to devices and the internet, as less-resourced students would feel disadvantaged (a problem that has a direct effect on satisfaction and desired equity). Another issue concerns out-of-class workload: certain students of BL courses believe that the format in fact requires more time (along with online assignments in addition to attendance), and that may be a stressor when not managed appro- priately. Stefanic et al. (2020) discovered that the general attitude towards the cross-cultural blended entrepreneurship course was generally beneﬁcial, though a certain part of students indicated an issue of greater self-discipline and time management, which are the demands of BL that may not be met by all students. This observation relates to the theme of satisfaction: highly motivated students performed well and were extremely satisﬁed with BL, whereas students who had difﬁculty managing themselves were overwhelmed at times. This indicates that some of the demonstrated beneﬁts for student satisfaction may be moderated by students’ existing digital skills, time management, and sup- portive structures. In other words, BL may make some students more satisﬁed, while simultaneously intensifying demands for others. Though our discussion here is on the means of satisfaction, some of the studies have also quantiﬁed academic performance or skill development and have discovered that BL was similar to or even better than the normal approach. As an example, Stefanic et al. (2020) found that students in their blended course had good learning results, and the results were correlated with satisfaction - those students who valued the blended course were more likely to participate and achieve better results. Lopez-Perez et al. (2011) (pre-2013 study) presented empirical evidence, which suggested that blended learning was related to reduced failure in undergraduate courses. This implies that this is more of a virtuous cycle; a good course on BL would make students more satisﬁed, which would, in turn, lead to higher engagement and, consequently, to higher performance, which would reafﬁrm satisfaction further. To recap it all, the literature indicates that in most cases, blended learning was intertwined with student satisfaction provided that some conditions were fulﬁlled. Those conditions encompass the student-oriented approach, active interaction, and a high level of support offered to learners during the course. About a third of all the coverage of the studies (eight out of 22) directly covered student satisfaction, and all except one found that students tended to like or give higher ratings of the blended experience than of traditional formats. These data show that BL is likely to work in cases where it is implemented considerately. On the other hand, with a bad implementation of BL (e.g., without any interaction, little instructor content, or technical obstacles), the advantages of satisfaction might be lowered or even negative, which a variety of authors also add. Thus, one of the insights that can be made is that high student satisfaction in BL means that special consideration must be paid to the design of courses, the reliability of technology, and the needs of the student population. But, as few studies were speciﬁcally concerned with satisfaction (about one- third of the studies have used self-reported measurements), such trends need to be considered with reservations.
Theme 3: blended learning and inclusive education

The third theme of this review is related to the area of inclusive education - whether and how BL can facilitate a learning environment where all students (cultural, linguistic, ability, etc., backgrounds) can be included on equal level and terms. Five of the 22 studies that were selected were focused on the effects of BL on inclusion or diversity (even though a few other articles mentioned the issues of engaging diverse learners or establishing the community between

different populations). The evidence around this area is rather slim since not many studies are directly investigated, and even the ones conducted were of an average quality according to CASP appraisal. Altogether, the results indicate that BL could advantage inclusivity through offering ﬂexible, multimodal learning modalities to learners with different backgrounds, including exposing the hardships of the reality of not letting equity prevail. One of the recurrent ﬁndings is that blended learning has the potential to lead to inclusivity through ﬂexibility and multiple forms of engagement that are highly accommodating to learners. In multiple studies, ﬂexibility and accessibility were recognized to be highly important beneﬁts of BL to the achievement of diverse student populations. Indicatively, Hajisoteriou and Sorkos (2023) discovered that a blended model made this possible, as students of varied linguistic and ethnic backgrounds could be involved through the combination of on-site and online inter- cultural learning projects. The involvement of minority students, who would have been marginalized in a traditional classroom, was made possible in their comparative study through BL, providing them with alternative channels (including online discussions) to express their opinions. The research emphasized that the multi-platform feature of BL is able to alleviate some of the obstacles, e.g., a student who is shy or whose native language is not the language of instruction may feel free to communicate in the written form online, thus balancing out participation. With the ability to study online at their own pace and then review the content during a classroom session, BL will be able to accommodate the needs of the students who learn by themselves and the ones who need additional support. It is especially crucial in inclusive education - learners who may have some difﬁculties in a one-size-ﬁts-all classroom (because of language barriers, other learning styles, etc.) tend to have more free time and materials that BL can offer. The other important feature of inclusiveness is learning materials accessibility. The digital content created by BL can also be frequently made more accessible (with captions, transcripts, compatibility with screen readers, and so on) than in the case of live in-person lectures. Although none of the reviewed articles directly assessed the accessibility features utilization, the availability of content in different formats also indicates the possibility of a larger group of learners. A combination of visual, auditory, and interactive material will help attract students who do not prefer to study the text, so as to suit the needs of diverse learning styles. Some (approximately four) studies (included in our sample) noted that BL may emerge as the means through which a stronger sense of community appears in learners, one of the foundations of inclusive education. According to Alshwiah (2016), online discussion groups within a BL environment also allowed students to develop strong connections and a sense of connectedness and respect towards others and the instructors. This implies that in the course of its extension of the communication that is beyond the classroom walls and the times of scheduled classes, BL provides continuous possibilities of community-building. Lonely students or those who are unwilling to speak up in a physical classroom (because of some social anxiety or belonging to a minority group) will have a voice there, and the combination of interaction styles is what will break some social barriers. This is inclusive in the sense that students will be more likely to feel that they belong to a learning community irrespective of their cultural and ability differences. It is, however, noteworthy that community building must be facilitated very keenly. Others warn that the online portion of BL might not result in actual inclusion but parallel play (students living together online, but not in the real world). Nonetheless, the studies on the whole paint the picture of BL as accommodating to the community: the blended classes usually included more student interaction and peer support compared to traditional classes since the students were interacting with each other in various contexts (e.g., commenting on the posts on a certain forum, then proceeding with the discussion face-to-face, etc.). The concept of inclusivity also implies the incorporation of different views into learning and multiple cultural content, and BL does not lack it. In an argument, Austin et al. (2017) suggested that local cultural narratives should be incorporated even in the design of a BL course in such a way that no one feels excluded or unwelheard. In a case study about community regeneration as a result of e-learning, they discovered that the deliberate incorporation of the local cultures into the BL curriculum made the process of learning more relevant and inclusive to the participants within the same communities. Likewise, Bragdon (2018), who concentrated on the library context, indicated that integrative education through BL enables students to experience the numerous cultures that exist in society, hence expanding their views and minimizing cultural prejudice. In the studies under review, the courses in which the material was provided that represented several different cultures, or the ones that allowed the students themselves to

exchange their opinions on their respective cultures, the learners grew more understanding and respectful of each other. This points to the possibilities of a democratized classroom with BL: online platforms allow each student to be granted the same space to present the material or examples of his/her background and diversify the scope of the curriculum, not merely based on the vision of the instructor alone. The review also established the difﬁculty in using BL to deliver inclusivity. Among them is the digital divide: not every student has the same access to the technology and internet connection that BL needs. Other researchers (e.g., Hajisoteriou and Sorkos, 2023) themselves admitted that unequal access to a trusted internet or device can create inequalities in that, on the one hand, well-resourced students gain more advantages of BL than less-resourced students do. This is a severe concern in an inclusive structure—the institutions that have implemented BL must make sure that it provides technology and technical support in such a manner that not a single student can be sidelined. This is another difﬁculty because educators require new competencies to deal with inclusive BL classes. Some of the articles indicated that a teacher is not necessarily ready to manage the variety of needs represented by a BL format, be it mediating an online conference to give voices to the less vocal students or modifying resources to make them accessible. An example is the commentary by Harrison (2019) on the emergence of BL, where the author argues that educators should change their pedagogy in order to address the needs of the students of the present time, and professional development is needed to answer the question of how teachers can use BL to help students embrace diversity. Regardless of these issues, the overall trend in the literature is positive with regard to the use of BL to create inclusivity. Although the number of studies that exclusively investigated inclusion was relatively small, a total of ﬁve studies were able to suggest positive outcomes regarding inclusion or diversity, with BL serving to level the playing ﬁeld for learners or open up participation. None of the reviewed articles stated that BL deteriorated inclusion; at most, some of them did not see signiﬁcant differences in some of their measures (such as one study did not see any difference in the rate of participation in traditional classes and BL classes in some student subgroups, implying that BL was not necessarily worse in terms of inclusion than the status quo) (See Appendix Table 5). In summary to this theme, it can be said that blended learning seems to be an assistive form of learning that offers adaptability, a diverse mode of interaction, and the ability of every student to contribute, thus catering to diverse learning needs. It fosters cross-cultural friendships and understanding, an enhanced sense of belonging, and provides an opportunity to incorporate diverse content that afﬁrms the identity of the students. The conclusions, however, are tentative considering the scarcity of evidence base. In order to achieve the full potential of the inclusive advantages of BL, it is essential that practitioners are conscious to ensure everyone gains access and receives proper support in the blended type of framework. Crucially, our recognition here of the inclusive promise is usually by implication, not explicitly. Most assumed inclusion from ﬂexibility, involvement or participation, or a sense of inclusion, but few from measures of accessibility or equity. This explains why in this area, claims are more limited than claims about intercultural communication, or communication satisfaction. To take a closer look, we further counted the number of studies in our sample that supported each particular sub- theme of inclusion. Six studies also mentioned ﬂexibility and accessibility in BL as one of its advantages. Three studies emphasized the application of multimedia in reaching a wide range of learning recipients. Heightened community among learners was reported in four studies. The three studies touched upon the integration of different cultural content into the curriculum. Therefore, it is recommended to carry out more comprehensive studies in this area and to develop new, equally effective frameworks that are more tolerant of negative emotions. Consequently, this is an area where increased and more rigorous research should be conducted, and new, less negative emotion- tolerant frameworks should be developed. These ﬁndings, when combined, demonstrate the various aspects through which BL can be used to foster an inclusive and diverse learning environment. To summarize, the results of this systematic review indicate that blended learning may positively affect each of the three domains studied. The results of cross-cultural communication improved comparatively in the BL setting (although it should be properly paid attention to cultural speciﬁcs). The use of BL in its thoughtful format that incorporated interactive and student-centered design was also found to increase student satisfaction. Based on the studies reviewed, we also ﬁnd that BL can improve inclusive education practices through its ﬂexibility and con- nectivity—but ensure that access is not inequitable. These ﬁndings lay the groundwork for our discussion, in which

we take these ﬁndings and explore how they can be applied to education and what it suggests for teaching and learning. Overall, these inferences suggest that impacts of blended learning are based on factors that are not inherent in the approaches. Intercultural communication appears to improve when intercultural interaction is explicitly structured and supported; satisfaction appears to increase when learning designs meet students’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and inclusion appears to increase only when ﬂexibility is combined with assuring access and designing for inclusion. In the next discussion, we discuss these patterns through established theories, such as intercultural compe- tence and social presence, Self-Determination Theory, and Universal Design for Learning. Across the three themes, an emerging refrain becomes apparent: BL is not best achieved through ﬂexibility in and of itself, but rather ﬂexibility and structure. Studies with better BL outcomes across multiple domains combined multimodal experience with facilitated interaction, scaffolding, and equity concerns. In contrast, studies that reported poorer or conﬂicting outcomes typically reported less-scaffolded interaction or uneven access to digital technologies; or design that moved responsibility to the student without providing adequate support. This across-theme ﬁnding suggests that it is pedagogic, rather than just modal differences, that account for many outcomes.
Discussion
Intercultural communication: intercultural competence and social presence

The studies reviewed here reported that many BL courses improved students’ culturally unaware or unresponsive, communicative, or empathy-interpretive skills. The effects were strongest in courses that structured intercultural encounters (e.g., online discussion spaces that paired culturally diverse students, online collaboration across campus sites, or virtual exchanges that were later discussed in face-to-face classes). The theoretical frameworks of intercultural competence theory help to explain why intercultural competence models (e.g., Byram; Deardorff) show us that intercultural skills grow as a result of exposure to difference, guided reﬂection, and opportunities to practise empathy, perspective-taking and respectful negotiation. This study’s BL courses typically offered scaffolded, multiple opportunities to interact with culture diverse peers, as well as activities that encouraged their interpretation and analysis. This “interaction and reﬂection” is consistent with theories of intercultural competence development. Our ﬁndings are also reﬂected in Social Presence Theory. Social presence is the degree to which learners in different online environments perceive each other as “present”, accessible, and engaging (Mulenga and Shilongo, 2025). In many of the courses we briefed, the use of multimedia (discussion boards, peer video conferencing, collaborative spaces) enabled learners to experience other distant learners as real people, not fantasies. The presence was tangible for the learners, and helped them ask questions, admit ignorance, and negotiate the meaning across cultures. Importantly, we did not have a victory plan. When the teachers simply added an online component without stimulation of cross-cultural contact, or generating initial trust, the intercultural beneﬁts were limited or absent. The students would sometimes retreat into their individual cultural group, or they socialized with each other only on the surface. It suggests that intercultural competence is promoted by BL largely when it is designed to increase cross- cultural contact and social presence, rather than being used simply due to techno-functional considerations. Overall, the results both uphold and extend intercultural competence and social presence theory. They support this by demonstrating that contact, reﬂection, and a sense of relational presence are important; but they also indicate that, in BL settings, these elements are sequence-sensitive. Trust and norms for conversation that are established early, along with instructor mediation, seem to be important precursors to intercultural contact, which means that social presence in blended environments is created, rather than bred by technology.
