Student satisfaction: a self-determination theory interpretation

The majority of the research focusing on student satisfaction indicated that students had a positive attitude towards blended courses, which were usually more positive than an entirely traditional course. The key characteristics of high- satisfaction cases were ﬂexibility (setting speed, location, or form), clarity and form (having expectations, getting feedback on time), and continued human interaction (availability of instructor and interaction with peers). Self-Determination Theory (SDT) provides a rational explanation of these trends. SDT believes motivation and content are enhanced where three fundamental psychological requirements are addressed, which are autonomy, competence, and relatedness. In highly-satisfaction BL classes, students reported being able to ﬁnd autonomy in ﬂexible pacing and typically in their freedom of choice in when or with what they relate to some online elements. They felt competent when content could be more easily comprehended through multimedia materials and quick feedback given by the instructor, clear assessment criteria, and through self-monitoring. This was associated with relatedness when the instruction was actively maintained by instructors seeing the students checking in, asking questions, prompting discussion, and when peers were actively present in online and face-to-face space. On the other hand, cases with unmet, differing, or neutral satisfaction results can be interpreted as holding all those needs unfulﬁlled. Indicatively, students were overwhelmed by work or the complexity of technology, which was probably demeaning their competence (Nowrin, Robinson, and Bawden, 2019). Others reported feeling isolated in the online portion when instructor presence and peer interaction were minimal, pointing to unmet needs for relatedness. In a couple of studies, autonomy was seen by learners as lower and responsibility higher (shifted to students without support). SDT is not autonomy support but a burden. So, with SDT, “students like blended learning” is a simpliﬁcation. Rather, students are satisﬁed when BL supports autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Satisfaction gains are lost if any of these needs is not met, as when ﬂexibility coincides with chaos. Thus, the review clariﬁes SDT in that ﬂexibility in BL is a pedagogic ambivalent resource. What is autonomy support in course design is, for students the removal of guidelines, the generation of confusion, and overloaded workload if sequencing, feedback, and workload-controlling strategies are poor. The mixed cases in our sample, then, do not challenge SDT; they advocate that autonomy, competence and relatedness in BL need to be simultaneously and continuously supported.
Inclusion and accessibility: a universal design for learning lens

The results for inclusive education were less consistent across studies than intercultural communication and satis- faction. In a few studies blended methods were seen to improve participation by providing multiple channels for accessing content, engaging in discussion, and for expressing knowledge. For instance, students who were slow to speak in class were more engaged in asynchronous forums; students who were time-constrained or had certain disabilities were able to revisit information and lectures; linguistically diverse students could more carefully craft their written responses without needing to respond in “real” time. These ﬁndings accord with Universal Design for Learning (UDL). UDL considers multiple means of engagement, representation, and expression to support variability in learning. Good BL practice lends itself to this: a course can be delivered in text, audio, and video; it can receive responses orally, in text, or multimedia; it can be synchronous and asynchronous. In the research studies where teachers speciﬁcally made use of these affordances, students who otherwise may be marginalised reported feeling more included in the course on more equal footing. However, the inclusion beneﬁts of BL weren’t always realised. Other courses were multimodal, but did not address accessibility. Inequality in access to devices and/or to a reliable internet connection created barriers for some students. Teachers sometimes assumed that creating online materials was the same as designing them in an accessible way, even when they were not (e.g., no captions, no video transcript, too much text). In these instances, the blended experience did little to alter students’ feelings of belonging or possibility.

Viewed through the lens of UDL, these inconsistent ﬁndings make sense. UDL emphasises proactive, deliberate design and access. BL opens up several options, but these options translate to the possibility of inclusion only if they are proactively advocated for, resourced and supported. This accounts for the mixed results we found about inclusion. Similarly, our ﬁndings complement, reﬁne and deepen UDL. They are largely in line with the principle of multiple means of engagement, representation and expression, but also demonstrate that multiplicity is not enough. In our review, the eligible studies suggest that multimodal design is likely to be inclusive if it is complemented by accessible materials, barriers-to-engagement-reducing pathways to participation, along with institutional support for technology and learner readiness. This suggests UDL in BL is more a matter of design and infrastructure than digital multiple choice.
A critical appraisal of the included studies

Before drawing theoretical and practical lessons from this body of work, it is worth pausing on how much weight it can actually bear. Read as a corpus rather than study by study, the 22 included reports share a cluster of metho- dological features that constrain the strength of any inference. The large majority were short, bounded to a single semester or a single course, so what is captured is the immediate response to a blended design rather than whether a gain in intercultural competence, satisfaction, or participation persists once the novelty of the format recedes. Outcomes leaned heavily on self-report—course-satisfaction surveys, reﬂective journals, and post-hoc interviews— and comparatively few studies triangulated these perceptions against independent or behavioural indicators of learning or participation. Self-report is informative about how students experienced a course, but it is exposed to social-desirability and recall effects, and it cannot on its own establish that the blended format produced the outcome attributed to it. Rigorous comparative designs were scarce: only a handful used a control or well-matched comparison group, randomisation was almost entirely absent, and where before-and-after gains were reported they were rarely insulated from instructor enthusiasm, cohort composition, or the simple fact that motivated students tend to self-select into—and persist with—ﬂexible formats. Finally, almost every study was anchored to one institution, discipline, and national setting, very often a single intercultural-communication or language course, which limits how far its ﬁndings can reasonably travel. These features matter for three reasons that surface repeatedly across the review. First, internal validity is uncertain: with few controls and a heavy reliance on perception data, it is difﬁcult to separate the effect of the blended mode from the effect of an engaged instructor, a self-selected cohort, or a well-resourced setting. Second, and as a consequence, the corpus does not license causal claims. The recurring association between blended designs and favourable outcomes is genuine and consistent, but under these conditions association is not the same as demon- strated effect, and we have accordingly written of what blended learning is linked to or associated with rather than what it causes. Third, generalisability is limited: context-speciﬁc samples, modest numbers, and the concentration of studies in higher education and in intercultural or language curricula mean that the observed patterns may not extend to schools, vocational settings, or to the diverse learners—students with disabilities, multilingual learners, and non- traditional learners—who matter most to questions of inclusion. We treat these as limits on the available evidence rather than on blended learning as such; but they are precisely why the conclusions that follow are framed as conditional and provisional rather than settled.
Theoretical contribution

Beyond using these frameworks to read the ﬁndings, applying all three lenses to the same corpus lets us feed something back into them. Because intercultural competence and social presence, Self-Determination Theory, and Universal Design for Learning were brought to bear on one shared evidence base rather than on three separate literatures, the review is positioned to specify boundary conditions—the circumstances under which each theory’s mechanism does and does not operate in blended settings—rather than merely to conﬁrm that the mechanisms exist.

We do not claim to overturn any of these frameworks. The contribution is more modest, and we think more defensible: a set of scope conditions that the evidence, for all its limits, points to with some consistency. For intercultural competence and social presence, the review suggests that social presence in blended environments is better understood as an achieved and sequenced condition than as a property of the technology. Presence, trust, and conversational norms had to be established ﬁrst—usually early in a course and usually through deliberate facilitation— before mediated contact produced intercultural learning; where that sequence was missing, the same tools generated parallel activity rather than exchange. This adds a temporal, design-dependent qualiﬁer to the contact-and-reﬂection mechanism that the theory in its general form leaves implicit. For Self-Determination Theory, the corpus invites a reframing of ﬂexibility, the feature most often credited for blended learning’s appeal, as motivationally ambivalent rather than inherently autonomy-supportive: the identical design that affords autonomy to a self-regulating student can, absent sequencing, feedback, and workload control, frustrate competence and relatedness for another. The implication is that SDT should be applied to blended learning at the level of how the three needs are jointly and continuously supported, not at the level of whether choice is nominally offered. For Universal Design for Learning, the evidence draws a line that the principle tends to blur in practice—between multimodality and inclusion. Offering content in several formats satisﬁed the letter of multiple means of representation while leaving accessibility, device and con- nectivity barriers, and learner readiness untouched; meaningful inclusion appeared only where multimodal design was coupled with proactive access provision. The reﬁnement is that, in blended settings, UDL operates as much through infrastructure and institutional support as through representational variety. These three qualiﬁcations share a common structure: in each case the blended medium supplies an affordance, but the theoretically predicted beneﬁt materialises only when pedagogy and institutional conditions convert that affor- dance into a realised mechanism. We offer this as a small but cumulative addition to theory—it moves each framework from a statement about what is possible in blended learning toward a statement about the conditions under which it is probable—and, consistent with the evidentiary caution set out above, we advance it as a hypothesis to be tested rather than as a settled ﬁnding.
Implications for instructors

Our interpretations of the theories have several pedagogic implications. First, to advance intercultural competence, teachers can’t presume that intercultural interaction will spontaneously occur online. Successful studies in this area involved more structured interaction across cultures, and an environment of safety and presence before deeper interaction. This is consistent with intercultural competence theory (facilitated reﬂection) and social presence theory (the feeling of genuine presence). More speciﬁcally, teachers can enhance intercultural results by incorporating structured pre-class prompts, small discussion groups with cultural representation, comparison and reﬂection tasks, and brief social engagement tasks (in person or synchronous) before expecting rich online discussions. Formally stated norms of communication and class discussions, given a debrief from the instructor, are particularly warranted if experience with intercultural exchange is varied. Second, to promote satisfaction, blended courses need to meeting the three SDT needs. Students should feel ﬂexible course options equate to autonomy, not neglect. The amount of work and navigating the course platform should not feel too complicated. To maintain relatedness, instructor and peer visibility in the online and face-to-face parts of the course should be preserved. To apply SDT in course design, instructors might work with weekly tasks that are sequenced to provide structure, provide the students with brief platform messages at the start of week, include small tasks that need to be submitted, and respond to students in online settings so that ﬂexibility does not become a source of confusion. Students’ satisfaction is more likely when online tasks relate to in-class tasks, and an appropriate amount of ofﬂine tasks are created. Third, BL needs to be built-in, and not bolted-on, to enable inclusion within the framework of UDL. Different forms of participation, different types of materials available, and alternative assessment might become a key con- tribution to the students who might be less communicative in class, or where there are practical/language challenges.

But they should be complemented with literal points (device, bandwidth, literacy) in order to avoid rhetorical inclusion. For inclusive design, practical choices and strategies include providing captioning for videos, making available low-bandwidth text materials, providing different options for participation (oral, written and asynchronous), and ensuring different methods of assessment (so work can be submitted and reviewed in different formats). When feasible, these design choices should be complemented with resources like access to devices, network support, and digital icebreaking programs. Because direct evidence on inclusion outcomes remains scarce, these are best treated as design principles to be evaluated in context rather than as established remedies.
Implications for institutions and policy

The other key strength identiﬁed in the review is the effect of the institution in the applications of blended learning. Training of teachers again proved critical: the ability for instructors to prepare their instruction in blended learning, universal design, and online facilitation meant more instructors could create opportunities that fostered intercultural communication, engagement, satisfaction, and access. Consequently, the institutions’ role is not just in provision of platforms, but the provision of training in instruction in line with the principles mentioned above. Providing access to technologies and infrastructure is also vital. Without access to technology and infrastructure, the “multiple pathways” to success that BL offers are no pathways at all. A number of studies warned that without institutional support to address access inequities, BL has the potential to entrench inequalities. Thus, institutions and policy makers should consider digital access as a key element of equity. Lastly, existing research discourages blanket recommendations for blended learning. The best instances were tailored to local conditions (for example, network speeds, scheduling, student demographics) and learning objectives (for example, cross-cultural exchange versus technology skills). Policies that promote ﬂexibility rather than uni- formity seem like better ﬁts to our ﬁndings about mixed evidence. At the same time, the evidence assembled here— limited in volume, heterogeneous, and especially thin for inclusion—is not strong enough to warrant prescriptive, system-wide mandates; it is better read as a case for funded experimentation under evaluation than for wholesale rollout.
Limitations of this review

Our conclusions are tempered by several limitations. First, we have an unbalanced body of evidence: many more studies addressed intercultural communication and satisfaction than did inclusive education, so any claims regarding inclusion necessarily draw on a smaller and more exploratory subset of the total body of evidence. Second, most studies were brief (one semester or one course) and used self-report data, so it is unclear whether the ﬁndings have lasting impact or reﬂect cause and effect. Third, designs, students and outcomes differed, and it was inappropriate to conduct a meta-analysis or to report a mean effect size; we therefore chose a thematic synthesis. The methodological constraints this entails—short follow-up windows, dependence on self-report, and a scarcity of controlled compar- isons—are examined directly in the critical appraisal of the included studies above, and they are the principal reason we have framed our conclusions as conditional. Last, we cannot rule out publication bias. Papers that found a positive effect of blended learning may have been published in indexed journals, while those that found no difference or even a negative effect may not. While we tried to include a small amount of grey literature, the evidence may still have a skew towards positive outcomes. Last, in attempting to address three themes (intercultural communication, satisfaction, and inclusion) simultaneously, we sacriﬁced detailed information on each in favour of an integrated perspective on how these themes interrelate.
Future research directions

Future jobs must not be limited to snapshots of one course. Longitudinal studies are required to understand the nature of the gains in intercultural competence or satisfaction as to whether they continue to be long-term (e.g., retention,

global collaboration skills). For understanding what features of blended design are contributing to success, studies with comparative and quasi-experimental design, preferably with some manipulation of instructors and course content, would be necessary. Most importantly, we need more longitudinal multi-site studies and better comparison groups, as well as detailed reporting of BL design features so that we can test, rather than just infer, mechanisms. When possible, random or well-matched quasi-experimental designs would isolate the effect of mode of delivery from the effect of instructor, cohort, and of selection. Importantly, more research on inclusive education is needed. Only a few studies have investigated learners with disabilities, multilinguistic learners, also non-traditional (working) learners. There is also a discussion of blended international collaboration (e.g., Collaborative Online International Learning) as an all-inclusive interculturalization process. Finally, as universities add more AI tutoring, adaptive, immersive media to blended environments, future research needs to explore how these technologies affect levels of autonomy, competence, relatedness, presence, and access. Future studies should also directly measure inclusion. Rather than focusing primarily on general values of participation or satisfaction, studies should include accessibility measures, subgroup analyses, and measures of beneﬁts, conditions, and costs. This is especially true for students with disabilities, multilingual learners, as well as non-traditional or working learners who are underrepresented in existing studies. In all, the review presents an optimistic albeit guarded view that blended learning can prompt intercultural engagement, student satisfaction, and inclusive student participation, but should be conducted pre-planned and institutionally supported in line with the theoretical mechanisms laid out above.
Conclusion

In summary, this review suggests that BL is most reliably linked to better intercultural communication, which is often driven by dialogue, reﬂection, and opportunities for long-term contact across difference. Also frequent are positive ﬁndings on student satisfaction, but these are more clearly dependent on course design and teacher presence, with limited workload. The ﬁndings on inclusion are encouraging but preliminary, and do not yet support sweeping conclusions without consideration of access, digital readiness, and institutional factors. Because the underlying studies are predominantly short-term, self-reported, and uncontrolled, the associations reported throughout this review are best read as provisional patterns rather than as demonstrated effects. These results add to current research on BL by suggesting that the three outcomes should not be considered separately; a given pedagogical design can advance or hinder intercultural learning, student satisfaction and inclusion simultaneously. Practice- and policy-wise, this is an indication that blended provision should be seen as a joint design challenge for curriculum, teacher learning, accessibility and technology. We are deliberately cautious about trans- lating this into ﬁrm prescriptions for inclusive education in particular, where the evidence is thinnest and rests as much on the logic of the guiding frameworks as on a robust body of empirical demonstration. As such, future research should break the short-term, self-reporting patterns of the past, and conduct longitudinal, comparative, and more rigorous studies to show the effectiveness of BL, with whom, why, and how.
